Item 001  ·  plain text
Academic writing is an integral part of tertiary education in Malaysia (Rahman & Rahim, 2016). At this level, undergraduates are expected to have the necessary linguistic skills to be able to produce writing that adheres to different genres and disciplines. However, among English as a second language (ESL) students, academic writing is often described as challenging, complex and often linked to writing anxiety. In particular, the comments made about Malaysian L2 writers are often bleak, imbued with issues that range from plagiarism (Habali & Fong, 2016), low selfefficacy (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015) to writing anxiety (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). As a result, such factors have been reported to act as barriers for students’ engagement and overall academic performance in the academic writing class (Badiozaman, 2015). Evidently, academic writing is not an easy skill to master especially in a second language (L2). Particularly with ESL or English as a F foreign language(EFL) students, research has attributed this to linguistics difficulties (Zhang, 2013) and the tacit nature of academic writing (Elton, 2010). Furthermore, since academic writing “serves different purposes in different units and requires students to assume different social roles ” (Zhu, 2004, p. 30), this has implications for the academic writing class in Malaysian universities, where students may be studying in different disciplines and have little to no academic writing experience For this reason, many higher learning institutions in Malaysia make it compulsory for students to undertake units such as Academic Reading and Writing, and Technical Report Writing. These units aim to equip students with the necessary language skills and the ability to read and write for academic purposes so that they can function effectively within an academic environment. Nonetheless, despite the fact that such units are ubiquitous in higher learning institutions in Malaysia, little is known about its effectiveness. The limited research on the improvements made by L2 learners in their academic writing in a L2 setting provided the impetus for this study. The focus on academic writing in this study is also due to the role of writing in tertiary education (Othman & Mohamad, 2009). Students’ achievements at tertiary level are evaluated mainly on written assessments, be it in the form of large extended writing (e.g. projects, proposal and reports) or short-response essays (e.g. examinations and quizzes). As the demand and participation in English-medium higher education increase, so is the expectation for students to have academic literacy skills. Hence, it is necessary to understand academic writing improvements that are made in academic literacy classes. Furthermore, factors involved in the development of academic writing such as organisation of ideas, identifying audience for various genres and synthesising from multiple sources are scarce. Therefore, this study aims to address this gap. In particular, it first seeks to explore how much impact the Academic Writing1 unit (AW hereafter) has upon the writing development of our ESL undergraduate students. Secondly, it will examine the transferability of skills to other academic units.

Item 002  ·  plain text
Formulaic language occupies a central place in academic writing, and its identification and description have been pursued through a range of corpus-based approaches, most prominently the extraction of lexical bundles (Biber et al., 2004; Hyland, 2008; Simpson-Vlach & Ellis, 2010) and phrase-frames (Lu et al., 2018). These approaches have generated valuable inventories of recurrent multiword expressions and have illuminated their structural and functional properties across registers and disciplines. However, methods that rely on continuous word sequences, or on sequences with a single open lexical slot, are limited in their ability to capture the more schematic and lexically variable patterns that pervade academic prose (Liu, 2012). Automatic extraction of such units often yields structurally incomplete items, and the restriction on lexical variation prevents these approaches from systematically revealing the formal and functional regularities of highly productive schematic patterns. Even the phrase-frame approach, which introduces flexibility by permitting one open slot, separates structurally and functionally similar phrases: a range of, a wide range of, a variety of, and a wide variety of, for instance, all instantiate a single underlying pattern but would be treated as distinct phrase-frames. One such highly productive schematic pattern is the N1 of N2 pattern, whose pervasiveness in academic discourse is well documented. Hyland (2008) found that the noun phrase with of-phrase fragment was the single most common structure in a large corpus of academic texts, and Biber et al. (2004) reported that roughly half of the most frequent referential lexical bundles were associated with this pattern. Lu et al. (2018) similarly observed that the N1 of N2 pattern accounted for a large proportion of the referential phrase-frames in social science research article introductions. A small body of work has examined the pattern directly, notably Sinclair's (1991) analysis of the functions of of and Cappelle and Grabar's (2016) PoS-gram-based investigation. Yet a comprehensive, functionally motivated account of the pattern in disciplinary academic writing remains lacking. Pattern grammar offers a principled means of addressing this gap. Growing out of corpus-based lexicography, it emphasises the pervasiveness of lexicogrammatical patterns and their associated meanings, treating a pattern as a frequent, lexically dependent word combination with a clear meaning (Hunston & Francis, 2000; Francis et al., 1996, 1998; Hunston, 2019). Pattern grammar aligns closely with construction grammar in prioritising form-function connections and recognising pattern-level meanings (Goldberg, 1995, 2006; Hunston, 2014). Constructions may be construed as encompassing patterns, and recent efforts to build “constructicons”—collections of construction descriptions—have generated interest in a rigorous, bottom-up research agenda for identifying and describing constructions (Lyngfelt et al., 2018). To date, however, construction-based and pattern-driven research has centred on a narrow set of verb-related (Ellis et al., 2016; Perek & Patten, 2019) and adjective-related (Hunston & Su, 2019) patterns, leaving nominal patterns such as N1 of N2 largely uninvestigated. The present study addresses this imbalance by applying a pattern-driven analytical framework to the N1 of N2 pattern in a corpus of applied linguistics research article introductions annotated for rhetorical moves and steps (Lu et al., 2020). We first retrieve all instances of the pattern, then analyse their functions to establish N1 of N2 constructions as systematic pattern-function mappings, and finally examine the rhetorical functions with which particular constructions are strongly associated. In doing so, we aim to provide a comprehensive functional description of the pattern in disciplinary academic writing, to demonstrate how the pattern-driven approach can be extended to schematic nominal patterns, and to contribute to the development of pedagogically useful constructicons of academic English.

M1-RRContemporary instructed language learning approaches emphasize on encouraging learners to actively take part in communicative tasks (Ellis, 2014). However, despite efforts made by teachers to provide such opportunities, it is very common for them to face learners who are reluctant to engage in verbal communication; which is due to various reasons (Zulkepli, Othman, & Khaja, 2013). The issue of reticence occurs not only among less proficient learners, but also the proficient ones such as preservice ESL teachers (Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016; Yousef, Jamil, & Razak, 2013; Zulkepli, Tajuddin, AlBakri, Atan, & Bakar, 2019). Empirical studies have long proven the strong link between speaking and learning a target language (Goh, 2014; Long, 2015; Swain, 2000). M1-CCThis has triggered interest among scholars in the area of willingness to communicate (WTC); resulting in numerous empirical studies that set to investigate the variables that affect this psychological construct (Pawlak, Mystkowska-Wiertelak, & Bielak, 2016; Shirvan, Khajavy, MacIntyre, & Taherian, 2019; Zhang, Beckman, & Beckman, 2018). M2-GapHowever, studies done on this area predominantly focus on in-class WTC where learners normally engage in interaction with “familiar interlocutors, such as teachers and peers, in relatively predictable L2 scenarios” (Lee & Hsieh, 2019, p. 64) To date, there is scanty research on out-of-class WTC where learners will speak with “unfamiliar acquaintances or strangers in somewhat unpredictable situations” (Lee & Hsieh, 2019: 64); which will be more challenging even for motivated and advanced learners. M3-OPThus, the purpose of the study is to identify the link between motivation and WTC among a group of advanced learners i.e., pre-service ESL teachers.

Item 004  ·  plain text
As authorised by the National Education Act (2002-2016) expressing the need for becoming autonomous and lifelong learners, the question of how Thai students can develop a more dynamic and responsible role in their own language learning is part of many teachers’ concerns (OECD/UNESCO, 2016). For this reason, learning reform through the learnercentred approach has been implemented widely, particularly the reform of curricula and learning processes. This research was initiated by the author’s concern about the reform movement in English language teaching (ELT) in the Thai university context and the interest in the Thai adult learners’ self-evaluation of their writing practice. Curriculum and syllabus goals in the Thai educational system encourage students to work more independently and take responsibility for their own learning, particularly the students in higher education (OECD/UNESCO, 2016). A review of the literature on evaluation (e.g., Nicol & MacfarlaneDick 2006, Rust et al. 2003, Sambell et al. 2013) also raises the researcher’s awareness of the importance of understanding the students’ own evaluation of their EFL writing performance as well as for the elaboration of evaluation procedures. Nevertheless, in Thailand, both students and teachers seem to have little previous experience of evaluation procedures in the language classroom as the evaluation has traditionally been the teachers’ exclusive privilege and obligation. Besides, there has been no research carried out on the conditions that govern adult learners’ participation in evaluation. Much of the previous research on formative evaluation and summative evaluation in language learning has focused on young learners learning a foreign language (Brown & Harris 2013, Lee 2017). According to Brown and Harris (2016), self-evaluation practices need to be explored in order to support the implementation of adult learners’ lifelong learning skill which is important for their language learning process. The focus on writing in the teaching of English as a foreign language was chosen because English is the language most Thai students learn, and writing has become more important in foreign language teaching at higher education level. Accordingly, as the role of writing in English as foreign language learning increases, the students’ ability to self-evaluate their writing skills is also important because selfevaluation could help reflect individual students’ understanding and possibility of improvement. This study will provide valuable insights into Thai adult learners’ selfevaluation in their English writing practice with regard to various aspects. As such, the research findings could, in turn, help improve the evaluation practice and bring about benefits to English language teaching and learning in this context. Moreover, it is expected that other useful implications can be formulated and would be applicable for the teaching and learning of other courses in university settings in Thailand. This research, therefore, aims to contribute to an understanding of whether the use of self-evaluation in the writing course of English as a foreign language in university can help develop lifelong language learning skills and further development of broader and fairer evaluation practices. The study centres on how the adult learners (or “students” hereafter in this study) self-evaluate their writing ability in general and their writing performance task based on the grading criteria of English writing compared with the evaluation of their teacher. The ultimate aim is to find out what the students and the teacher have experienced from the self-evaluation practice in the writing class. The results could be useful for further developing the students’ English writing ability. Three main research questions are developed based on the objectives of the study: 1) How do the students self-evaluate their English writing performance compared with the evaluation of their teacher? 2) Based on the evaluation criteria, how do the students’ self-evaluate their English writing performance compared with the evaluation of their teacher? 3) What do the students and the teacher experience from the use of students’ selfevaluation of English writing performance to further develop the students’ writing ability?

M1-CCCURRICULUM IS CENTRAL TO THE processes of schooling. M2-CTRecently, scholars in language education have called for more re- search and theoretical perspectives to be brought to bear on the complexity of curriculum1 in language classrooms. M1-RRIn the introduction to an edited volume on critical approaches to language materials research, Gray (2013a) pointed out that the bulk of the publications on curriculum materials have focused on materials development rather than materials use, or what Eisner (2002) called curriculum enactment.2 Gray urged re- searchers to conduct “materials research” (p. 13) that asks critical and fundamental questions in analyses of curriculum content and its enactment. In the Perspectives column (Tarone, 2014) in this journal on the significance of Guerrettaz and Johnston’s (2013) study—which examined the functions of textbooks in one English-as-a-second- language (ESL) classroom—Garton and Graves (2014) registered a similar concern and argued that “the field is generally undertheorized” (p. 654). Contributors to this column under- scored the importance of studying curriculum materials in relation to classroom discourse, Kongji Qin 843 as featured in Guerrettaz & Johnston (2013). M3-OPTaking up these calls for research and curriculum theorizing, this article brings together perfor- mativity theory (Butler, 1990, 1997) and critical race theory (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson– Billings & Tate, 1995) to explore the relationship between language curriculum and learners’ subjectivity, drawing on a critical ethnography of immigrant adolescents’ language learning in one U.S. high school. Specifically, this study takes a discourse analytical approach to analyze instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews to understand two research questions: RQ1. How did the teacher-designed curricu- lum for vocabulary instruction in one .ESL classroom construct subjectivity for students? RQ2. How did three immigrant students in this classroom negotiate their subjectiv- ity in relation to the curriculum con- tent M3-APRThe focal participants, Tiger, Chris, and Abdullah, 3 are from Taiwan, Malawi, and Libya, respectively. M3-OPThis analysis explores their nego- tiation of racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities through language use during a vocabulary activity. M1-RRBy subjectivity, I mean “our conscious and unconscious sense of self as medi- ated through symbolic forms [such as language]” (Kramsch, 2009, p. 18). It is “the particular ways in which a person gives meaning to themselves, others, and the world” (Davies & Banks, 1992, p. 2). In this poststructuralist theorizing of self, a person is a subject, in the sense that as a social being we are subject to various forms of symbolic constraints and forces, such as normative ways of understanding gender, race, and learners. M3-APRThe analytic foci of this study—the construction of subjectivity by curriculum texts and learn- ers’ subjectivity negotiation during curriculum enactment—are prompted by Kramsch’s (2009) argument that learners’ subjectivity, or their sense of self as a subject, is an integral aspect of language learning and needs to be attended to in language education research and practice. M3-OPThe goal of this analysis is twofold: The first goal is to make a conceptual contribution to lan- guage curriculum research by bringing in a post- structuralist lens of performativity. M1-RRPerformativity theory highlights the power of language in con- stituting subjectivity and social realities (Kramsch, 2009; Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004). Departing from the traditional, technical view of curricu lum as a linguistic resource for language learn- ing and of language instruction as a tool for de- veloping students’ linguistic and communicative competence, this poststructuralist lens views lan- guage learning as a process intertwined with the construction of learners’ subjectivity, that is, their sense of being and becoming a certain kind of learner and individual (Davies, 2014). It allows re- searchers to ask how curriculum texts and class- room talks around the curriculum constitute lan- guage learners’ subjectivity M3-OPThe second goal is to illuminate the interactional process in which cur- riculum is taken up and appropriated by the three immigrant adolescent participants for subjectivity negotiation. M1-CCThe issues involved at the nexus of curriculum, learning, and subjectivity are compli- cated for immigrant youths like the participants in this study. Understanding their discursive negoti- ation of self in language classrooms is of critical relevance as current debates around immigration and displacement are often mired with racism, xenophobia, and nationalist ideologies (Greene, 2018).

Item 006  ·  plain text
Tourism has become one of the most dynamic and economically significant industries of the contemporary world, and language stands at the very heart of its operation. Long before travellers reach a destination, they encounter it as a text: a brochure, a website, a guidebook, or a television commercial that constructs an image of the place and invites them to become part of it. In this sense, tourism is not merely a matter of movement between locations but a phenomenon that is discursively produced and mediated. As Dann (2012) observes, the language of tourism was originally conceived as part of the modernist project, a largely monological discourse framed within parameters of social control, though it has more recently been transformed by digital communication into a more egalitarian, dialogic exchange between the industry, the tourist, and the toured. Whether monologue or trialogue, however, the persuasive vocation of tourism discourse remains constant: it seeks to attract, to entice, and ultimately to convert the reader into a traveller. It is precisely this persuasive orientation that makes tourism texts a fertile ground for linguistic analysis. The study of tourism discourse has expanded considerably over recent decades, drawing on a range of theoretical perspectives and methodologies. Some scholars have approached tourism as a language of social control and authenticity (Rokowski, 2001; MacCannell, 1989), while others have examined the psychological and identity-related dimensions of the tourist experience (Bruner, 1991; Thurot, 1989). A substantial body of work has focused on the promotional and marketing functions of tourism texts, investigating destination image, publicity programmes, and the ways in which national and regional tourism organisations construct and disseminate representations of place (Dore & Crouch, 2003; Choi et al., 2006). With the proliferation of the internet, considerable attention has turned to official tourism websites and their role in constructing the identity of destinations, communities, and even nations (Doolin et al., 2002; Burns et al., 1999; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Alongside these text-based studies, a growing multimodal tradition has explored how visual design, layout, and image interact with verbal content to produce meaning in promotional materials (Kress & van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon & Scollon, 2004; van Leeuwen, 2004; Pan et al., 2010). Case studies of particular genres and cultural contexts, such as travel brochures in Hong Kong (Ip, 2008), contrastive analyses of cohesion in English and Chinese tourist texts (Cui et al., 2012), and analyses of tourism discourse in relation to place and community (Santos et al., 2008), have further enriched the field. Genre analysis, too, has offered valuable insights into the structure and communicative purposes of promotional texts within professional settings (Bhatia, 1993; Gotti, 2008), while research on the language of persuasion more generally has clarified the linguistic mechanisms by which texts influence their audiences (Hosman, 2002). Despite this breadth of scholarship, the verbal content of travel brochures has received comparatively less systematic attention than either the visual dimension of tourism promotion or the discourse of tourism websites. Brochures remain a central genre in the promotional repertoire of the tourism industry, and although they overlap in function with travel guides and web-based materials, their compact, densely persuasive language merits examination in its own right (Molina & Esteban, 2006). More importantly, few, if any, studies of tourism discourse have analysed the evaluative language of travel brochures from the perspective of the appraisal model. This is a notable gap, since evaluation lies at the very core of what tourism texts do: they do not simply describe destinations, but assess, magnify, and celebrate them in order to render them desirable. An approach that foregrounds evaluation therefore promises to illuminate a dimension of tourism discourse that has remained largely implicit in prior work. The appraisal framework, developed within Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) as an extension of the interpersonal metafunction, offers a particularly well-suited instrument for this purpose. Elaborated most fully by Martin and White (2005), the model provides what Bednarek (2010) describes as the only systematic, detailed, and elaborate framework of evaluative language among critical approaches to text evaluation. Appraisal comprises three interacting systems: attitude, which concerns the expression of feelings, judgements, and appreciations; engagement, which concerns the negotiation of positions and voices; and Graduation, which concerns the scaling up and down of values. The framework has been productively applied across a wide array of discourse types, including academic writing (Hood & Martin, 2005; Hood, 2010; Hood, 2005), narrative and its ethical work on readers (Macken-Horarik, 2003), student argumentative essays (Mei & Allison, 2003; Yang, 2016), cross-cultural news and media discourse (Liu & Stevenson, 2013; A'Beckett, 2009), and persuasive genres such as advertising (Patpong, 2009). This accumulating body of research demonstrates the versatility of appraisal as a tool for uncovering how writers construe interpersonal meaning and align readers with particular evaluative stances. Yet its application to the promotional discourse of tourist brochures has remained conspicuously underexplored. Among the three appraisal systems, the present study focuses on Graduation. This choice is motivated by both theoretical and practical considerations. Graduation possesses a distinctive generality within the appraisal architecture: attitudinal and engagement values are themselves gradable, that is, they can be intensified, quantified, or made more or less prototypical, so that Graduation pervades and modulates the operation of the other two systems (Hood & Martin, 2005; Martin & White, 2005). This pervasiveness makes Graduation worth studying in its own right, and it is especially significant in tourism discourse, which is widely characterised as a language of exaggeration, superlatives, and amplification. Graduation operates through two main subsystems: force, which grades meanings according to intensity or amount, and focus, which grades non-scalable categories according to prototypicality through sharpening or softening. These subsystems, in turn, branch into further categories such as quantification and intensification. Given the tendency of tourist texts to magnify the number, extent, and quality of the attractions and services they promote, and given their preoccupation with authenticity, which is closely tied to the resources of focus (MacCannell, 1989; Dann, 1996), Graduation offers a particularly revealing lens on the evaluative work performed by travel brochures. Concentrating exclusively on this system, rather than attempting to survey the entire appraisal model, allows for a more comprehensive and finely grained analysis of the lexicogrammatical resources through which evaluation is realised. The present study accordingly sets out to examine how Graduation strategies are deployed in the promotional discourse of travel brochures and to identify the lexicogrammatical resources through which these strategies are encoded. Two main questions guide the investigation: first, what statistical variations characterise the use of Graduation strategies, and their constituent subsystems, in tourist brochures; and second, what lexicogrammatical resources are preferred for the construal of these strategies in the texts. To address these questions, a dataset of 50 e-brochures released by tour operators across the United States between 2012 and 2013 was assembled, with one brochure drawn from each state in order to ensure a fair geographical distribution and to target an English-speaking readership. The analysis proceeds on two complementary levels. A quantitative analysis, conducted with the aid of statistical software, establishes the frequencies and distributions of the values of force and focus and their subcategories, while a qualitative analysis illustrates the range of grammatical structures through which these values are realised and interprets the promotional functions they serve within their contexts. In revisiting tourism discourse through the appraisal model, this study aims to contribute in several ways. Theoretically, it tests the descriptive power of the Graduation system as an instrument for text analysis in a genre to which it has not previously been applied, thereby extending the reach of the appraisal framework beyond the academic, narrative, and journalistic contexts in which it has more commonly been used. Descriptively, it maps the specific lexicogrammatical resources favoured in the coding of Graduation in tourist brochures, offering a detailed account of how tourism texts grade and amplify their evaluations of destinations. Practically, the findings hold potential value for those working within the tourism sector, providing a frame of reference for the design and assessment of effective promotional materials and clarifying the linguistic resources through which brochures are made to resonate with the expectations of prospective travellers.

Item 007  ·  plain text
Writing is widely regarded as one of the most demanding skills for learners of English as a foreign language (EFL). It requires learners not only to master linguistic knowledge such as grammar, vocabulary, and mechanics, but also to organise ideas coherently and to communicate them effectively to an audience. In many EFL contexts, however, the limited hours allocated to writing instruction and the scarcity of opportunities for authentic writing practice beyond the classroom make it difficult for students to develop this skill. This challenge is even more pronounced in courses where English is taught for specific purposes and where writing competes with other language skills for classroom time. Consequently, teachers have increasingly sought ways to extend writing practice outside the classroom while at the same time engaging students in meaningful, authentic communication. The rapid development of Internet technologies has opened new avenues for language teaching and learning. Among these technologies, blogs have attracted considerable attention as tools for teaching writing because they combine writing activity with virtual social interaction and easy web publishing (Abu Bakar & Ismail, 2011; Nepomuceno, 2011). Blogging enables students to write for a real and often global audience, to receive feedback from peers, teachers, and other readers, and to respond to comments on their own posts. In this way, writing becomes an interactive and social process rather than a solitary task performed only for the teacher. Blogs also expose learners to authentic reading texts, allowing them to observe the conventions of writing as they engage with the language as it is used beyond the classroom (Nepomuceno, 2011). A growing body of research has examined the potential of blogging to support EFL and ESL writing. Zhang (2009) argued that blogs are effective tools for improving English writing and for engaging students in reflective learning. Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) reported that blogging encouraged students to go beyond the classroom and to write more constructively in English. Other studies, however, have shown that blogging alone does not guarantee better writing achievement, and that the writing instruction accompanying the activity plays a decisive role in learners' progress (Özdemir & Aydin, 2015). This suggests that blogging is likely to be most beneficial when it is integrated with a sound pedagogical approach to teaching writing rather than treated as an isolated technological add-on. Against this background, the present study set out to improve the writing skill of EFL nursing students by incorporating a blogging activity, carried out on a social network website, into a writing course taught through the process-genre approach. Employing action research with mixed methods over two cycles, the study sought to determine whether such integration could enhance students' writing performance and to explore students' perceptions of the blogging activity.

Item 008  ·  plain text
The basis of this paper is clarification and interpretation of relations originating at the intersection of three phenomena: quality in education, preschool education and parents of children as consumers of this education. We share opinions supporting the importance of pre-school education, which have resonated in pedagogic discourse during the last decades The increasingly stronger voices of all those who are involved in education of children before they start primary school are based on a growing amount of empiric evidence that systematic institutional education of children of pre-school age is effective for both society in its more distant perspectives and also for the further development of each individual child. The parents of the children always appear in context concerning any analyses in relation to pre-school education, but they are only minimally considered important actors on a declarative level. Oft-repeated statements of the high rate of return on pre-school education do not always contain the adjective “high-quality”. We consider it important to mention that the benefits of pre-school education must be clearly linked to its quality, which means clarification of this concept and its overlap into practice. Regardless of whether we mean a high-quality educational system, quality in preschool education, high-quality pre-school education, a high-quality nursery school or other pre-school facility The objective of this paper is to seek answers to the question of what status the perspectives of parents have in these concepts on the background of a discussion of the concepts of quality of pre-school education. For this, we utilise the synergy originating from a combination of analysis of existing discourse about the quality of pre-school education and the parents’ position in this and subsequent synthesis resulting in conclusions about how this parental voice can be defined. Within the terms of analysis, we therefore reveal the interpretation of quality in pre-school education, and we endeavour to reflect various properties of phenomena and elements, which represent it. This particularly includes parent culture (parent cultures are perceived here in the broader context as the life styles of parents with children of pre-school age, which includes their convictions, attitude, shared values, preferences and the nature of the family’s social-cultural background, which they create. We also interpret it as a structure of values in which they move, which they utilise and mediate to their children). We do not consider synthesis here to be simple assembly of partial elements into a whole, this is an operation based on revealing new relations and rules in regard to the issue in question. Combination of the outputs of this analytical approach leads to the conclusion that the voice and status of parents is strong, but is only utilised to a limited degree in the reality of education when evaluating quality. The final synthesis should form a basis for correct decisions, of which one could also more or less purposefully focus on the perspectives of parents and their children in relation to the actual quality of education.

M1-RRLarsen-Freeman (2006) understands language as a complex, dynamic system and language use/acquisition as dynamic adaptedness to a specific context. This, in her own words (2006: 590) “proves a useful way of understanding change in progress, such as that which occurs with a developing L2 system”. As Larsen-Freeman states, because language is complex, progress cannot be totally accounted for by performance in any subsystem. She refers to van Geert and Steenbeek (2005) to explain that linguistic subsystems, dimensions of language proficiency (accuracy, fluency, and complexity), and even individual elements of language interact in ways that could be both supportive and competitive. This perspective sees “linguistic signs not as autonomous objects of any kind, either social or psychological, but as contextualised products of the integration of various activities by [particular] individuals in particular communicative situations” (Larsen-Freeman, 2006: 594). Written competence is a subset of learners’ language competence, with an emphasis on writing-specific abilities such as the production of a variety of genres and rhetorical features, but also including language-specific abilities like the use of a range of vocabulary and syntactic structures (Wolfe-Quintero, Inagaki & Kim, 1998: 2). M1-MTGWritten competence as a subset of language competence is also complex and can only be explained by the interaction of different dimensions of language proficiency. M1-RRMoreover, fluctuations in one component, such as fluency or complexity, might be associated with various fluctuations in another (Skehan, 1998, 2009). M3-APRAs our framework for the present study, the notions of complexity, accuracy, and fluency which make up the Common Assessment Framework (CAF) are regarded as the principal constructs to capture the multidimensionality of L2 written performance. M3-OPWithin this framework we intend to examine two dimensions of written language proficiency, namely, grammatical complexity and accuracy, considering the relationships and interactions between them. Moreover, the aim is to study and analyse the errors in the written English of EFL learners as an indicator of their developmental stage in morphology, syntax and lexis. M3-APRThis study examines learners at two levels of proficiency, upper intermediate (B2) and advanced (C1) users according to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) for Languages (Council of Europe, 2001).

M1-MTGPreschool education constitutes a formative period in which children acquire the linguistic, social and cognitive foundations upon which their later schooling is built. M1-CCDuring this stage, play, communication and adaptation to the culture of the school and the classroom are central to development (Katrancı, 2016). It is widely accepted that early childhood education plays a decisive role in preparing children for formal schooling and in supporting their emotional, social and cognitive growth. Because so much of what happens in the preschool classroom depends on communication between teachers and children and among the children themselves, language occupies a particularly important place at this level of education. When children arrive at school already competent in the language of instruction, the socialisation process unfolds relatively smoothly; when they do not, the entire dynamic of teaching, learning and peer interaction is affected in ways that merit careful investigation. M1-MTGBilingualism is a common reality in many parts of the world, and Turkey is no exception. In several regions of the country, and especially in the Southeastern Anatolia region, large numbers of children grow up speaking Kurdish at home and encounter Turkish, the official language of education, for the first time when they begin school. M1-CCReading is universally regarded as one of the most powerful and indispensable means of learning. For this reason, the development of a sustained reading habit among learners has long been considered essential for a life-long learning experience. A society that reads is a society that grows, and the cultivation of a reading culture has consistently been treated as a matter of national importance by educators, librarians, and policy makers (van der Ploeg, 1998). Reading extensively, and reading for pleasure, is widely viewed as a foundation upon which the quality of a nation's graduates ultimately rests. M1-MTGYet the environment in which contemporary students read has changed dramatically. M1-RRJohnsson-Smaragdi and Jönsson (2006) note that both visual and ICT media are frequently presented as a threat to books and the reading of literature, accused of drawing time and interest away from children and adolescents by offering more approachable alternatives. Social media—defined as Internet-based applications that allow the creation and exchange of user-generated content (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010)—has become deeply woven into the daily lives of the young generation, with platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter attracting overwhelming numbers of student users (Junco, 2012; Mastrodicasa & Metellus, 2013). Contemporary research on academic discourse rests upon the premise that it is a form of social practice and as such inherently interactive (Hyland, 2004). By examining the concepts, such as hedging (Hyland, 1998), metadiscourse (Hyland, 2005), stance (Biber, 2006), etc., research has illuminated how academics use language to build their arguments, express viewpoints, engage with previous research, evaluate the content with an appropriate level of certainty or doubt, etc. to create a text that readers will find convincing and eventually accredit as a valid contribution to the existing disciplinary knowledge (Hyland, 1998). One of the central pragmatic phenomena underlying the interactive nature of academic discourse is hedging, broadly defined as a rhetorical strategy used to decrease the strength of one’s claims (Hyland, 1998) In academic discourse, hedging is concerned with express ing possibilities, tentative judgments, and speculations rather than categorical and factual statements Though claims may be mitigated in multiple ways, hedging is typically associated with the use of modality devices (e.g. may, possible, perhaps, likelihood) (Hyland, 1998). In terms of syntax, hedged stance can be expressed by means of that-complement clauses (e.g. We hypothesize that…), in particular extraposed that-clauses (e.g. It is possible that…) (Hyland & Tse, 2005). The latter are preceded by a matrix it-clause which allows writers to express stance towards the content of the complement clause without revealing the source(s) of the claim (Hewings & Hewings, 2002). A congruent syntactic pattern in Croatian is a complement da-clause (Cro. kompletivna, dopumbena rečenica), as in e.g. Pretpostavljamo da…’We hypothesize that…,’ broadly defined as a dependent clause in which a matrix clause subjectively qualifies the content of the complement clause (Pranjković, 2001). An equivalent clause type to the extraposed that-clause refers to a declarative subject clause (Cro. izrična subjektna rečenica), which consists of a dependent clause controlled by the conjunction da and a matrix clause with an impersonal structure, such as an adverbial (e.g. Moguće je da…’It is possible that…’) (Silić & Pranjković, 2005). Extraposed clauses are relatively frequently employed for expressing various attitudinal meanings in academic prose, such as (un)certainty, necessity, affect, etc. (Biber et al., 1999). Likewise, Silić (2008) maintains that impersonal structures of matrix predicates of da-complement clauses are commonly used in academic writing in Croatian. By taking a cross-linguistic perspective, the primary focus of the current study is to explore how the given syntactic patterns are used as hedges in research article writing in English and Croatian. Though previous research has examined the pragmatic functions of that-complement clauses (including extraposition) in expert (Hyland & Tse, 2005) and student writing in English (Hewings & Hewings, 2001), the present study aims to enrich the former by providing a more comprehensive account of the hedging potential of extraposed that-clauses in research articles in psychology. More specifically, it examines the lexical choices of the matrix predicates, their distribution as well as hedging functions across the IMRAD structure. The study is extended by accounting for the hedging functions of the declarative subject clauses controlled by the conjunction da in the comparable corpus of research articles in Croatian, which to the best of the author’s knowledge has not been previously examined. By providing a corpus-based, cross-linguistic analysis of the target patterns, the present study aims to deepen our knowledge and raise awareness of the way hedged stance is conveyed in the disciplinary writing in each language This is particularly important for the linguistic account of the Croatian academic writing, which has been, understandably, significantly less researched than the English. At the same time, it aims to provide important evidence-based insights into the patterns of cross-linguistic similarities and differences in the distribution and the hedging potential of the target clauses Thus, the findings and the issues raised in the paper may inform the classroom practice in the given non-native English academic context and generally contribute to better understanding of crosscultural academic writing.

Second language (L2) speech fluency has long been recognized as an important indicator of L2 proficiency, capturing the smoothness and effortlessness with which learners produce speech (Chambers, 1997; Lennon, 1990). Within the Complexity–Accuracy–Fluency framework (Housen, Kuiken, & Vedder, 2012), fluency in its 'narrow sense' is typically operationalized through temporal features of speech such as speaking rate and pausing, distinguishing it from the broader, nontechnical understanding of fluency as general oral proficiency (Lennon, 1990). These objective and measurable features of utterance fluency are generally regarded as reflecting a speaker's underlying cognitive fluency (Segalowitz, 2010). Contemporary research commonly organizes fluency measures into three dimensions—speed, breakdown (pausing), and repair (false starts, repetitions, and reformulations)—each of which has been widely used to characterize learner performance and to relate it to overall proficiency (Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2012; Kormos & Dénes, 2004). While numerous factors influencing L2 fluency have been examined, the influence of first language (L1) fluency on L2 fluency remains comparatively poorly understood. Early theorists noted that even L1 speakers vary considerably in their fluency (Goldman-Eisler, 1968; Lennon, 1990), a finding that has been repeatedly confirmed empirically. If individual differences shape L1 fluency, they are likely to be reflected in L2 fluency measures as well (De Jong et al., 2015; Huensch & Tracy-Ventura, 2017). Indeed, several studies have reported large standard deviations in the use of filled pauses and repetitions in both native and nonnative speech (Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014), suggesting that at least these aspects of fluency are subject to substantial individual variation. It has further been proposed that pause length may reflect individual speaking style more than L2 proficiency, and that temporal features such as speech rate and pausing carry over from a speaker's L1 speaking style into L2 production (Raupach, 1980; Segalowitz, 2010; Towell et al., 2005). A small but growing body of work has addressed the L1–L2 fluency relationship more directly. Derwing et al. (2009) conducted the first systematic longitudinal investigation, comparing Slavic and Mandarin learners' productions in their L1 and L2 English. They found significant correlations between L1 and L2 fluency that shifted over time and differed between groups, leading them to conclude that fluency cannot be regarded as a purely 'traitlike' feature. De Jong et al. (2015) subsequently demonstrated significant correlations between L1 and L2 fluency for all measures examined, with L1 fluency explaining substantial variance in L2 fluency; they also showed that correcting L2 measures for L1 behavior could strengthen their predictive value for proficiency. Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2017) extended this work longitudinally, showing that the contributions of L1 fluency and cross-linguistic differences shifted across development, becoming more prominent after study abroad. Studies outside the L2 fluency tradition have likewise underscored the influence of L1 speaking style on L2 pause patterns and speech rate (Möhle, 1984; Towell et al., 1996). Despite these advances, previous studies have relied almost exclusively on quantitative, group-level analyses, thereby underemphasizing the individual variation that appears especially prominent in learners' use of stalling mechanisms such as filled pauses, drawls, fillers, and repetitions (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998; Götz, 2013; Hilton, 2014). Such phenomena are multifunctional and idiosyncratic, and their connections between L1 and L2 may be obscured when examined only through aggregate statistics. The present study addresses this gap by adopting a mixed methods approach that combines quantitative analyses (rank-order correlations and regression) with a complementary qualitative examination of selected learners' L1 and L2 productions. Speech samples were collected from 42 Finnish learners of English at two school levels, allowing the role of proficiency in the L1–L2 fluency relationship to be considered while also introducing a previously understudied language pair. Guided by this approach, the study addresses three research questions: (RQ1) which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with measures of L2 fluency; (RQ2) to what extent measures of L2 fluency can be predicted from L1 fluency measures; and (RQ3) what kinds of individual differences can be identified in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency through a qualitative analysis of learners' productions with high frequencies of stalling mechanisms.

The spread of English as a lingua franca (ELF) has profoundly reshaped the way languages are used, learnt and taught across the world. English now functions as the dominant means of international communication, a status that sets it apart from any other foreign language and that has generated a substantial body of applied linguistic inquiry into its nature, its varieties and its pedagogical implications (Seidlhofer et al., 2006; McKay, 2018). Much of this discussion has centred on how best to conceptualise ELF: as a variety, a register, or a function. Friedrich and Matsuda (2010) argue that understanding ELF merely as a linguistic variety fails to capture the reality of international communication, which is always context and situation specific, while Mollin (2006) similarly questions whether ELF can be integrated into nation-based models such as Kachru's as a variety at all. Seidlhofer (2009) further stresses the common ground shared by world Englishes and ELF research, both of which assume that English belongs to all who use it. These debates matter because the way English is defined shapes the way it is taught in classrooms. Alongside the rise of ELF, a growing awareness of multilingualism has emerged as our default reality, with monolinguals increasingly the exception. This shift has sharpened the tension between English as a language for communication and as a language for identification, a distinction articulated by House (2003), who argued against the assumption that English inevitably threatens national languages and multilingualism. Jenkins et al. (2001), in describing an emerging Euro-English, similarly point to the complex ways in which English is being reappropriated across the continent. In Europe specifically, the omnipresence of English creates a potential conflict with the ideals of societal multilingualism and individual plurilingualism (Seidlhofer et al., 2006), a conflict that European policy guidelines such as the CEFR attempt, not always successfully, to resolve. Despite this rich literature on the status and function of ELF, comparatively little attention has been paid to how a plurilingual and ecological understanding of English can be operationalised in the primary classroom, particularly in relation to the role of the mother tongue in learning the foreign language. Existing pedagogical approaches, including the popular CLIL model, remain largely monolingual and native-based in practice, with British and American models still defining authentic materials and cultural appropriateness. Moreover, cross-national comparisons that examine how differing language policies translate into differing learner attitudes and outcomes are scarce. It remains unclear whether an approach that deliberately uses the L1 as a scaffolding tool, and that presents English as a language belonging to no single nation, can improve learning independently of the student's mother tongue. This paper addresses that gap by proposing and testing a plurilingual and ecological approach to English language teaching in primary school. Drawing on the initial results of an international research project conducted in three very different contexts, and presenting here the first phase involving 133 Year 6 students in Spain and Norway, we compare plurilingual and monolingual teaching through written tests, an oral activity and an attitudinal questionnaire. In doing so, we distinguish between languages for communication and languages for identification, examine the language policies of the participating countries, and analyse cross-linguistic and cross-cultural perspectives. We argue that a plurilingual approach using the L1 as a connecting tool improves English learning while fostering an ecological understanding of languages in which all languages are valued within a shared linguistic ecosystem.

Teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) is commonly considered a challenging practice by teachers. Some challenges arise from the capability of the students to interact and communicate with their teachers in the target language. Others derive from stakeholders who continue to insist on an English-only policy as they still believe it is the best approach to acquire a foreign language This issue has increasingly become a great obstacle to students in the classroom. Whenever the idea of plurilingualism is brought up for discussion a long dispute can be expected. This dispute is understandable, but a space for constructive discussion is needed, especially nowadays, when new theories are evolving with regard to allowing students’ first language to be used together with the target language in EFL classrooms. Plurilingualism is not the exception; indeed, it is quite popular around the world, especially where multicultural and national backgrounds coexist (Blommaert, 2010; Lamb, 2015). The phenomenon of plurilingualism, according to Marshall and Moore (2018, p. 19), concerns: “…the study of individuals’ repertoires and agency in several languages, in different contexts, in which the individual is the locus and actor of contact; accordingly, a person’s languages and cultures interrelate and change over time, depending on individual biographies, social trajectories, and life paths.” In other words, it is seen as an individual characteristic, in contrast to multilingualism, which is considered a societal phenomenon (García & Otheguy, 2020). This individualist feature affords individuals within societies their preference of linguistic choices for the purpose of communication and improving their communicative competence. Hence, plurilingual speakers are aware of their plurilingual practice and also pay attention to others’ plurilingual practice. This awareness raises the attention of speakers and supports their goal of achieving linguistic competence. In addition, plurilingualism concentrates on the language itself and attempts to help monolinguals become bi/multilinguals with a view to building a “repertoire of languages” (García & Otheguy, 2020, p. 21). This case study, therefore, aims to explore the idea of plurilingualism in terms of the views held by EFL teachers in intermediate and secondary schools in the Qassim region, Saudi Arabia. A questionnaire was distributed among EFL teachers concerning their awareness of the term “plurilingualism” and their perspectives regarding the inclusion of the two languages, mother tongue and target language, in the classroom. A focus group interview was then conducted to attain a deep understanding of their thoughts and concerns about plurilingualism and its application in the classroom.

Teaching English as a foreign language at an early (7-12) and even at a very early (under 7) age is becoming increasingly popular and accessible worldwide. This growing interest is often driven by parents, who see the demands of a globalizing world and wish to ensure their children can thrive in a future in which English plays a central role (Tekin 2015). Indeed, in many contexts, from the Gulf Region to Korea and Central Europe, parents invest heavily in their children's English education and begin this process at ever-younger ages (Linse 2011, Tekin 2015). As a result, teachers of very young learners frequently face pressure and expectations from parents regarding the nature and quality of instruction they provide. Parents, then, are essential stakeholders in the teaching of English to young and very young learners, since it is largely the family that decides when and what language a child begins to learn and shapes the child's attitudes towards the languages studied. It follows that understanding parental attitudes is beneficial for the future of the field, allowing practitioners and policy makers to ensure that expectations and outcomes meet. A considerable body of research has addressed the age question, examining the benefits and possible threats of an early start (Nikolov and Djigunović 2006, 2011, Hanušová and Najvar 2005), while other studies have surveyed public and professional opinion about the ideal starting age (Purdjaková 2006). A parallel strand of research has explored parental beliefs about early EFL, identifying links between attitudes and demographic factors such as maternal education, parental age, and sociocultural background (Griva and Chouvarda 2012, Tekin 2015, Linse 2011). Attitudes towards accent and native-speaker norms have likewise attracted much attention, revealing that native varieties are often accorded greater prestige while non-native, including local, accents are frequently disfavoured. However, comparatively little is known about how parents of very young learners in Hungary view the pronunciation of the teacher, and whether such attitudes vary according to the age at which parents prefer language learning to begin, their own self-rated proficiency, their plans to move abroad, or the formal or informal context in which their children learn. Addressing this gap, the present study examines the attitudes of fifty Hungarian parents of children aged 0-7 towards teacher accent and the ideal age to start learning a foreign language, drawing on an online questionnaire that included an 8-item attitude scale measuring responses towards American, British, and Hungarian pronunciation. In doing so, we aim to shed light on the extent to which native-speakerism persists among these key stakeholders.

Language is a complex communication tool consisting of language layers analysed according to their respective linguistic disciplines; however, speakers use its entire range of means concurrently and appropriately for the particular act of communication. In the current period of globalization, speakers often communicate in foreign languages, the use of which brings new aspects to communication Levis (2005) presents a draft of a Speaker-Listener Intelligibility Matrix for communication between native and non-native speakers. Communication between two native speakers presumes shared strategies and the successful transfer of information. In reality, the extent to which this communication succeeds depends on many factors such as the use of nativized varieties of English (e. g. India). When native speakers speak and non-native speakers listen, it resembles the typical non-native way of foreign language learning. On the contrary, non-native speakers bear a higher degree of responsibility for successful communication when native speakers are listening. Two non-native speakers use a given foreign language as their lingua franca. Therefore, context is important for the outcome of this communication Jenkins (2002) claims that currently English is spoken by a higher number of non-native speakers than native speakers, thus investigation into possible issues is required. Pronunciation is one of the key aspects of speech, which is reflected in the recent growth in research into pronunciation teaching. At the beginning of the new millennium, Derwing and Munro (2005) commented on the lack of investigation into pronunciation teaching to non-native learners due to the study of pronunciation shifting to the field of applied linguistics. In approaches to nonnative language teaching relevant to that period improved pronunciation was a result of exposure to the target language (Foote et al., 2016). Subsequently, teachers were given few guiding principles and some non-native teachers avoided teaching pronunciation (Munro & Derwing, 2005). Almost a decade later, Thomson and Derwing (2014) observed a clear growth in interest in pronunciation research and carried out an analysis of 75 studies focusing on how non-natives learned pronunciation, concluding that non-native learners benefit from the explicit explanation of pronunciation rules. Pronunciation is viewed as different from other aspects of language proficiency, as the ability to imitate sounds is not tied to language proficiency (Thomson & Derwing, 2014). However, Nair et al. (2017) suggest, some non-native language teachers believe that the ability to learn an accent is based on talent or exposure to the target language. The specific pronunciation features non-native learners of English should command are determined by the listeners’ ability to identify the meaning of words pronounced differently from the form presented as models. The difference in nonnative pronunciation may be caused by an error as well as the use of an accent or a pronunciation variety While native speakers are allowed to use their native accents (social, geographical), often with greater variation than non-native speakers; non-native speakers are taught to imitate Received Pronunciation or General American English accents (Jenkins, 2002). Levis (2005) argues that even though the majority of native speakers speak neither of these accents, a large part of instructional materials presents them as prestigious models and their use in actual communication may not be effective. She suggests including non-native accents to pronunciation teaching. Jenkins (2002) believes that pronunciation teaching makes the most compromises when compared to the teaching of other language layers and adds that “[t]he links between accent and identity on the one hand and accent and articulatory motor skills on the other are, it seems, so ingrained that traditional English pronunciation teaching is destined to fail for all but a small minority of L2 learners” (Jenkins, 2002, p. 86) The position of pronunciation training has not been stable over the different periods of English language teaching. While the early approaches to language teaching (the Direct Method or Grammar Translation) either ignored pronunciation or taught it through drills and repetition to achieve native-like pronunciation, the Reform Movement or Audiolingual/Oral Method viewed pronunciation instruction as an important part of non-native language learning (Celce-Murcia et al., 1996) Today pronunciation teaching concentrates on those aspects of English pronunciation that constitute and carry meaning and aims to respect the natural accent of English learners (Celce-Murcia et al., 1996; Jenkins, 2002; Levis, 2005; Saito, 2012). Those theories (e. g. the Critical Period Hypothesis, Flege, 1987) that assume that learner’s age may limit achieving accent-free pronunciation of non-native English learners in English were challenged soon after their presentation (e. g. Patkowski, 1990). Regarding acceptance of the concept of comprehensible pronunciation with an accent among non-native learners of English, new goals to pronunciation teaching were formulated. Levis (2005) compares the terms nativeness and intelligibility. The nativeness principle is based on the assumption that native-like pronunciation and the ability to imitate target sounds by non-native learners of foreign languages can be achieved by motivation, exposure to the target language and pronunciation training. This principle has not been fully accepted due to a lack of evidence; however, this principle seems to be reflected in many textbooks on pronunciation practice. On the contrary, the intelligibility principle is based on the assumption that “learners simply need to be understandable” (Levis, 2005, p. 370) and deviations from model pronunciation compromise the comprehension to a different degree. Intelligibility is a universally accepted term; however, there are different classifications and instruments used to measure it. In the past, intelligibility was evaluated using cloze tests, transcriptions or rating scales Crowther et al. (2015) list the evaluation methods for both approaches – while nativeness is evaluated using accentedness ratings, comprehensibility (intelligibility) is rated via the listener’s relative difficulty to understand an utterance. The data indicate that listeners take into account the speaker’s native language as well as the type of utterance. A large role in the evaluation of speakers’ performance and intelligibility is played by evaluator bias against the phenomena, accents, speakers as well as their experience with a particular accent or pronunciation feature (Derwing & Munro, 2005). The concept of intelligibility has been variously subclassified (comfortable, functional, overall; for details, see Isaacs, 2008) with the same general conclusion – the listener should understand the speaker’s message without the need for repetition or rephrasing the utterance. Derwing and Munro (2005) therefore identified two main concerns in pronunciation teaching – intelligibility that allows the non-native learner to communicate successfully with different groups of native and non-native English speakers and secondly the non-native accent that has an impact on the social interactions between non-native speakers and their listeners. The needs of different learners from different linguistic backgrounds vary, as Wells (2008) pointed out. Pronunciation features challenging speakers of one language may be easy for speakers of another language and can be caused by a different set of phonemes in each language. Crowther et al. (2015) add that pronunciation of sounds in a foreign language contains elements traceable to native language and the non-native learners of English who share one native language display similar pronunciation features in the foreign language. The linguistic homogeneity or heterogeneity of a group of non-native learners and the instructor’s native language are a major factor in pronunciation teaching (Foote et al, 2016). All these factors are accompanied by the individual ability of non-native learners to produce and recognize specific sounds.

Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has become one of the most dynamic and rapidly expanding pedagogic trends in European education over the last two decades (Dalton-Puffer, Nikula & Smit, 2010; Pérez-Cañado, 2011). Embraced enthusiastically by policy-makers as a means of promoting plurilingualism and boosting foreign language competence, CLIL has spread throughout the continent as a language enrichment measure integrated into mainstream schooling. In Spain, this expansion has been particularly striking, with successive waves of bilingual programmes being launched across autonomous communities, including monolingual regions such as Castilla-La Mancha, where contact with foreign language speakers has traditionally been limited and where proficiency in English and French has historically been low. Against this backdrop, bilingual education has been positioned not merely as a linguistic reform but as a flagship educational initiative capable of raising the quality and international standing of schools. The considerable enthusiasm generated by CLIL has, however, run ahead of the research base needed to justify it. As several scholars have warned, CLIL has often been presented as a near-panacea, credited with a wide array of benefits, not all of which are firmly supported by empirical evidence (Bruton, 2011; Paran, 2013). Much of the earlier research into CLIL effectiveness has been criticized for methodological shortcomings, most notably the failure to control for the selective nature of CLIL populations, whereby programmes tend to attract already high-achieving students both in language and content (Bruton, 2011; Paran, 2013). This critique has provoked a lively debate about how to move beyond both an overly optimistic and an overly dismissive stance towards CLIL, and has generated calls for a balanced, methodologically sound research agenda (Pérez-Cañado, 2016; Cenoz, Genesee & Gorter, 2014). Studies examining the actual gains associated with CLIL have accordingly produced mixed and sometimes confined results, whether in relation to language competences (Nieto Moreno de Diezmas, 2016), cross-curricular and digital competences (Nieto Moreno de Diezmas, 2018), affective factors and motivation (Lasagabaster & Doiz, 2015; Navarro Pablo, 2018), or content acquisition (Szmalec et al., 2025). What is increasingly clear is that, after more than a decade of implementation, the moment has come to take stock and reflect critically on the points of tension, needs, shortcomings and unresolved issues that accompany bilingual education in practice (Dalton-Puffer & Smit, 2013; Pérez-Cañado, 2016). Within this broad research agenda, the perceptions and beliefs of the stakeholders directly involved in CLIL have emerged as a particularly fruitful and, at the same time, underexplored field of inquiry. As Dalton-Puffer and Smit (2013) argue, the investigation of stakeholders' perceptions of CLIL and its success constitutes an essential dimension of policy-oriented research, since the implementation of CLIL is best understood as a form of extended language policy that links language management, practice and beliefs, rather than as a purely top-down legislative measure (Hüttner, Dalton-Puffer & Smit, 2013). Beliefs and so-called lay theories held by teachers and learners exert a powerful influence on how CLIL is enacted at the local level, and these constructions of CLIL and of CLIL success may diverge considerably from those of experts or policy-makers (Hüttner et al., 2013). Listening to learners and providing them with a voice has likewise been shown to enrich our understanding of what constitutes successful learning across CLIL contexts (Coyle, 2013). A growing body of research has therefore begun to elicit the opinions, attitudes and expectations of the different groups involved, at both primary and secondary levels and in tertiary settings (Dafouz, Nuñez & Sancho, 2007; Pladevall-Ballester, 2014; McDougald, 2015; Fernández-Costales, 2015; Martínez & Barrio Llavador, 2016). Despite this expanding interest, most of the existing studies have tended to focus on a restricted set of participants, typically students, content teachers, or, in some cases, parents (Pladevall-Ballester, 2014). Comparatively few investigations have simultaneously considered the full range of teaching professionals who share responsibility for making CLIL work. A notable exception is the line of research pursued by Doiz and Lasagabaster (2017), who examined whether management teams and teaching staff share the same beliefs about CLIL programmes, thereby drawing attention to the crucial but frequently overlooked role of school leaders. Coordination between content and language teachers has similarly been identified as one of the key drivers of successful CLIL, and one that hinges on teachers' perceptions of their own professional identities and roles (Pavón Vázquez & Méndez García, 2017). Yet the perspective of English teachers, of CLIL programme coordinators and of management teams has rarely been examined together with that of content teachers and students within a single study, leaving important gaps in our understanding of how the various stakeholders view one another and where friction between them may arise. Another recurrent theme in the literature concerns the beliefs surrounding native speakers and native language assistants, who occupy a prominent place in the imagination of stakeholders involved in bilingual programmes. Research in the Spanish context has explored the use of native assistants as language and cultural resources (Tobin & Abello-Contesse, 2013) and has analysed the narratives and ideologies of bilingualism that circulate in schools, including in Castilla-La Mancha, where questions of who counts as the legitimate teacher of English and whose English is legitimated have proved especially salient (Relaño-Pastor, 2018). Such work suggests that the idealization of the native speaker constitutes a shared lay theory whose pedagogical foundations warrant closer scrutiny. The present study seeks to contribute to this field by exploring the shared beliefs and perceptions of the full spectrum of stakeholders involved in CLIL programmes at secondary level. Unlike most previous research, it gives voice not only to students and content teachers, but also to English teachers, to CLIL programme coordinators and, crucially, to the members of the management teams, whose views are seldom considered in tandem with those of the teaching staff. Drawing on data gathered from 114 participants in two state secondary schools located in the provinces of Albacete and Cuenca in Castilla-La Mancha, both selected as examples of good practice and continuity, the study combines Likert-type questionnaires with open-ended questions and interviews in order to capture both the quantitative distribution of opinions and the more nuanced qualitative reasoning behind them. The bilingual programme in Castilla-La Mancha offers a particularly relevant setting for such an inquiry, given the rapid expansion of provision and the succession of regulatory changes that have reshaped its structure in recent years, changes whose effects on the quality of the programmes and on the satisfaction of those who implement them remain to be fully understood (Ruiz Cordero, 2021). By identifying the shared perceptions, mutual regard and points of tension among these different categories of participants, as well as the lay theories they hold and the shortcomings they detect, this paper aims to shed light on the strengths and, above all, the areas in need of improvement in the implementation of bilingual education. In so doing, it responds to the call for localised, context-sensitive research capable of informing effective CLIL practice and of ensuring that the potential contribution of all stakeholders is neither overlooked nor squandered.
