Assessment lies at the heart of the teaching and learning process, and over the past three decades the role of assessment in shaping classroom learning has attracted growing international attention. Assessment plays a crucial role in any educational milieu (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017), and the recognition that it can be a resource for learning rather than merely a means of measuring it has given rise to a large body of scholarship on formative assessment (FA). Formative assessment is an instructional approach that has received considerable international attention because of its potential to improve teaching and learning. Although a single definition has not emerged among researchers and practitioners, common elements recur across the literature: formative assessment is understood as a cyclical process involving interactions between teachers and students, in which information about learning is elicited, interpreted, and used to provide feedback that helps students confirm or improve their understanding (Bennett, 2011). In contrast to summative assessment, which summarises and ranks what students have learned, formative assessment is embedded in instruction and used to diagnose learning needs and adjust teaching accordingly. The influence of formative assessment on learning outcomes has been documented in a number of seminal studies. Black and Wiliam (1998) reviewed a large volume of evidence and concluded that strengthening the practice of formative assessment produces significant learning gains, particularly for lower-achieving students. Subsequent research reinforced these claims: Wiliam, Lee, Harrison, and Black (2004) reported a mean effect size of 0.32 in favour of classrooms in which teachers developed formative assessment strategies, and Hattie (2009) placed feedback and assessment-related practices among the more powerful influences on achievement in his synthesis of hundreds of meta-analyses. Building on these findings, scholars have described the knowledge and skills that teachers require in order to enact formative assessment effectively, including domain knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, knowledge of students' prior learning, and knowledge of assessment itself (Heritage, 2007), as well as concrete classroom moves such as posing good questions, probing responses, and involving students in assessing their own and others' learning (Duckor, 2014). Formative assessment has also been examined at the level of higher education, where it has been theorised as a driver of pedagogic enhancement (Yorke, 2003), and within teacher education, where its integration into instruction has been proposed as a route to more coherent teaching and learning (Shavelson, 2006). Much of this scholarship, however, has concentrated on the benefits and effects of formative assessment on student engagement and learning achievement (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017). A parallel strand of research has begun to stress that whether and how these benefits are realised depends heavily on teachers themselves. The beliefs teachers hold about assessment influence their classroom practices and reflect broader cultural and societal differences (Brown, Hui, Yu, & Kennedy, 2011). Teachers' conceptions of formative feedback and their assumptions about their students shape the input they provide and the follow-up actions they take, and these conceptions are further mediated by contextual factors such as professional development opportunities, collegial support, and the pressures of high-stakes testing (Harrison, 2013; Rink & Mitchell, 2002). Investigating classroom assessment practices, then, requires attention not only to what formative assessment can achieve, but also to teachers' attitudes, intentions, and self-reported behaviour (Stiggins, Conklin, & National Education Association, 1992). One fruitful framework for connecting attitudes and intentions to behaviour is Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen, 1985, 1991), which holds that behaviour is predicted by intention, which in turn is shaped by attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control. Drawing on this framework, Yan and Cheng (2015) developed the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ) and used it to examine primary teachers' attitudes, intentions, and practices, operationalising the constructs through subscales measuring affective attitude, instrumental attitude, subjective norm, controllability, self-efficacy, intention, and behaviour. Their study, and related work applying planned-behaviour models to teacher assessment (Yan, 2014), revealed an intriguing disjuncture: although teachers generally reported positive attitudes and strong intentions towards formative assessment, these did not translate consistently into frequent classroom use, with the behaviour subscale correlating only weakly with the other measures. This tension between what teachers believe about formative assessment and what they actually do has been observed repeatedly across contexts (Black & Wiliam, 1998), and it points to the importance of understanding teachers' conceptions in detail rather than assuming that favourable attitudes will automatically produce widespread practice. Despite the wealth of research on formative assessment and its impact on learning, there has been little in-depth study describing teachers' own understandings of formative assessment and how their perspectives shape their follow-up actions. The gap is particularly acute outside the English-speaking and East Asian contexts in which most of the existing instruments and models have been developed and validated. In many EFL settings, teachers work within examination-driven cultures and with limited resources, and it cannot be assumed that findings from primary science classrooms in Singapore or Hong Kong will generalise to their circumstances. In the Iraqi context specifically, the study of English language teaching and assessment literacy remains underdeveloped, and to the best knowledge of the present researcher no study has investigated the contributions of teachers' attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment to student learning in Iraqi universities and schools. Given the growing emphasis on language assessment literacy as a component of teacher professionalism (Atmani et al., 2021), and the recognition that changing assessment cultures requires attention to teachers' beliefs rather than resources alone, there is a clear need to describe how Iraqi EFL teachers conceive of and enact formative assessment. The present study addresses this gap by exploring the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding formative assessment. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior, it seeks to investigate not only whether these teachers value formative assessment but also the extent to which the various components of their attitudes are related to their actual application of it, and whether such attitudes vary by gender and level of education. The study also aims to highlight the applicability of formative assessment in EFL classrooms, particularly the alignment of appropriate strategies with assessment purposes, and to identify pedagogical implications for teacher education in Iraq. To this end, four research questions guide the investigation: (1) What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards formative assessment? (2) How frequently do Iraqi EFL teachers use formative assessment? (3) To what extent are the different components of attitudes to formative assessment related to its application? and (4) Do Iraqi teachers' attitudes to formative assessment differ in terms of sex and level of education? To answer these questions, the study administered an Arabic version of the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (Yan & Cheng, 2015) to 102 EFL teachers working across primary schools, high schools, private institutes, and universities in Iraq. The instrument was translated and back-translated, and its validity was examined through confirmatory factor analysis before descriptive and inferential statistics were computed to characterise teachers' conceptions and to test relationships among the constructs. By providing the first empirical account of Iraqi EFL teachers' formative assessment attitudes and practices, the study may inform the design of professional development programmes and contribute to a fuller understanding of the conditions under which positive assessment beliefs are, or are not, converted into classroom practice.

Fairclough (1993) argues that academic environment has also been marketized because of the fact that universities are required to operate as businesses, selling their products to consumers. Through the use of discoursal and rhetorical elements which function to enhance the perceived value of one’s research (Bhatia, 2005), writers promote their research to others. Bekenkotter and Huckin (1995: 43) also argue that “today’s scientists seem to be promoting their work to a degree never seen before.” For them, one of the main reasons for the increase of promotion is rooted in the current promotional culture, which is changing discoursal practices and creating hybrid genres. Promotion can be expressed in various forms as it can be “realized by means of those linguistic choices that seek to change or affect the opinions or behaviors of an audience in terms of positively assessing the research contribution” (Martin & Perez, 2014: 1). It has been studied as a discourse feature realized through evaluation (e.g. Hunston & Thomson, 2000), metadiscourse (e.g. Hyland, 2005), and lexicogrammatical features such as selfreference and self-citation (e.g. Afros & Schryer, 2009; Harwood, 2005a, 2005b; Hyland, 2000, 2005). Some other strategies have also functioned as promotional elements, such as explicitly highlighting the novel contributions of the study to the discipline or commenting briefly on the findings in the introduction section (Martin & Perez, 2014). Most of the studies related to promotion have investigated the introduction sections of RAs (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Berkenkotter & Huckin, 1995; Bhatia, 2004; Lindeberg, 2004). This section has been a major focus of attention since it “generally entails a great deal of complexity in terms of rhetorical options, among them the possibility of including promotional elements” (Martin & Perez, 2014: 2). Analyzing the rhetorical structure of introductions has proved to be the most fruitful method in order to gain an in-depth understanding of, among other things, how promotional elements are employed by the authors of RAs. M1-CCSwales’ (1990) seminal work on the rhetorical structure of introduction has been revolutionary in the analysis and teaching of academic writing. He came up with a model, namely the Create a Research Space (CARS) model, which has been the basis of numerous subsequent studies (e.g. Bhatia, 1993; Burgess, 2002; Fredrickson & Swales, 1994; Loi, 2010; Nwugo, 1991). M1-RRSwales’ (1990) CARS model is a framework proposed to describe the organizational patterns of writing the Introduction sections in academic research articles. This model assumes that writers, in an attempt to develop an effective introduction to their research articles, follow a general organizational pattern. The model comprises three main actions referred to as ‘Moves’, each of which consists of a number of ‘Steps’ as illustrated in Table 1 and briefly explained below. As Table 1 shows, Move 1 generally sets the ground for introducing the research topic. Step 1 of the first move is claiming centrality, which is defined by Swales (1990) as appeals through which authors argue that their research is “part of a lively, significant or well established research area” (p. 144). In Step 2, statements are made about the current state of knowledge and the need for further investigations in the area. In Step 3, authors review one or two studies that they consider to be relevant to the establishment (Swales, 1990). In Move 2, authors try to persuade readers that their research is important and valuable (Swales, 1990). In Step 1A, authors point out the limitations of the general research area; in Step 1B, authors develop a research problem around a gap in the literature; in Step 1C, they raise key questions in the area; and in Step 1D, authors generally pose a weaker challenge to the prior research, aiming to expand or clarify a specific research problem (Swales, 1990). In Move 3, writers discuss the contribution and organizational structure of their paper (Swales, 1990). In Step 1A, they indicate their main purpose(s); in Step 1B, they describe the main features of their research. In Step 2, authors provide a general summary of key findings, and in Step 3, they bring statements about the structure of the remainder of the article (Swales, 1990). Later in another book, Swales (2004) made some revisions to his model, which are minor and have not changed the basic structure. As can be seen in Table 2, the moves are roughly the same in the revised version of the model, with a minor difference in the wording of the third move. The steps have undergone relatively more changes, with some steps in the original model omitted and some others added. The order of the steps and their wordings have also been revised. The theoretical concern with authorial self-representation has deep roots in the seminal works of Bakhtin, Foucault, and Ivanič, in which authorial presence is situated within the relations between self and others, between the author's voice and the audience, and between the writer and the writer's identity. Pre-school education is increasingly recognised as a foundational phase of lifelong learning, offering children their first sustained encounter with peers and non-familial adults, and shaping developmental trajectories in ways that resonate far beyond early childhood (OECD, 2019; Herschkowitz et al., 2002). This early period, coinciding with accelerated brain development, is regarded as both formative and critical, and its influence on the child's later educational career and overall wellbeing is closely tied to the quality of the care and education provided (Ugaste et al., 2013). Economists have argued persuasively that investment in high-quality early education yields among the highest rates of return across the entire continuum of lifelong learning, particularly for children from disadvantaged environments, and that such investment supports both social equity and economic growth (Heckman, 2011, 2013; European Union Commission, 2006; Ball, 1994). Yet, as numerous authors caution, the positive effects of pre-school education are not automatic; they are contingent upon quality, and the pre-school sector remains one of the least understood, most fragmented and least uniformly regulated segments of education (OECD, 2019; Janta et al., 2016; Melhuish et al., 2015; Slot, 2017). This makes the concept of quality itself a central and yet notoriously elusive object of study. Discussions of educational quality are frequently confused by a lack of shared understanding of what the term actually means (Tawil et al., 2014). Rather than a single definition, the literature offers a diverse and value-laden conceptualisation: quality is understood as multi-dimensional, relative, dynamic and context-dependent, perceived differently by the various parties involved—students, parents, teachers, employers and inspectors (Dahlberg & Moss, 2007; Průcha, Walterová, & Mareš, 2009). Interpretations range across structural and process dimensions (Slot, 2017; Litjens & Taguma, 2010; Janta et al., 2016), across objective and subjective standpoints (Parrila, 2002), and across the multiple perspectives that Katz (1999) identified for evaluating programme quality. Crucially, research has tended to privilege the 'top-down' perspective of experts, while the perspectives of children, families and communities remain comparatively neglected (Rentzou, 2011; Rentzou & Sakellariou, 2013). Among these under-examined standpoints, the position of parents is particularly striking. Parents occupy a strong and multifaceted role in pre-school education: they select institutions, articulate expectations, participate in daily processes, and contribute to the very dimensions through which quality is constructed (Rabušicová et al., 2004; Glenn-Applegate et al., 2016; Sevinc, 2006). Their evaluations, however, are often shaped by subjective needs, cultural values and socio-economic circumstances, and consequently tend to differ in semantics from the assessments of experts (Malovic et al., 2017; Brodin et al., 2015; Bayrak & Koksal, 2017). This tension raises a question that has received insufficient theoretical attention: how, if at all, should the parental perspective be incorporated into the conceptualisation and definition of quality in pre-school education? The present theoretical study addresses this question through an analysis of research discourse drawn largely from the past two decades. It proceeds in three stages: first, examining the importance and benefits of systematic pre-school education for the child and for society; second, clarifying the concept of quality and its interpretation in education; and third, elaborating the interesting yet undervalued position of parents in relation to how the quality of pre-school education is defined and evaluated.

M1-MTGLearning a foreign language is a gradual process during which learners inevitably encounter gaps between what they intend to express and the linguistic resources they have acquired. M1-RRA common feature observed in the foreign language classroom is the way learners draw on communication strategies to manipulate a limited linguistic system in order to convey their intended meaning (Dörnyei & Scott, 1997). M1-CCRather than abandoning the message when faced with such gaps, learners frequently devise creative means of getting their point across, and these strategic behaviours have become an important focus of second language acquisition research over the past few decades (Faerch & Kasper, 1984; Yule & Tarone, 1987). M1-RRCommunication strategies have been variously classified, but a broad distinction is often drawn between interlingual strategies, which borrow from another language, and intralingual strategies, which resolve difficulties within the target language itself through devices such as approximation, word coinage and restructuring (Brown, 2000; Dörnyei & Scott, 1997). M1-CCOne of the greatest challenges learners face is the inadequacy of the lexical items they have mastered, whether because words have been forgotten or because they cannot be retrieved or used with confidence (Poulisse, 1993; Ringbom, 2006). M1-MTGThese difficulties are compounded when the target language differs markedly from the learner's native language. M1-RRAs Trager and Lado (1957) noted in their pioneering work on contrastive analysis, the structures and habits of the mother tongue directly shape the way a second language is learnt, and interference is most acute where the two systems diverge. M1-RRThe Chinese writing system exhibits an irregular sound-to-symbol correspondence, and its pronunciation contains phonemes that have no equivalents in languages such as Malay or English (Everson, 1988). Consequently, learners must develop new approaches to both recognising and producing Chinese words. The English article system is widely recognised as one of the most challenging aspects of English for second language learners to master, particularly for those whose first language lacks a comparable system (Master, 1997; Hewson, 2017). The system comprises the definite article 'the', the indefinite article 'a/an', and the zero article Ø, and the correct choice among them depends on interrelated features such as countability, number, definiteness, and specificity. Because these distinctions are grammaticalised differently across languages, learners frequently transfer patterns from their first language, resulting in systematic errors (Hasbún, 2012). Research on EFL learners has repeatedly shown that overuse of articles, especially the definite article 'the', is a common feature of learner production and is at least partly attributable to first language interference (Hasbún, 2009). Pashto, a widely spoken language in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan, has no article system as such. Definiteness and indefiniteness are instead conveyed, to some extent, through demonstratives and indefinite numerals such as /yaw/ (one). This mismatch between Pashto and English raises questions about how adult Pashto speakers acquire and use English articles. Although the acquisition of English articles has been extensively studied among speakers of many languages, very little research has examined Pashto learners specifically. The present study addresses this gap by investigating the types, nature, and loci of the errors that adult Pashto learners make when using English articles, examining these errors from the perspectives of both noun types and noun phrase environments, and considering the role of first language transfer.

University English as a foreign language (EFL) programs often pressure instructors and teachers to use generic, globally published EFL textbooks for reasons more socio-political than pedagogical (Chang, 2009). Considering instructors and students need to make the best of matters in EFL under those circumstances, the present study proposes a framework that echoes Fox (2004) arguments that a curriculum is a rhetorical accomplishment. The discursivity to which Fox (2004) refers can be conceptually amalgamated in a term: curricularivity. Curricularivity is additionally informed by arguments supporting critical approaches to EFL learning (i.e., Canagarajah, 2016; Kumaravadivelu, 1999, 2006). The approach, aimed at finding a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC), encourages reflexive praxis rooted in one’s beliefs, assumptions, and knowledge (BAK) about language teaching (Banes, Martínez, Athanases, & Wong, 2016; Meschede, Fiebranz, Möller & Steffensky, 2017; Pennycook, 2008; Woods, 1996) that any EFL instructor can use for their respective classes. The “zone” was inspired by Rogan’s (2007) Zone of Feasible Innovation in curriculum and Vygotsky’s (1978) Zone of Proximal Development. In the context of Korean, university EFL courses, the ZPC establishes a “level of potential development as determined through problem solving under guidance” (Vygotsky, 1978, p. 86). Instead of blindly plowing through textbook content, that often serves as the course curriculum in many EFL programs (Richards, 2001; Tomlinson & Masuhara, 2011), without concern for one’s students, who may feel culturally marginalized by lesson contents that can be counter-intuitive to their cultures (i.e., Song, 2013; Weninger & Kiss, 2013), instructors can recontextualize textbook content to raise the value of student language learning investment However, as Fredricks (2007) notes in their application of culturally relevant alterations to EFL textbook content, a systemic framework would greatly improve the reflexive praxis that most instructors do internally when negotiating textbook content in EFL classes. This study endeavors to address that gap in EFL teaching practice.

Not understanding a foreign language is the major obstacle that prevents audiences from enjoying these television programs and films. Subtitling and dubbing are the mechanisms which facilitate the interpretation of international programs and films. In the field of AVT, one of the most challenging tasks is translating animated cartoons, which can play a vital role in children’s emotional and social development and education, and have a direct influence on their cognition and behaviour (Ghilzai, Alam, Ahmad, Shaukat, & Noor, 2017). Throughout the course of translation, as different new areas are drawn into sharp focus, identities are lost, allowing ways for new ones. This is why translators take strong caution when approaching subjects that are considered unacceptable like religion, humour, and taboos that often constitute a major challenge for translators. Those subjects are discussed thoroughly in this paper. In this study, the researchers have classified cultural constraints into three categories, namely, religious remarks, jokes and humour of proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks in this paper refer to any unacceptable offensive religious reference that has been included in Family Guy. Jokes and humour of proper nouns refer to cross-cultural names that have been used in a humorous context. This paper also investigates taboos, which can be defined as immoral or explicit content that is deemed inappropriate by the target audience. According to Allan (2001, p. 148), “tabooed words are those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent when used in certain contexts” The reason behind this classification is that religion might be the number one red zone for almost all societies and cultures. The followers of a particular religion do not tolerate mockery or disdain of their beliefs nor invading the sacredness of their religion. Therefore, when a popular television show provokes the audience by offending their religion for creating controversy, the translator shall avoid rendering such provocative utterances by resorting to one of the translation strategies. The second category, jokes and humour of proper nouns, shows how a translator can deliver an item that is well known to the source culture but not the target culture, without losing the humorous effect. The third category, taboos, is included owing to the fact that the explicit rendition of taboos often comes as shocking and unpleasant, let alone that conveying an idea that is acceptable by a particular society to a more conservative one might taint the identity and customs of it. The purpose of this study is to investigate and identify the strategies translators opted for while subtitling cultural constraints in an American animated sitcom, Family Guy, into Arabic. M1-RRIn tone languages, pitch is not merely a paralinguistic embellishment but a phonemic property that distinguishes lexical and grammatical meaning. A small change in the pitch of a word can result in an entirely different meaning, so that speakers rely on pitch height and contour to interpret one another correctly (Agawu, 1988; Chan, 1987). M2-QRThis centrality of pitch raises a question that has intrigued linguists and ethnomusicologists for nearly a century: what happens to linguistic tone when words are sung? Because melody imposes its own pitch trajectory upon a text, singers face a potential conflict between the requirements of the language and the requirements of the tune. A logical question for those who document tone languages, then, is whether singers preserve linguistic tone when they sing and, if so, to what degree. M1-RRStudies addressing this so-called tone-tune relationship have produced strikingly inconsistent, sometimes contradictory, results. Some investigations report a high degree of correspondence between the direction of linguistic tone and the direction of melodic movement (Mendenhall, 1975; Leben, 1983; Chan, 1987; Schellenberg, 2009; Morey, 2009; Ketkaew & Pittayaporn, 2014; Lissoir & Démolin, 2015), while others find that tone and tune are only minimally related or even unrelated (Agawu, 1988; List, 1961). Still others report mixed findings in which some songs closely reflect linguistic tone while other songs in the same language do not (Herzog, 1934; Richards, 1972; Tanese-Ito, 1988). A recurring explanation for this variability is musical genre: songs whose primary function is to convey meaning tend to preserve tone, whereas songs whose primary function is aesthetic or ceremonial appear to permit greater deviation from spoken pitch (List, 1961; Schellenberg, 2009). M2-QRYet the evidence for such a genre effect rests on comparatively small corpora, and researchers have cautioned that broad generalizations remain premature (Schellenberg, 2009). Perhaps more importantly, the very meaning of a reported percentage of tone-tune 'matching' is unclear, since the literature has never established what threshold of correspondence would be required for a song to remain intelligible to native speakers. Much of this uncertainty may stem from the methods that have been used. M1-RRThe dominant approach compares the directionality of linguistic tone transitions to the directionality of note transitions in a musical score, tallying agreements and disagreements and reporting percentages of correspondence (List, 1961; Richards, 1972; Chan, 1987; Agawu, 1988; Ketkaew & Pittayaporn, 2014). Such directionality comparisons treat note transitions and tone transitions as though they belong to a single commensurable domain. M2-GapHowever, if a musical notation fails to capture significant movements in the fundamental frequency of a sung performance, the method will manufacture apparent mismatches that do not reflect what singers actually produce. M1-RRRefinements to this basic procedure, including the analysis of downdrift and tone sandhi (Leben, 1983) and the treatment of contour tones as decomposable sequences of level tones (Ketkaew & Pittayaporn, 2014; Proto, 2016), have shown that different methods applied to the same data can yield opposing conclusions. M2-CTThis methodological sensitivity motivates a comparison of procedures rather than reliance on any single approach. M2-GapA further gap concerns the languages that have been studied. The overwhelming majority of tone-tune investigations have focused on Asian and African languages. For the Otomanguean family of Mesoamerica, there exists only one study, Pike's (1939) brief qualitative abstract on a song in an unspecified variety of Mixtec, in which he concluded that the melody was largely independent of linguistic tone and that Spanish loanwords appeared to influence the tonal melody more than native words did. The acquisition of vocabulary through spoken input has attracted growing interest in recent years, yet it remains substantially less well understood than vocabulary learning through reading. A recurring finding in the literature is that gains from listening tend to be lower than those from reading (Vidal, 2011), and that listening may primarily develop earlier-acquired aspects of vocabulary knowledge such as form recognition. How much learners gain, however, may depend on their level of proficiency, whether general proficiency, prior vocabulary knowledge, or listening proficiency specifically. Existing vocabulary knowledge might be expected to shape learning through spoken input, given that vocabulary breadth correlates with listening comprehension, yet findings across studies have been contradictory, partly because the relationship between vocabulary knowledge and listening is more complex than that between vocabulary knowledge and reading, with learners drawing on factors beyond word knowledge when interpreting speech. Vocabulary learning during listening can also be enhanced through a lexical focus-on-form approach (Laufer, 2005), in which the salience of items is heightened to increase noticing (Schmidt, 1990) and involvement load (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001). Different forms of teacher explanation—including second-language, codeswitched, and contrastive crosslinguistic explanations (Kroll & Stewart, 1994; Jiang, 2002)—may prompt differing degrees of processing and hence learning. A small number of studies have examined how such explanations interact with learner proficiency, but they have treated proficiency as a categorical rather than continuous variable, losing potentially subtle variance, and have paid little attention to school settings. Consequently, the role of proficiency and its interaction with explanation type remains unclear. Returning to data from Zhang and Graham (2019), the present study therefore examined how preexisting vocabulary knowledge and listening proficiency, treated as continuous predictors, interact with test time points and four types of vocabulary explanation among Chinese secondary-school learners of English.

M1-RRFoster and Skehan (1996) conceptualised accuracy as the relative absence of errors and grammatical complexity as the use of progressively more elaborate language and a greater variety of syntactic patterning, associating complexity with growth and change in the interlanguage system and accuracy with control at a given developmental point. M2-QRInvestigating how these dimensions behave as proficiency increases has therefore become a fruitful, though far from settled, line of enquiry. Despite a substantial body of work, findings on L2 writing development remain notably inconclusive. Some studies report gradual improvement in holistic scores and in accuracy and complexity as proficiency rises (e.g. Larsen-Freeman, 2006), whereas others fail to detect such gains, observing improvement only in fluency or holistic ratings. Equally, the pattern of error development is contested: while certain studies suggest a broadly linear reduction of errors, others describe non-linear trajectories characterised by stabilisation and even regression. These divergent results indicate that the relationship between proficiency and written accuracy and complexity is more intricate than a simple linear model would predict. Analogical reasoning is a fundamental aspect of human cognition, allowing us to transfer knowledge from a familiar situation to a novel one (Gentner et al., 2001). In the domain of natural language processing, analogies of the form "A is to B as C is to D" have proven to be a fruitful framework for reasoning about the relations between words. When these relations concern the different inflected forms of a word—such as write is to writes as watch is to watches—the task becomes one of morphological relational reasoning, in which the aim is to predict an inflected target word given a query word and a demonstration of the relevant morphological transformation. Understanding and modelling word inflection is central to the processing of morphologically rich languages, where a single lemma may correspond to a large number of distinct surface forms. The problem of solving morphological analogies on words has a long history. Lepage (1998) proposed an influential rule-based algorithm that computes the changes in prefixes, infixes, and suffixes between a pair of demonstration words and then applies the same operations to a query word to derive its target form. Related algebraic formulations treat analogical learning as a two-step process of establishing a mapping between a memorised situation and a new situation and then transferring the corresponding knowledge (Yvon, 1997). Such approaches are elegant and require no training data, but they are limited in generality: because they essentially copy affixes, they struggle when the query word follows a different inflectional pattern from the demonstration, and they cannot easily accommodate the orthographic and phonological alternations that pervade natural language morphology. A closely related family of tasks is morphological inflection and reinflection, which received considerable attention through the 2016 and 2017 SIGMORPHON shared tasks (Cotterell et al., 2016a, 2017). In these tasks, a word is transformed into a target form that is specified by an explicit enumeration of morphological features encoding number, gender, case, tense, aspect, and so on. Following early rule-based systems (Koskenniemi, 1984) and learned string transducers, this area has recently been dominated by character-level neural network models (Faruqui et al., 2016; Kann & Schütze, 2016). Character-based modelling brings important advantages: the vocabulary is reduced to a small finite alphabet, out-of-vocabulary words are essentially eliminated, distributional properties of both frequent and rare words can be captured (Luong & Manning, 2016), and no tokenisation is required. Because they operate at the subword level, such models are particularly well suited to tasks that demand an awareness of morphology. A quite different perspective on word relations comes from the word-embedding literature, where analogies have been used both to demonstrate and to evaluate the quality of learned representations (Mikolov et al., 2013a, 2013b). The famous observation that vector arithmetic over embeddings can recover analogous relations gave rise to benchmarks for syntactic analogies, and later work sought to inject morphological structure into embeddings directly (Cotterell & Schütze, 2015). However, word-level embedding approaches inherit a fixed vocabulary, require large amounts of unsupervised training data, and are expensive to query, since a prediction is obtained by comparing a computed vector against every word in the vocabulary. Despite this substantial body of work, an important gap remains. Existing solutions to morphological transformation tasks either rely on rigid rules that cannot generalise across differing inflectional patterns, or they depend on the availability of an explicit set of morphological tags describing the desired target form. Such tag inventories are not always available, and they presuppose that the relevant morphological categories have already been analysed. What has received little attention is a feature-free approach that infers the intended transformation implicitly, from a single demonstration pair, while at the same time generalising robustly across the varied inflectional patterns and orthographic and phonological regularities found in real languages. To address this gap, we present the Neural morphological analogy system (NMAS), a character-based recurrent neural network for morphological relational reasoning. Rather than being supplied with explicit morphological features, the model is given a demo pair (such as write:writes) that implicitly specifies a relation, together with a query word, and it must predict the target form. The architecture employs three separate encoders—two sharing weights to encode the demonstration relation and one to encode the query—and a single attention-based decoder that generates the target as a raw character sequence. We evaluate the model on five typologically diverse languages: English, Finnish, German, Russian, and Swedish. Our experiments show that the exact target form can be predicted with high accuracy, reaching 94.85% for English and consistently outperforming rule-based and embedding-based baselines. Crucially, the model is not limited to copying affixes: it generalises to words with varying inflectional patterns, learns disentangled internal representations of the morphological relations without any explicit tag supervision, and can abstract away from the orthographic surface to the level of morphological form.

Academic writing is widely acknowledged as one of the most important and enduring means of communicating knowledge within the academic community. It is a central concern in higher education, where the quality of students' written work not only demonstrates the acquisition of new knowledge but also determines their standing and identity within discipline-specific discourse communities (Zhu, 2004; Rahman & Rahim, 2016). As students progress through university, the communicative expectations placed upon them shift, requiring them to move from general academic tasks to more specialised, discipline-specific writing (Nesi & Gardner, 2012). This trajectory is particularly demanding for Malaysian students transitioning from secondary school to higher learning institutions, many of whom study at international branch campuses where English is the medium of instruction. The acquisition of academic writing skills is a challenging endeavour, especially for second language (L2) writers. Academic writing is an elaborated and grammatically complex form of discourse, produced under carefully planned and edited conditions (Staples, Egbert, Biber, & Gray, 2016), and it requires students to advance their own ideas within a framework of disciplinary knowledge (Hyland, 2002). For ESL students, difficulties stem not only from inadequate English language proficiency but also from a lack of experience with formal writing and an incomplete understanding of academic writing conventions and expectations (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015; Zhu, 2004). International students, in particular, have been shown to negotiate new academic writing conventions with considerable tension and apprehension (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). These challenges are compounded by cognitive and metacognitive demands, as well as by the affective dimensions of self-concept and confidence that shape learners' engagement with writing (Adi Badiozaman, 2015). In response to such challenges, many foreign university branch campuses in Malaysia make it compulsory for students to undertake academic literacy units, such as Reading for Academic Purposes or Academic Writing (AW), in order to equip them with the language, reading and writing skills required for tertiary study. Despite the ubiquitousness of these units, surprisingly little is known about their actual effectiveness. Studies investigating the development of academic writing have yielded mixed findings; while some report gains following explicit strategy instruction (Zhang, 2013), others have found no significant improvement despite students completing English for Academic Purposes or writing-intensive courses. Research examining the improvements L2 learners make in their academic writing within an L2 medium setting remains few and far between, and this scarcity provides the impetus for the present study. This longitudinal, mixed methods study aims to address this gap by exploring the effectiveness of an AW unit at an international branch campus of an Australian university in Malaysia. Specifically, it seeks to investigate (i) students' self-concept in academic writing, (ii) the perceived impact of the AW unit on their writing development, and (iii) the transferability of the skills acquired to other academic units. This paper reports on the first, quantitative phase of the study, drawing on questionnaire data gathered from undergraduates who had completed one semester of the unit. In doing so, the study aims to disclose the challenges these students face and to inform a more objective and grounded approach to the pedagogy of academic writing in L2 settings.

The development of the notion of communicative competence in the language testing and evaluation field has had a great impact on theories of second language (L2) learning in the past decades. This concept not only refers to individuals’ underlying knowledge of grammatical and structural forms of language (Chomsky, 1965), but also to their capacity in using this insight in real conversations (Hymes, 1972). This move from mastery of mechanical aspects of language to the mastery of functionally or pragmatically appropriate language use, greatly influenced the development of theories and models of communicative proficiency in the field of language learning and assessment (e.g. Bachman, 1990; Bachman and Palmer, 1996, 2010; Canale, 1983; Canale & Swain, 1980; Celce-Murcia et al., 1995). Within various frameworks of communicative language ability, pragmatic capacity is a core ability that learners of a new language require to acquire. Pragmatic capacity is mainly about how meaning is created and understood in a specific context (Bachman & Palmer, 2010). In fact, it is the study of actions performed intentionally by individuals for some purposes, and it encompasses individuals’ beliefs, opinions, intentions, and actions (Thomas, 1995). That is, it is not the words, speakers, or even hearers that are responsible for creating or conveying meanings, per se; rather meaning is constantly negotiated, in a dynamic interaction, between speakers, hearers, and the context of interaction. In pragmatics, the focus is on meaning, particularly, on the functional aspect of language whereby language use is described as a form of social behavior that people exhibit through their utterances. Due to the significance of pragmatic knowledge in the flourishing of interactive language ability of language learners, many research studies have been centered upon speech acts comprehension and production (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Felix-Brasdefer, 2007; Matsumura, 2001, 2003; Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). Equally important in the realm of pragmatics is the investigation of implicit meaning or implicature Despite this importance, a few researchers have examined L2 comprehension of conversational implicatures (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2010; Tagouchi 2002, 2005, 2007). Implicature as a notion refers the functional aspect of language; it identifies how individuals comprehend meanings that are not stated in an explicit way in their speech (Archer et al., 2012; Levinson, 1983; Verschueren, 1999). In fact, implicature is produced as a result of interlocutors' interpretations and it conveys meanings beyond the surface structure of the utterances (Archer et al., 2012). Identifying the gap between surface and deep meaning, when comprehending implied meanings, creates a major difficulty for learners of a second or foreign language. This is due to the fact that factors such as cultural background, L2 exposure, implicature type, and general L2 proficiency influence learners’ comprehension (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2010; Tagouchi 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013). Studies on implicature comprehension (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2010; Tagouchi 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013) have largely contributed to the field of second language learning. However their approach to the notion of conversational implicature has not been adequate and comprehensive enough, particularly, with regard to matters such as the type of the instruments used, the construct, and its subtypes. Moreover, it has been argued that face management is one of the major factors responsible for violating the maxim of relevance. Nevertheless, as far as the available literature shows, no empirical research study has systematically set out to develop and validate an original instrument that tests conversational implicature taking into account the insights from relevance maxim and face management theory. Accordingly, the present study set out to eliminate this gap through the construction and validation of an authentic measurement that test the degree to which EFL learners in Iran have developed pragmatic inferential skills in comprehending conversational implicature used in every day spoken English

In the Indonesian educational landscape, English holds the status of a foreign language, learned in classrooms rather than acquired through everyday communicative exchange. This position gives English learning in Indonesia a particular character: students master the language not only as a means of communication but, in the case of prospective teachers, as a subject that must eventually be taught to others. The importance of equipping English Education students with strong literacy skills is therefore considerable, since the quality of future EFL teachers is closely tied to the quality of their own reading and writing competence. As Mappiasse and Sihes (2014) have argued, improving the marketability and readiness of prospective EFL teachers depends on strengthening the role of English within the curriculum. Understanding how these students respond to learning basic reading and writing skills is thus central to improving instruction at the tertiary level. Reading and writing occupy an intertwined place in the development of English literacy. Reading provides learners with the background knowledge and exposure to varied text types that shape their overall image of themselves as literate users of the language (Kuhn & Rasinski, 2009). Effective reading, however, draws on the interaction of cognitive, psychological and ecological components (Joshi & Aaron, 2011), and requires learners to develop both language knowledge and general comprehension skills (Grabe, 2004). Writing, by contrast, is a more complex undertaking, demanding control of grammar, syntax, coherence and mechanics (Ibnian, 2011), together with sustained practice and feedback (Salma, 2015; Zaman & Azad, 2012). Because the amount of reading a learner does directly influences the quality of their writing, the two skills reinforce one another within the growth of a student's literacy. A growing body of research has examined how Indonesian and other EFL learners respond to English and its constituent skills. Muliawati (2017) found that senior high school students in Banda Aceh differed markedly in their attitudes toward English depending on their academic stream, suggesting that internal conditions strongly influence learner motivation. Sukandi and Sani (2017) similarly reported that university students prefer some skills over others, with reading emerging as the most desirable skill among learners of academic essay writing. Taguchi et al. (2004) further demonstrated that fluency alone does not guarantee successful reading, underscoring that the development of literacy is a gradual and ongoing process. Together, these studies indicate that EFL learners hold varied and skill-specific preferences that carry implications for classroom instruction. Despite these contributions, relatively little research has captured, in a single study, how EFL students in Indonesian higher education respond to the specific experience of learning basic reading and basic writing side by side. Much of the existing work addresses either reading or writing in isolation, or focuses on secondary-level learners, leaving the responses of tertiary English Education students to the combined learning of these foundational skills insufficiently documented. What preferences these students hold, which text types they read, which linguistic aspects they find most difficult, and what strategies they adopt when facing difficulties remain questions that merit closer empirical attention in this context. The present study addresses this gap by surveying the responses of 120 students enrolled in Writing 1 and Reading 2 courses in the English Education Study Program of STKIP PGRI Sumatera Barat. Using a questionnaire administered to the whole population, the research investigates students' skill preferences, their reading material choices, the aspects of reading and writing they find most difficult, and the strategies they use when encountering difficult words. The findings offer a contextualised account of learners' responses that may inform how instructors design and support basic reading and writing instruction, and may encourage stronger motivation and richer literacy development among prospective EFL teachers.

Phraseological units in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) research have been operationalized using a range of constructs with nuanced differences in definitional criteria, such as lexical bundles (Biber, 2006; Biber, Conrad, & Cortes, 2004; Cortes, 2013), formulas (Simpson-Vlach & Ellis, 2010), and phrase-frames (Fletcher, 2002e2007), among others. Research with these constructs has yielded pedagogically useful lists of fully lexically instantiated (e.g., lexical bundles, formulas) and nearly fully lexically instantiated (e.g., phrase-frames) multi-word expressions. However, these widely studied constructs have been criticized for structural incompleteness (Liu, 2012) and separation of structurally and functionally similar patterns. More importantly, schematic patterns with high lexical variance (e.g., patterns with two or more open lexical slots) have been left unexamined with these operationalizations. From the perspective of usage-based construction grammar, schematic patterns are at least as important as lexically instantiated patterns in language processing, use and learning (Goldberg, 1995, 2006; Bybee, 2010; See Section 1.3 for a discussion of the similarities and differences between constructions and schematic patterns). In this theoretical framework, language is seen as an inventory of constructions, defined as form-meaning/function pairings, and language learning is in essence a piecemeal, frequency-biased process of accumulating these constructions (Bybee, 2013; Ellis, Romer, € & O’Donnell, 2016). Schematic patterns constitute a crucial part of language knowledge as they create “an important top-down component to the process of linguistic communication” (Ellis, 2003, p. 67) and carry constructional meanings independent of lexical meanings. Biber et al. (2004) argued that “the overall importance of multi-word units in discourse can be fully understood only by undertaking empirical research studies from different perspectives” (p. 372). The need for more perspectives on multi-word sequences was also indicated in the fact that researchers often used multiple constructs of phraseology in their analysis. For example, Stubbs (2007) examined “n-grams” (“a recurrent string of uninterrupted word-forms”), “phrase-frames” (“an ngram with one variable slot”), and “PoS-grams” (“a string of part of speech categories”) in his corpus investigation of phraseological units (pp. 90e91) In a similar vein, the current study aims to examine the potential of a complementary approach, the pattern grammar approach (Ellis et al., 2016; Hunston & Francis, 2000; Hunston & Su, 2019; Perek & Patten, 2019), to the analysis of schematic multi-word units. Grammar patterns are more schematic than lexical bundles, formulas, and phraseframes, as they contain more than one open lexical slot (e.g., N1 of N2 vs. the end of the road or the end of the N), but less schematic than PoS-grams, as they specify some lexical items in the pattern (e.g., N1 of N2 vs. NOUN PREPOSITION NOUN). This study investigates the use of the N1 of N2 pattern in written academic discourse, defined by the corpus-based Collins COBUILD Grammar Patterns (Francis, Hunston, & Manning, 1996, 1998) as consisting of a noun phrase followed by the preposition of and another noun phrase, regardless of the number of articles, adjectives, and other linguistic elements within the pattern (e.g., the focus of this research, the rapidly growing field of second language, etc.). A number of corpus-based studies (Biber et al., 2004; Francis, Hunston, & Manning, 1998, 1996; Hyland, 2008; Lu, Yoon, & Kisselev, 2018) have lent evidence to the pervasiveness of the N1 of N2 pattern in academic discourse, indicating the importance of a systematic examination of this pattern.

THE IMPORTANCE OF LISTENING comprehension ability in second language (L2) learning is uncontroversial given the current pedagogical emphasis on achieving communica- tive competence. Such approaches to language teaching underscore the need to practice listen- ing skills with the main goal of comprehension, which is usually operationalized in terms of per- formance on a test. Vandergrift and Goh (2012) explained that this view of listening as a product predominates most language classrooms today but does not take into account the importance of “teaching them [learners] how to process and manage input” (p. 13). The product approach to listening comprehension, perhaps, reflects our lack of understanding of this construct. Indeed, historically speaking, scant attention has been di- rected toward defining listening comprehension and empirically testing variables (e.g., learner or text related) assumed to facilitate or hin- der the process of L2 listening comprehension (Vandergrift & Baker, 2015). Numerous factors are argued to influence the difficulty of L2 listening (e.g., Bloomfield et al., 2010; Imhof & Janusik, 2006), such as passage characteristics (e.g., length of passage, linguistic complexity, speed of speech), listener charac- teristics (e.g., second language proficiency, first language [L1] listening ability, prior knowledge), and listening contexts or testing conditions (e.g., formal or informal real-life listening, time limi- tations, number of exposure times). However, as pointed out by Vandergrift & Goh (2012), while “knowledge of these factors and how they hinder or facilitate successful comprehension is impor- tant for informed teaching of L2 listening ( ...) there is still very little research to provide empiri- cal evidence for a causal relationship” (p. 57). The present study thus seeks to contribute to the L2 listening strand of research by empirically exam- ining the impact of two passage characteristics— speech rate and utterance length—and one listener characteristic—L2 oral proficiency—on the listening comprehension of Spanish as a second language. In doing so, we provide recom- mendations to best inform pedagogical practices on developing L2 listening skills and materials.

M1-CCAffective variables have long been recognised to play a crucial role in the process of learning a second language (L2). Over the last decades, emotional aspects such as Foreign Language Anxiety (FLA) have been the focus of much debate. Specifically, this affective factor is thought to be a major obstacle to learning and production of the target language) (Horwitz, 2001; Krashen, 1985; Pavlenko, 2011; Phillips, 1992), regardless of the language teaching methodology (see Liu, 2013). M1-RRHorwitz et al. Those authors highlight the distinctive feature of FLA as a situation-specific type of anxiety associated with L2 learning contexts MacIntyre (1999: 27) described FLA as the “worry and negative emotional reaction aroused when learning or using a second language”. This emotional state may interfere with production of the new language causing apprehension, nervousness, worry, and tension related to L2 learning (MacIntyre & Gardner, 1994, 1991). Thus, many research studies provide evidence of a significant negative correlation between FLA and L2 achievement) (Horwitz, 2001; Onwuegbuzie, Bailey & Daley, 2000; Williams & Andrade, 2008). According to researchers, foreign language classroom situations are especially anxiety-provoking contexts due to their interactive nature (Yang, 2012). In fact, although FLA has been linked to different language skills, oral production is viewed as the greatest source of anxiety in the L2 classroom mainly due to students’ fears to communicate publicly by means of a language they do not master completely (Aida, 1994; Choi, 2016; Horwitz et al., 1986; MacIntyre & Gardner, 1991; Mak, 2011; Matsuda & Gobel, 2004; Park, 2014; Woodrow, 2006; Young, 1992). According to Pellegrino (2005: 7), “to learn another language is to redefine yourself publicly, socially, and personally.” In the same vein, some authors point out that the difficulties experienced at trying to express themselves in the L2 may challenge students’ self-concept and identity as competent speakers, which can easily result in worry and frustration (Ortega-Cebreros, 2003; Schumann, 1978). Thus, although some studies have suggested that FLA may have a positive effect on language learning, drawing a distinction between beneficial/ facilitating vs. inhibitory/ debilitating anxiety (Bailey, 1995; Dörnyei, 2005; Spielman & Radnofsky, 2001), most researchers report the detrimental or debilitating effects of FLA (Cheng, Horwitz & Shallert, 1999; Horwitz, 2001). These latter effects can manifest in many different ways such as avoidance behaviour (e.g. arriving late, avoiding participating in the classroom or interacting, skipping classes), face-saving (e.g. joking) or minor physical symptoms (e.g. sweating, headaches, etc.) (see Gregersen, 2007; Horwitz & Young, 1991). FLA is, therefore, believed to hinder learning and affect the efficiency of language learning (Onwuegbuzie et al., 2000). Horwitz et al., (1986) designed the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS) to measure the level of anxiety of L2 learners while learning the target language in the context of the classroom. The FLCAS has been extensively used in language anxiety studies across different disciplines (i.e. psychology, education, applied linguistics, etc.) due to its high reliability and validity (see Aida, 1994; Arnaiz & Guillén, 2012, 2013; Choi, 2016; Kruk, 2018; Mak, 2011; Park, 2014; Park & French, 2013; Rodríguez & Abreu, 2003). The scale deals with general foreign language anxiety although it especially highlights speaking and listening skills. According to these authors, FLA can be associated with three main interrelated types of anxiety: communication apprehension, test anxiety and fear of negative evaluation. Communication apprehension is described as fear about communication with people or in front of others. Apparently, the lack of proficiency in the L2 can lead to anxiety, frustration and self-consciousness in some learners. Test anxiety refers to fear of failure or failing in tests. Test-anxious students tend to feel constantly evaluated and are usually afraid of making mistakes. Finally, fear of negative evaluation is related to learners’ worry about peoples’ negative judgement or evaluations. In order to reduce the possibility of obtaining negative evaluations from their teachers or classmates, anxious students may avoid interacting in the L2, which prevents them from improving and developing their oral communication skills in the L2 (Arnaiz & Guillén, 2012; Gregersen, 2007). Therefore, these three main interrelated factors negatively affect the learning of the L2 (Horwitz et al., 1986). The globalized spread of English has made textbooks central artifacts in English as a foreign language (EFL) education, particularly in expanding circle communities where globally published materials dominate university programs (Kachru, 1992; Richards, 2001). These textbooks are frequently adopted for reasons that are more socio-political than pedagogical, and instructors and students in Korean post-secondary programs are often pressured to use them by their departments (Chang, 2009; Song, 2013). As pedagogical artifacts, textbooks carry a legitimacy conferred by the very adjective 'school,' validating the social norms they project (Curdt-Christiansen & Weninger, 2015). Critical applied linguists have long argued that what passes for knowledge in such materials is ideologically founded and can 'other' non-inner-circle learners, marginalizing their cultures and harming their educational experience (Canagarajah, 2016; Pennycook, 2008; Song, 2013). A growing body of work has examined how culture and ideology are represented in EFL textbooks, and some scholars have called for more dynamic, semiotic approaches to understanding how learners engage with texts and images (Weninger & Kiss, 2013). Yet while multimodal discourse has been recognized as an under-appreciated source of dominant social narratives, few studies have investigated how these narratives are negotiated 'in situ' in the classroom. Existing frameworks tend to analyze the textbook as a static object rather than as content actively reconstructed by instructors drawing on their beliefs, assumptions, and knowledge (Woods, 1996) and their understanding of curricular commonplaces (Fox, 2004). To address this gap, the present study proposes a two-step model for achieving a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC), which requires instructors to understand both the curricular commonplaces of their EFL program and the power and ideologies within the multimodal discourse of their textbooks. Demonstrated through vignettes of two EFL courses at Chung-Buk National University in Korea, this study asks: Does an instructor's understanding of curricular commonplaces and of ideologies in multimodal textbook discourse appear to help them achieve a ZPC, and how do their students respond?

Over the past few decades, English has become the world's foremost contact language, used more often between speakers who do not share a first language than between native speakers themselves. This demographic shift, driven by globalisation and the deepening interconnectedness of contemporary social life, has fundamentally transformed the way English is used and conceptualised (Dewey 2007). Where speakers of different linguistic and cultural backgrounds meet, English functions as a lingua franca (ELF), and this use has grown from a minority interest within applied linguistics into a major field of study in its own right (Jenkins 2012). Central to the ELF perspective is the recognition that English used in lingua franca interactions is not a deficient version of native English (ENL) but a legitimate form of communication occupying its own space, one that is neither English as a foreign language nor failed native English (Jenkins 2006). Since the pioneering work of Firth (1996), ELF scholars have sought to describe the phenomenon empirically, arguing that ELF must be well grounded in systematic description in order to gain acceptance as a legitimate variety (Jenkins 2009). Research has revealed patterns of change and linguistic fluidity emerging across all levels of language, including phonology, pragmatics, and morphosyntax (Jenkins et al. 2011, Cogo 2010). One of the most significant insights to emerge from this body of work is that many of the deviations from ENL norms observed among ELF users are not errors resulting from inadequate knowledge, but principled adjustments motivated by the pragmatic demands of communication. Cogo and Dewey (2006), for instance, demonstrated how pragmatic or functional motives such as efficiency, added prominence, and the exploitation of redundancy can lead to lexico-grammatical innovation, revealing an intimate interrelationship between pragmatics and morphosyntax. Similarly, Ranta (2006) showed that ELF speakers extend the use of the progressive aspect for expressive purposes, drawing on the 'attractiveness' of its form and meaning rather than misapplying a rule. Within Asia, where the numbers of English users have grown exponentially and where distinct varieties continue to develop, questions of proficiency and norm have become especially pressing (Bolton 2008). Thailand offers a productive site for such inquiry. Although the country has no official second language and its population is overwhelmingly Thai-speaking, English serves as the de facto second language and is used across a wide range of domains including business, tourism, and higher education. As a member of ASEAN, which has adopted English as its official working language, Thailand relies on English as a lingua franca linking it culturally, intellectually, and commercially with its neighbours and the wider world. Given this status, it is reasonable to expect that identifiable features of ELF used by Thai speakers will emerge, and a study of this group promises to reveal both features particular to Thai users and broader characteristics of the nature of ELF communication. Despite the growing interest in the morphosyntax of ELF, relatively little attention has been paid to how proficient Thai users handle specific grammatical systems, and even less to why they deviate from ENL norms when they do. Verbal inflectional suffixes provide a revealing test case because they carry information that is frequently redundant, being recoverable through other means, yet they remain heavily emphasised in traditional L2 pedagogy, which treats grammatical accuracy as central to success (Dewey 2014). Following the principle that ELF description should be drawn from communication between proficient users so that systematic patterns can be identified (Cogo & Dewey 2006, Jenkins 2009), the present study examines the academic writing of advanced and upper-intermediate Thai English-major students. It focuses on three suffixes: the third person singular present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing. The study addresses two questions: in what ways do Thai ELF learners deviate from ENL norms in their use of these three suffixes, and what linguistic and functional causes underlie these deviations? By analysing the circumstances in which learners omit the tense suffixes and extend the meaning of the progressive, this study aims to determine whether such deviations constitute emerging ELF features, to clarify the relationship between morphosyntax and pragmatics, and to draw out implications for the teaching of English in international settings, where distinguishing core features from unproblematic variants is of considerable pedagogical value (Seidlhofer 2005).

In the field of applied linguistics and English language teaching, evaluation constitutes an integral component of effective teaching and learning. Traditionally, the responsibility for evaluating language performance has rested primarily with the teacher, who assigns grades, provides feedback, and determines whether learners have achieved the goals set out in a course. Increasingly, however, scholars have recognised that involving learners themselves in the evaluation of their own performance can transform the way learning takes place. Self-evaluation, as an alternative form of assessment grounded in the critical applied linguistics perspective, has attracted considerable attention as a means of empowering learners rather than suppressing them, of encouraging them to think and learn more, and of underpinning their development as autonomous and lifelong learners. Within English as a foreign language (EFL) writing in particular, self-evaluation offers a promising route through which students can identify where they stand in their writing development and take greater responsibility for their own learning. A substantial body of research has emphasised the value of engaging students in assessment processes. Rust et al. (2003) demonstrated that student learning can be improved significantly, and durably, when students are helped to understand assessment criteria and the assessment process through structured intervention. Brown and Harris (2013) similarly highlighted the importance of self-assessment in empowering students to identify their strengths and areas for growth, while later work (Brown, 2016) situated self-assessment within a broader consideration of the human and social conditions that shape how assessment is experienced. In the context of second language writing specifically, Lee (2017) has examined how classroom writing assessment and feedback can be reconceived to support learners more effectively. Together, these studies suggest that self-evaluation may function not merely as a measurement device but as a genuine learning tool, particularly when it operates alongside teacher feedback and a clear understanding of evaluation criteria (Sambell et al., 2013). Despite this growing interest, there has been comparatively little empirical research on students' self-evaluation of task-based writing performance, and fewer studies still that examine how self-evaluation aligns with teacher evaluation in authentic classroom settings. Much of the existing work has been conducted in Western higher education or in nursing and general education contexts, and questions remain about how self-evaluation operates among adult EFL learners in Asian contexts. In Thailand, where English-medium graduate study places substantial demands on students' academic writing (OECD/UNESCO, 2016), it is unclear whether adult learners are able to evaluate their own writing performance in ways that correspond meaningfully with a teacher's judgement, or how both learners and teachers experience the practice of self-evaluation within a writing course. If students are able to evaluate their own performance more or less in accordance with the teacher's evaluation, important questions arise concerning what is actually being evaluated and how the criteria for assessing writing are understood on both sides. These gaps warrant closer investigation, especially given the potential of self-evaluation to foster the autonomy and lifelong learning that graduate-level EFL programmes increasingly aim to cultivate. This study therefore sets out to investigate how Thai adult learners self-evaluate their English writing performance in relation to their teacher's evaluation, and what both the students and the teacher experience from the self-evaluation practice. Specifically, the research addresses three questions: how closely students' self-evaluations of their writing tasks correspond with the teacher's evaluation; how self-evaluation relates to students' satisfaction with particular writing skills; and what views and experiences students and their teacher hold regarding the use of self-evaluation to develop writing ability. To pursue these questions, the study draws on data from 32 Thai graduate students and one experienced Thai EFL writing teacher, collected through students' self-evaluation and teacher's evaluation forms, two writing tasks, and individual interviews, with qualitative and quantitative data considered together to gain a comprehensive picture of the issue under investigation. In addressing these aims, the study offers insight into the extent to which adult EFL learners can serve as a valid source of information about their own writing achievement. Its findings are expected to highlight the importance of students' self-evaluation for developing the teaching of EFL writing and for promoting learners' autonomy, while drawing implications for the design of independent learning goals within graduate writing courses and pointing to directions for future research.

In academic writing, the ways in which writers position themselves in relation to their claims and to their readers have attracted considerable attention over the past decades. The linguistic resources through which writers convey stance, evaluation, and interaction have become central concerns of research on academic discourse (Biber, 2006; Hyland, 1998; Hyland & Tse, 2005). Among these resources, hedging has emerged as a particularly important object of study, since the tentative negotiation of knowledge claims lies at the heart of scientific argumentation. As Hyland (1998) has shown, the pervasive use of possibility and tentativeness in research writing is intimately connected to the social and institutional practices of academic communities, and is central to the way in which knowledge comes to be socially accredited through texts. One grammatical construction that lends itself readily to the expression of hedged stance is the extraposed that-clause, in which the heavy or more complex part of the sentence is shifted to a post-predicate position and replaced by the anticipatory pronoun it, as in It is possible that the results were misinterpreted. The impersonal form of the matrix predicate allows writers to express attitudes and epistemic judgments without overtly assuming responsibility for the claim, thereby rendering an essentially subjective evaluation more objective and formal (Biber, 2006). It is precisely this property that makes extraposition particularly convenient for hedging in academic discourse. Corpus-based research has consistently documented the more frequent use of extraposition in the academic register than in other registers, and has explored its role across a range of perspectives, including professional versus student writing (Hewings & Hewings, 2001, 2002) and the thematization of evaluative meaning through the evaluative that-clause (Hyland & Tse, 2005). Hewings and Hewings (2001) further identified several metadiscoursal functions of matrix predicates, among which hedging predominated in expert writing. Despite this rich body of work on English, cross-cultural comparisons of English extraposition with equivalent structural patterns in other languages remain rather scarce, particularly with respect to academic writing. Where such comparisons exist, they have tended to focus on a limited number of language pairs and genres. For Croatian, the situation is even less developed: the linguistic literature offers only limited descriptions of the congruent clause type, namely the declarative subject da-clause, whose matrix predicates are controlled by antecedents denoting a mental, verbal, or emotional activity (Pranjković, 2001; Silić & Pranjković, 2005). While descriptive accounts of the Croatian scientific style point to the phraseological status of such matrix predicates and to the predominantly impersonal and neutral characterization of academic writing in Croatian (Silić, 2008), empirical, corpus-based investigations of their pragmatic functions are largely missing. Consequently, little is known about how hedged stance is realized through this construction in Croatian academic prose, or about how its use compares with that of extraposed that-clauses in English. Given the structural and rhetorical congruence of the two clause types, a comparative analysis is both feasible and potentially revealing. Against this background, the present study explores the use of extraposed that-clauses in a corpus of research articles in psychology published in English-medium journals, and compares it with the use of declarative subject clauses controlled by the conjunction da in a comparable corpus of articles published in Croatian-medium journals. Specifically, the study addresses three questions: what is the frequency of the target clauses in the two corpora; how is their use distributed across the IMRAD structure of the articles; and which matrix predicates are most frequent in each corpus, and what hedging functions do they perform. To this end, the study combines corpus linguistic and qualitative methodology, drawing on Hyland's (1998) polypragmatic model of scientific hedging to interpret the contextual functions of the matrix predicates. By examining these congruent constructions cross-linguistically, the study aims to shed light on the similarities and differences in the way writers convey hedged stance in English and Croatian disciplinary writing. Beyond its descriptive contribution to the still understudied field of Croatian academic discourse, raising awareness of the rhetorical conventions governing hedged stance in cross-cultural academic writing may offer valuable implications for academic writing instruction, particularly in a non-native English context where the demands of international publishing make such awareness increasingly important.
