The rapid expansion of online and distance education has transformed the ways in which learning occurs, placing interaction at the centre of contemporary pedagogical debate. Interaction has long been recognised as a defining feature of meaningful learning, particularly within constructivist perspectives that emphasise the social genesis of knowledge and the value of engaging with the perspectives of others (Bosnot et al., 2006). From this vantage point, learning is not the passive transmission of fixed bodies of information but an active process in which learners construct knowledge through reciprocal exchanges with content, instructors, and peers. Such an understanding has become increasingly urgent as institutions of higher education move instruction online and seek to preserve, and even enhance, the interactive dimensions of the classroom (Swan, 2002). A substantial body of scholarship has examined the role of interaction in technology-mediated environments. Alavi (1994) demonstrated that computer-supported collaborative learning can produce higher levels of perceived skill development, self-reported learning, and even improved test performance compared with non-supported collaborative approaches. Subsequent work has continued to elaborate the social and interpersonal dynamics that underpin online learning (Alavi & Dufner, 2004), while Anderson et al. (2019) developed instruments to assess teaching presence within computer-conferencing contexts, drawing on the influential model of critical thinking and practical inquiry proposed by Garrison, Anderson, and Archer. Swan (2002) further underscored that building learning communities online depends fundamentally on carefully designed interaction, and Kolloff (2019) articulated concrete strategies for fostering effective student-to-student interaction in online courses. Collectively, these studies confirm that interaction is not a peripheral feature of online education but a core determinant of its quality and effectiveness. Among the theoretical accounts that seek to integrate these insights, the Online Interaction Learning Model offers a comprehensive framework grounded in constructivist learning theory. Conceived as an input-process-output model, it treats a range of moderating variables—the characteristics of courses, instructors, learners, and technology—as inputs that shape the interactive processes through which learning outcomes are generated (Benbunan-Fich et al., 2004). This model provides a structured means of understanding how the various components of an online learning environment combine to influence learners' experiences and achievement. Prior research has identified several categories that appear indispensable to any online interaction model. Endres, Chowdhury, and Frye (2009), for instance, isolated course materials, instructor performance, and access to technology as central elements, while other work has drawn attention to the importance of learning practices and student-to-student interaction (Kolloff, 2019). Building on this cumulative body of evidence, the present study conceptualises the Online Interaction Learning Model as comprising five constructs: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology. Despite the theoretical maturity of the Online Interaction Learning Model and its adoption by numerous researchers, a notable gap persists in the literature. Feedback and assessment have long been regarded as powerful tools for improving teaching and learning (Mandouit, 2018), yet there exists no validated and reliable instrument specifically designed to measure the Online Interaction Learning Model as an integrated whole. While tools have been developed to capture particular aspects of online learning, such as teaching presence (Anderson et al., 2019) or the broader Community of Inquiry framework (Garrison, Anderson & Archer, 2000), the multidimensional model that combines course-, instructor-, learner-, and technology-related factors has not been operationalised through a psychometrically sound questionnaire. In China, English language testing occupies a uniquely prominent position within the educational system. With a testing tradition that can be traced back nearly two thousand years to the imperial examination system, contemporary China administers standardized English tests to billions of learners, for whom success on these assessments frequently determines academic advancement and broader life prospects (Cheng, 2008). Among these high-stakes examinations, the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), a compulsory component of the National College Entrance Examination (commonly known as the Gaokao), is arguably the most consequential. Taken annually by millions of high school graduates seeking admission to higher education institutions, the NMET functions as a unified national placement test that distinguishes learners across the full spectrum of English proficiency (Cheng & Qi, 2006). Unlike more comprehensive admissions systems used in Western contexts, where standardized test scores are weighed alongside extracurricular records and personal statements, the Gaokao relies on a single set of examination questions to determine eligibility, a design intended to safeguard fairness and equity across a vast and socioeconomically diverse population (Farley & Yang, 2019). Beyond its selection function, the NMET has also been explicitly designed to serve as an agent for pedagogical change, aiming to promote reform in English language teaching and learning in schools (Qi, 2005, 2007). However, research on the washback of the NMET has consistently demonstrated that these dual purposes are frequently in tension. Qi (2005, 2007) found that the selection function and the intended reform function of the NMET often conflict with one another, rendering the test a powerful trigger for teaching to the test but an ineffective vehicle for the classroom changes envisioned by its designers and policymakers. Similarly, Yan (2015) documented a persistent implementation gap between the goals of curriculum reform and teachers' classroom practices, attributing this gap in large part to the pervasive backwash effect of the examination-oriented culture that dominates Chinese schooling. These studies collectively suggest that the characteristics of the NMET itself exert a profound influence over what and how students learn, making the systematic examination of the test's content a matter of considerable practical and theoretical importance. Given this influence, the reading comprehension component of the NMET warrants particular attention. Reading comprehension accounts for a substantial proportion of the total score, and the texts that students are required to process constitute a central determinant of the demands the test places on learners. According to widely accepted models of reading comprehension, the features of a text—its vocabulary load, linguistic structure, discourse organization, and genre—directly shape the representations readers construct and thereby influence comprehension outcomes (Snow, 2002; Alderson, 2000). For second language readers in particular, textual characteristics such as rhetoric, genre, and text complexity play a critical role in shaping understanding, especially among intermediate-level learners (Hornof, 2008; Guthrie, Klauda, & Ho, 2013). Text complexity, understood as the set of measurable linguistic properties of a text that can be analyzed independently of any particular reader (Mesmer, Cunningham, & Hiebert, 2012), therefore provides an especially informative lens through which to interrogate the changing demands of a high-stakes reading assessment. If the complexity of NMET reading passages has shifted over time, such shifts would carry direct implications for the expectations placed on learners, the alignment between the test and national curriculum policy, and the equity considerations that underpin the Gaokao's design. Despite the extensive scholarship on the washback and policy dimensions of the NMET, comparatively little research has systematically examined the linguistic properties of its reading passages, and even fewer studies have tracked how these properties have developed over an extended period. Recent advances in corpus linguistics and natural language processing now make it possible to measure text complexity at multiple linguistic levels with far greater precision, reliability, and comprehensiveness than traditional readability formulas or manual analysis allow (Benjamin, 2012; Crossley, Greenfield, & McNamara, 2008). A suite of freely available automated tools—including those designed to analyze lexical sophistication, lexical diversity and density, syntactic complexity, and textual cohesion—enables fine-grained, batch-processed analyses of large text collections across lexical, syntactic, and discourse dimensions. These developments open the possibility of a rigorous, longitudinal investigation into whether and how the reading demands of the NMET have evolved. The present study addresses this gap by examining the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the national version of the NMET over the past 25 years, from 1996 to 2020. Drawing on a corpus of 206 reading passages, the study measures text complexity at the lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels using established natural language processing tools and compares these measures longitudinally across the years. Specifically, the study asks how lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level text complexity have changed over this period, and it further evaluates the observed patterns against the relevant national curriculum standards and examination guidelines. By tracing the trajectory of text complexity and situating the findings within the policy context, this study aims to contribute empirical evidence to inform test design, curriculum alignment, and pedagogical practice for reading comprehension in the Chinese EFL context and beyond.

Analogical reasoning is an important part of human cognition (Gentner et al. 2001). Resolving analogies by mapping unknown data points to known analogous examples allows us to draw conclusions about the previously unseen data points. This is closely related to zero-shot and one-shot learning: strategies that are useful when training data is very limited, such as when explicit labels may not be available, or only sparsely available. In linguistics, analogies have been studied extensively, e.g. phonetic analogies (Yvon 1997) and semantic analogies (Mikolov et al. 2013a). In general, an analogy is defined as a quadruple of objects A, B, C, and D having the analogical relation: A is to B as C is to D, and the problem is to predict D given A, B, and C. In this work, we study morphological analogies where A, B, C, and D are words. The pair (A, B) represents a demo relation representing some morphological transformation between two word forms, and the problem is to transform the query word C from the source form to the target form as specified by the demo relation. The task may be illustrated with a simple example: see is to sees as eat is to what? A good solver for morphological analogies can be of practical help as writing aids for authors, suggesting synonyms in a form specified by examples rather than using explicitly specified forms. Furthermore, models that can generate words with correct inflection are important building blocks for many tasks within natural language processing. Studying how systems can learn the right abstraction to generate inflected words using limited supervision, can help us learn how to create systems for more complex language generation tasks, such as machine translation, automatic summarization, and dialogue systems. Previous work has tackled the problem of predicting the target form by identifying the string transformation (insertions, deletions, or replacements of characters) in the demo relation, and then trying to apply the same transformation to C (Lepage 1998). For instance, this algorithm correctly solves the example given above, since it just needs to add an s to the query word. However, such solutions are brittle, as they are unable to abstract away from the raw strings, failing when the given relation is realized differently in A and B than in C and D. On a basic level, the model needs to take into account phonological processes such as umlaut and vowel harmony, as well as orthographic quirks such as the rule in English that turns y into ie in certain contexts. Furthermore, an even more challenging problem is that the model will need to take into account that words belong to groups whose inflectional patterns are different – morphological paradigms. In all these cases, to be successful, a solution needs to abstract away from the raw character-based representation to a higher level representation of the relations. In this work, we propose a supervised machine learning approach to the problem of predicting the target word in a morphological analogy. The model is based on character-level recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which have recently seen much success in a number of morphological prediction tasks (Faruqui et al. 2016; Kann and Schütze 2016). This model is able to go beyond the simple string substitutions handled by previous approaches: it picks up contextual string transformations including orthograpic and phonological rules, and is able to generalize between inflection paradigms. Machine learning approaches, including character-based RNNs, have been successfully applied in several types of prediction problems in morphology, including lemmatization, inflection and reinflection (see Section 2.2). However, those tasks have either been more restricted than ours (e.g. lemmatization), or relied on an explicit enumeration of morphological features, which may not be available in all cases. In contrast, our model is a completely feature-free approach to generating inflected forms, which can predict any form in a morphological paradigm. The fact that our model does not rely on explicit features makes it applicable in scenarios with under-resourced languages where such annotations may not be available. However, since the model is trained using a weaker signal than in the traditional feature-based scenario, it needs to learn a latent representation from the analogies that play the same role as the morphological features otherwise would, making the task more challenging.

Oral fluency, the “flow, continuity, automaticity, or smoothness of speech” (Koponen & Riggenbach, 2000, p. 6), is a prime characteristic of successful language communication that has recently become central to many studies of second language acquisition (SLA). Investigating fluency helps researchers to understand how a second language (L2) is processed, produced, and acquired In addition, exploring fluency enables them to examine some abstract dimensions of SLA, including implicit knowledge, proceduralization of newly learned structures, and automatization of the processes of speech production (Loewen & Sato, 2018; Paradis, 2009; Suzuki & DeKeyser, 2017). For this reason, fluency is often examined in relation to other aspects of language processing and performance The current study belongs to this body of research in aiming to investigate the relationship between fluency and use of formulaic language. The interest in this relationship is built on psycholinguistic research evidence suggesting that use of formulaic language reduces the amount of language planning and processing, and therefore facilitates oral production (see Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018, for a review). One line of research in this area has focused on the use of multiword sequences (MWSs)—combinations of words that appear together highly frequently in a target language (Garner & Crossley, 2018)—and on its relationship with proficiency (e.g., Nattinger & DeCarrico, 1992; Pawley & Syder, 1983; Wood, 2015; Wray, 2002; see Granger, 2018, for a review). Findings suggest that more proficient L2 users have a better command of MWSs in terms of range, frequency, and sophistication (e.g., Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle & Crossley, 2015; Paquot, 2019). The findings also indicate that use of MWSs is related to oral fluency (Boers, Eyckmans, Kappel, Stengers, & Demecheleer, 2006; Stengers, Boers, Housen, & Eyckmans, 2011; Tavakoli, 2011; Wood, 2009, 2010). Although the existing research evidence highlights the relationship between fluency and MWSs, no study thus far has examined this relationship systematically across a range of assessed levels of proficiency to see if there is a linear relationship between the two. Understanding the relationship between MWSs and fluency at different levels of development is important for the study of SLA in shedding light on the processes of speech production. In addition, such knowledge can help the language testing discipline to develop a valid assessment of learner phraseological knowledge and its relationship to fluency at different levels of proficiency. The current study aimed to contribute to these areas by investigating, both quantitatively and qualitatively, the relationship between MWSs and fluency in 56 participants at four levels of proficiency assessed via the speaking paper of the Test of English for Educational Purposes (TEEP).

The proliferation of foreign television programmes across the Arab world has made audio-visual translation an increasingly significant field of enquiry. Since television screens first entered Arab homes, the subtitling and dubbing of foreign animation have grown steadily, bringing with them the need for stricter control and ethical supervision of the language that reaches viewers (Díaz Cintas, 2009). Animated series, in particular, occupy an unusual position: while animation is frequently associated with children, a substantial number of contemporary animated sitcoms are produced for adult audiences and rely heavily on satire, irony, and culturally embedded humour. This tension is significant because cartoons and animated programmes have been shown to exert considerable influence on the language and behaviour of their viewers, especially the young (Ghilzai et al., 2017). Consequently, translators working into Arabic are expected not only to transfer linguistic meaning but also to act as cultural gatekeepers who mediate between the values of the source culture and those of the target audience. Among the animated sitcoms broadcast in the Arab world, the American series Family Guy stands out as a particularly demanding case for the translator. Created by Seth MacFarlane, the show is built around provocative and irreverent humour that repeatedly engages with sensitive matters such as sex, alcohol, religion, and politics. What functions as ordinary comic material for its original American audience may be received with concern and caution, or outright rejection, in Arab societies whose ideological and religious frameworks differ markedly from those of the West. Film translation possesses a strong potential to shape the beliefs and opinions of its audience, arguably more than other forms of translation, which is precisely why questions of censorship and appropriateness become so pressing in this context. The translator of Family Guy is therefore confronted with content that not only resists straightforward linguistic transfer but also collides with the deeply held convictions of the receiving community. The relationship between translation and culture lies at the heart of this challenge. National identity is culturally diverse, bound up with race and ethnicity, and expressed through a particular language and culture (Venuti, 2005); in the process of translation, identities may be lost and reshaped as new cultural material is brought into focus. It is for this reason that translators exercise strong caution when approaching subjects deemed unacceptable, and it is this caution that motivates the present study. Because translation and culture cannot be separated, the transfer of cultural aspects during subtitling can be extremely challenging, and at times impossible, given the wide gap that may exist between source and target cultures. Film translation in particular carries the power to influence audiences profoundly (Szarkowska, 2005), which places a heavy responsibility on the subtitler to render content in a manner that is both intelligible and culturally acceptable. For the purposes of this study, the cultural constraints that emerge in subtitling Family Guy into Arabic are grouped into three broad categories: religious remarks, jokes and humour that revolve around proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks refer to any offensive or unacceptable religious reference contained in the show; jokes and humour of proper nouns concern cross-cultural names deployed within a humorous context; and taboos are understood as immoral or explicit content deemed inappropriate by the target audience. Following Allan (2001, p. 148), tabooed words may be defined as ‘those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent when used in certain contexts’. This threefold classification is deliberate. Religion arguably constitutes the foremost ‘red zone’ for most societies, since adherents of a faith rarely tolerate mockery of their beliefs or intrusion upon what they hold sacred. Humour, meanwhile, poses distinct difficulties, as comic references familiar to the source culture may lose their effect when transferred; indeed, earlier research has shown that target texts tend to contain fewer humorous elements than their source texts, partly because translators lack the means to render culturally specific humour (Jankowska, 2009). Taboos are included because the explicit rendition of sexual or otherwise indecent content can be experienced as shocking and unpleasant, and because conveying an idea acceptable in one society to a more conservative one risks tainting the latter's identity and customs. Despite the growing body of scholarship on audio-visual translation into Arabic, relatively little attention has been paid to Family Guy, notwithstanding its notoriety and the intensity of the cultural clashes it provokes. This study seeks to address that gap by investigating and identifying the strategies that subtitlers adopt when confronting cultural constraints in the Arabic version of the programme. In doing so, it draws on the cultural approach to translation, which treats the translated text not as a mere replica of the source but as a product shaped by the norms, history, and ideology of the receiving culture. Specifically, the study is guided by the following research question: what are the strategies used by the subtitlers of Family Guy to (A) translate unacceptable religious remarks, (B) reflect on the target audience the humorous effect that revolves around proper nouns, and (C) render taboos into Arabic? By answering these questions, the study aims to illuminate the vital role that the target audience's ideology and culture play in determining which constraints govern the translation process.

Language testing occupies a central position in foreign language education, since the decisions made about learners' placement, progress, and achievement depend heavily on the quality of the instruments used to measure their abilities. As the demand for efficient, dependable, and economical assessment of general language proficiency has grown, so too has the interest of researchers in developing test formats that yield accurate information about learners while placing minimal demands on time and resources. Among the various approaches proposed for this purpose, tests grounded in the reduced redundancy principle have attracted sustained attention. The underlying assumption is that knowledge of a language necessarily entails the ability to function even when redundancy is reduced, so that learners with greater command of the language can more successfully exploit the redundancy of natural discourse to reconstruct a mutilated text (Spolsky, 1968; Klein-Braley, 1997). The C-Test, first proposed by Raatz and Klein-Braley in the early 1980s, is the most prominent representative of this family of reduced redundancy tests. A C-Test typically consists of several short authentic passages in which the second half of every second word is deleted, and test-takers are asked to restore the missing parts by drawing on all they know of and about the language. Because a single C-Test comprises a number of independent texts rather than one passage, it samples a wide range of linguistic knowledge and is less vulnerable to the influence of a test-taker's familiarity with a particular topic than a conventional cloze test (Baghaei & Grotjahn, 2014a; Baghaei & Grotjahn, 2014b). Over the past four decades, numerous scholars have advocated the use of the C-Test as an economical, realistic, quick, accurate, and reliable indicator of overall competence in a second or foreign language (see the extensive body of work reviewed in Baghaei, 2011). The reported reliability coefficients of well-constructed C-Tests are impressive, frequently exceeding 0.85 for shorter versions and 0.90 for longer ones, which makes the format especially attractive for practical assessment purposes. The question of what the C-Test actually measures, however, has generated considerable debate. The strongest claim made on its behalf is that it is a measure of general language proficiency, so that examinees' scores can be interpreted as reflecting their overall foreign language ability. A number of construct validation studies employing Rasch modeling and confirmatory factor analysis have supported this claim, demonstrating that C-Tests tend to be highly reliable and unidimensional instruments that tap the same general dimension as tests of reading, listening, writing, and speaking (Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006; Grotjahn, 2016; Eckes & Baghaei, 2015). Baghaei's (2008a, 2008b, 2010, 2011) programme of work likewise provides evidence, through Rasch analysis, for the coherence of the C-Test construct, while investigations into the factorial validity of the format have consistently reported results favourable to the general proficiency interpretation (Raatz, 1984; Raatz, 1985). More recently, the C-Test has even been proposed as an integrative measure of crystallized intelligence, extending its potential range of application well beyond conventional language assessment (Baghaei & Tabatabaee, 2015). Nevertheless, this interpretation has not gone unchallenged. Because the C-Test does not directly engage learners in oral or aural skills, some scholars have argued that its scores are better understood as measures of reading and writing ability than of listening or speaking proficiency (Alderson, 2002; Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006). The correlational evidence bearing on this issue is decidedly mixed: studies have reported coefficients ranging from as low as 0.24 between a French C-Test and self-ratings of speaking to as high as 0.76 for listening comprehension, with correlations for speaking generally lower than those for listening. These inconsistent findings indicate that the extent to which the C-Test can legitimately be interpreted as a general proficiency measure remains an open empirical question, one whose answer may well depend on the particular population, language, and version of the test involved. Despite the wealth of validation research accumulated in European, and to a lesser degree Middle Eastern, contexts, the great majority of these studies have been conducted with German, English, and Iranian learners. To date, there appears to be no published research examining the psychometric qualities of the C-Test among Afghan students of English as a foreign language. This is a notable gap given the distinctive circumstances of English language education in Afghanistan, where a large number of teachers have neither received training in test development nor acquired the expertise needed to construct sound assessment instruments (cf. Coniam, 2009). In such a setting, a test that is both easy to construct and economical to administer, yet capable of delivering reliable information about learners' general proficiency, would be of considerable practical value. Whether the encouraging validity evidence obtained elsewhere generalises to Afghan EFL learners cannot simply be assumed and needs to be established empirically. The present study addresses this gap by investigating the reliability and validity of the C-Test as a measure of overall English language proficiency among Afghan EFL learners. To this end, one hundred advanced English majors were administered a C-Test composed of four authentic passages, three drawn from written discourse and one from spoken discourse, alongside a criterion measure consisting of the listening, reading, and writing sections of a standard English proficiency test. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha reliability estimates, Pearson correlation coefficients, and factor analysis were employed to examine the concurrent and construct validity of the C-Test against these criterion measures. It is anticipated that establishing the C-Test as a reliable and valid indicator of general proficiency in this context would offer practical benefits for teachers, test administrators, and students in Afghanistan, providing an efficient alternative to lengthier and costlier proficiency tests for placement and general assessment purposes, and would extend the international body of C-Test validation research to a hitherto unexamined population.

Worldwide, more than 90 million U.S. adults lack adequate literacy, and vast numbers of immigrant adults arrive in new countries having had little or no opportunity for formal schooling in their first language (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012; UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2020). For these learners, becoming literate is not merely a matter of transferring existing print skills to a new script; rather, they must develop print literacy for the very first time, often while simultaneously acquiring an entirely new language. Despite the growing presence of such learners in publicly funded adult education classrooms, they remain markedly underrepresented in second language acquisition (SLA) research. As Bigelow and Tarone (2004) have argued, who we choose to study fundamentally shapes what we come to know about second language learning, and the field's reliance on easy-to-recruit, well-schooled participants has left the needs of socially excluded, low-educated adult learners largely unaddressed (Young-Scholten, 2013). The subfield of Low-Educated Second Language and Literacy Acquisition (LESLLA) has emerged to fill this gap, generating a body of practice-oriented scholarship focused on instruction, teacher preparation, and the distinctive demands facing adults with emergent print literacy (Strube, 2009; Vinogradov, 2009; Young-Scholten, 2015). Much of this work has concentrated on oral skills, reading, and the professional knowledge instructors require to teach this population effectively (Carter, 2020). Comparatively little attention, however, has been paid to the earliest stages of writing development—the point at which adults must learn to hold a writing implement, form recognizable shapes, and copy text before they can compose independently. This omission is significant. Writing, even in its most rudimentary form of copying, entails a remarkable convergence of motor, perceptual, orthographic, semiotic, and linguistic skills. Whereas L1 children typically spend years engaged in play writing and shape formation before entering formal schooling, adults new to print literacy often have had no such preparatory experience. Moreover, unlike children, these adults frequently cannot map meaning onto the words they are copying, since they are simultaneously acquiring the L2 lexicon in which those words are written. The cognitive burden entailed in what may appear to be a simple copying task is therefore considerable, and current language content standards—which reduce beginning writing to targets such as tracing or printing letters—fail to capture this complexity. Given that ethical treatment of L2 writers requires understanding learners, placing them in suitable contexts, and providing appropriate instruction (Silva, 1997; Carter & J. M, 2020), it is essential to develop a clearer picture of how adult emergent print literacy actually unfolds. Drawing on the well-developed literature on children's orthographic and motor development as a lens, this ethnographically situated study documents four adult students, each with 0–1 year of prior formal education, as they copied classroom text over a five-month period at a Northern California adult school. Specifically, it asks: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability—copying—in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy?

M3-OPThis article presents a quantitative study that seeks to establish how discursive means of self-mention are represented in research sections of the leading universities in Estonia and the United Kingdom (the UK), respectively. M1-RRResearch sections of university websites serve as digital artifacts that are used to communicate, disseminate and promote research (Tomášková 2015). M1-MTGTypically, the university’s research communication on its website involves discursive means of self-mention, i.e. how the university refers to itself on the website. M3-OPThe specific aim of this study is to identify and juxtapose self-mentions in the research sections of the university websites in Estonia and the UK. M3-APRThis study is grounded in the theoretical premises of self-mention in academic discourse that are formulated by Hyland (2001, 2008) and the construal of the Inner, Outer, and Expanding Circles of the English language in the sense postulated by Kachru (1985). M1-RRAccording to Kachru (1985), the Inner Circle of English is represented by the countries where English is the mother tongue, e.g., the UK, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Ireland. In the Inner Circle, English is “a mother tongue that is passed on to infants naturalistically across generations” (Bruthiaux 2003: 159). In the countries of the Inner Circle, English is used in a normative manner as a linguistically codified and socially accepted set of norms or standards that are regarded as norm-providing to the Outer and Expanding Circles (Bolton 2006; Kachru 1985). The Outer Circle is associated with the speakers of English as the second language (ESL) in the former British colonies (e.g., India, Jamaica, Singapore, etc.), where “English is only one of the community languages in what are clearly multilingual societies” (Bolton 2006: 3) In contrast to the Outer Circle, the English language in the Expanding Circle of English does not have an official or semi-official status. The Expanding Circle is theorised to be associated with English as an international language in those countries where English is taught as a Foreign Language, or EFL (Bolton 2006: 3). English in the Expanding Circle is assumed “to be exonormative in that speakers, educators, and policy-makers have traditionally looked to American or British models for linguistic norms” (Bruthiaux 2003: 159-160). Arguably, the use of English in the Expanding Circle is norm-dependent, since EFL speakers need to be provided with a model or a codified norm of English associated with the Inner Circle (Bolton 2006). The aforementioned characteristics of the Expanding Circle of English could be illustrated by the case of Estonia. Whilst English does not have an official status there, the importance and prestige of the English language increases in today’s Estonia (Lazdiņa, Marten 2019) due to the country’s participation in the “collective West”, as a member-state of the EU, NATO, OECD and other international organisations that use English as a lingua franca (Jurkynas 2020). In addition, the use of the English language in Estonia is facilitated by an increased number of international students at Estonian universities (Soler, Björkman, and Kuteeva 2018). After Estonia regained its independence after nearly 50 years of Soviet occupation, the teaching and learning of English have aligned with the practices that are found in the West (Alas, Liiv 2009: 20). Given the increase in international co-operation and university mobility, Estonian universities maintain and regularly update websites in English (van Doorslaer, Loogus 2020; Virkus 2008). M1-MTGPresumably, English-mediated university websites in Estonia could be regarded as digital discursive artifacts that construe university-specific narratives associated with a variety of aspects, i.e. the presentation of the university’s structure, university’s identity, university student life, enrollment, and research activities. M1-RRIn this regard, it should be noted that university websites in Estonia and the UK alike could be theorised as a complex multimodal discursive space, where verbal and non-verbal discursive means are employed in order to achieve the pragma-communicative goals of promoting the university to the public (Tomášková 2015). M3-OPIt could be assumed that, by serving the aforementioned pragmacommunicative aims, the use of the English language on the English-mediated university websites reflects the realities of the Circles of English, as well as the cultural, educational, and socio-economic realities. Consequently, the discursive means of self-mention on the university websites might differ, due to the disparities between a university that is situated in a country of the Expanding Circle of English (e.g., Estonia) and a university in the UK that belongs to the Inner Circle of English. M2-GapCurrently, however, little is known about whether or not self-mentions are linguistically similar and/or different on the English-mediated university websites in the Expanding Circle of English (e.g., Estonia) and the Inner Circle of English (e.g., the UK). Furthermore, there are no prior studies that investigate self-mentions in the research sections of Estonian university websites in order to compare their use with that of the UK’s university websites M3-OPThe present study seeks to address this under-represented issue. M3-ISThis article is structured as follows. First, I will provide a review of the current literature associated with self-mention in academic writing in English and in computer-mediated discourse in section 2. Then, I will introduce and discuss the present study with its research questions, corpus, methodology, and results, and provide a detailed discussion of the major findings in section 3. Finally, the article will be concluded with the summary of the results in section 4

M1-RRWriting is a way of connecting individuals with each other in ways that carry particular special meanings, and the process of writing is a rich collection of elements (Hyland, 2003). Specifically, Hyland (2003) points out the merits of genre-based writing, which unlike process approaches to writing, offers students “explicit and systematic explanations of the ways language functions in social contexts” (Hyland, 2003, p. 18). Genre-based writing is writing based on the assumption that the features of a similar group of texts depend on the social context of their creation and use (Hyland, 2003). It is based on the idea that members of a community are usually able to recognize similarities in texts they use on a frequent basis, and are able to draw on repeated experiences with such texts to read, understand and perhaps write such texts (Hyland, 2007). M1-MTGAs such, genre-writing enables L2 users to use language to interpret communicative situations, combining language together with content and context. Kern (2008) emphasizes the point that texts enable learners the opportunities to position themselves in relation to viewpoints and cultures, and to “make the connection between grammar, discourse, and meaning, between language and content, between language and culture, and between another culture and their own” (Kern, 2008, p. 380). Canagarajah (2011) looks at translanguaging in writing, which can bring discourse and rhetorical issues into focus (p. 402). M1-MTGWriting is different to speaking which is more spontaneous, and unlike the relatively spontaneous speech act, the monitored and somewhat detached activity of writing involves strategic options and choices. Students have to develop a critical awareness of the choices that are rhetorically more effective. In his study, Canagarajah presents a model featuring identity, role, subjectivity and awareness with the aim of exploring how these “find amalgamation in the textual voices of multilingual students” (p. 2). “Identity” relates to features such as language, ethnic, and national affiliations that are part of one’s history. According to Canagarajah, the roles one plays come with expectations about the voice one should adopt in communicative interactions. “Subjectivity” is an “ideological construct” which indexes the discourses that shape one’s voice as they find expression through genre conventions, communicative norms, and value systems (Canagarajah, 2014, pp. 2-3). Item 081  ·  plain text
The ability to use and interpret language appropriately in social contexts has long been acknowledged as a central dimension of communicative competence. Since Chomsky's (1965) distinction between competence and performance, applied linguists have sought to broaden the notion of what it means to know a language. Hymes (1972) introduced the concept of communicative competence, arguing that linguistic knowledge alone is insufficient for successful communication and that learners must also acquire knowledge of when, where, and to whom particular utterances are appropriate. Subsequent models expanded this idea. Canale and Swain (1980) and Canale (1983) proposed frameworks encompassing grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse, and strategic competencies, while Celce-Murcia, Dörnyei, and Thürrell (1995) later refined the construct to include actional and sociocultural components. Across these formulations, pragmatic competence—the ability to convey and comprehend meaning in context—emerges as an indispensable element of second and foreign language ability (Bachman & Palmer, 1996). Despite this recognition, pragmatic competence remains one of the least investigated components of communicative language ability. Much of the research in interlanguage pragmatics has concentrated on the production and comprehension of speech acts, particularly requests, apologies, and refusals, often within cross-sectional or study-abroad designs (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Matsumura, 2001; Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). The instruments used in these studies are frequently framed by the speech act paradigm, drawing on discourse completion tasks and related elicitation techniques. In contrast, comparatively little attention has been paid to conversational implicature, the process by which hearers infer meanings that go beyond the literal content of utterances (Grice, 1975; Levinson, 1983; Verschueren, 1999; Archer, Aijmer, & Wichmann, 2012). The comprehension of implied meaning is arguably as crucial to successful communication as the recognition of illocutionary force, yet it has been examined by only a modest body of research (Bouton, 1988, 1994; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2013; Taguchi, 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013). The available evidence indicates that cultural background, second language exposure, implicature type, and general L2 proficiency all shape learners' ability to interpret implicatures the way native speakers do. Bouton (1988, 1994) demonstrated that non-native speakers from different cultural backgrounds derive divergent meanings from implicatures and that idiosyncratic implicatures are learned slowly when not deliberately taught. Taguchi's (2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013) series of studies established that proficiency and exposure influence the accuracy and speed of implicature comprehension, with more conventional implied meanings proving easier to interpret than nonconventional ones. Roever (2006, 2013) similarly reported that learners' knowledge of implicature increases with proficiency, and he stressed that comprehension depends on learners' recognizing the divergence between surface and intended meaning. A recurring concern in this literature is the need for valid and reliable instruments capable of measuring implicature comprehension, an area where the field lags well behind the assessment of other aspects of L2 competence (Roever, 2006; Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Kane, 2011). The present study addresses this gap by constructing and validating a test of conversational implicature comprehension for use in the Iranian EFL context. Drawing on Grice's (1975) conversational maxims and Goffman's (1967) insights on face management, and following the model articulated by Holtgraves (1998), the construct of conversational implicature is defined in terms of hearers' inferential responses to violations of the relevance maxim. Face management is treated as a principal motivation for indirectness, since interlocutors employ implicatures to protect their own and others' face (Brown & Levinson, 1987; Thomas, 1995). Within this framework, four subtypes of implicature—indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes—are hypothesized to constitute the underlying structure of the construct. Two lines of evidence are pursued to establish construct validity: confirmatory factor analysis through structural equation modeling, testing whether a four-factor model fits the data, and a differential group study, examining whether learners of differing proficiency levels differ significantly in their comprehension. By developing a validated listening-based instrument and applying rigorous statistical procedures, this study aims to extend the scope of second and foreign language pragmatic research and to offer a practical tool for assessing an under-researched dimension of EFL learners' communicative ability.

M1-CCQuestioning lies at the heart of classroom interaction and academic inquiry. The capacity to formulate questions that span the full range of the cognitive domain—from remembering and understanding to analysing, evaluating, and creating—is central to effective teaching, yet it is far from an innate ability. This is especially true for English as a second language (L2) learner teachers, many of whom enter teacher training programs having received little or no explicit instruction in how to ask questions purposefully and strategically. For these teachers, developing awareness of questioning strategies is a demanding cognitive and linguistic task that intertwines their command of English with their emerging pedagogical repertoire. M1-RRResearch on questioning has accumulated across several distinct traditions. Within first language (L1) English contexts, a substantial body of interventional studies examined how children develop questioning ability through training, modelling, and awareness-raising (Blank & Covington, 1965; Zimmerman & Pike, 1972; Nelson & Earl, 1973). Later work analysed how children use questioning to make sense of the world, uniting the forms and functions of inquiry in authentic texts (Lindfors, 1999). A parallel line of work in language learner strategy research established that learners invest strategically in acquiring language skills (Cohen & Macaro, 2007; Oxford, 1992), though critical reviews have cautioned that L2 strategic behaviour should not be reduced to decontextualised taxonomies of self-reported processes (Ortega, 2009). Studies of teacher questioning have compared display and referential questions and their effects on classroom discourse, producing notably inconsistent findings: while some report that referential questions elicit more elaborate responses (Brock, 1986; Nunan, 1990), others conclude that display and closed questions are more effective in eliciting student responses in particular contexts (Wu, 1993; Cotton, 1989). Research on the functions of questions in institutional discourse has further shown that context and institutional structure shape what counts as, and how one performs, a question (Ehrlich & Freed, 2009; Koshik, 2009). Studies of teacher questioning as scaffolded assistance similarly foreground its interactive role in supporting learning (Hall & Verplaetse, 2000; Yaqubi & Mozaffari, 2010). M2-GapDespite this breadth, the development of adult L2 teachers' own questioning ability remains strikingly under-investigated. Adults, unlike children, approach language learning more analytically and are frequently the subjects of strategy instruction research (Grenfell & Macaro, 2007), yet interventional work has focused overwhelmingly on question formation as a syntactic developmental task rather than on the cognitive levels and purposes of questioning. McDonough and Mackey (2006, 2008), for example, demonstrated that productively using a question form is more beneficial for development than mimicking it, but their participants were EFL undergraduates rather than learner teachers who need such development most acutely. M1-RRSurvey and content-analytic studies have exposed teachers' lack of specific questioning strategies and revealed persistent misconceptions about convergent, divergent, and cognitive-level question types (Sun, 2012; Döş et al., 2016). M2-CTThese findings have generated repeated and explicit calls for the teaching of questioning strategies and for in-service and pre-service training programs to strengthen teachers' classroom questioning behaviours (Döş et al., 2016; Davoudi & Sadeghi, 2015). M2-GapTo date, however, no experimental study has taught L2 learner teachers questioning through the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), and interventional research on developing L2 teacher questioning is scarce. M2-CTLearner teachers educated in non-Socratic contexts, who receive limited questioning instruction in their prior schooling, therefore need contextualised training to catch up on the questioning education they have missed. M3-APRThe present study addresses this gap. It reports an eight-week quasi-experimental study that operationalises the Revised Taxonomy to develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of questioning strategies—specifically, formulating questions at varying cognitive levels and generating Divergent Questions for scaffolding purposes—through intensive restructuring activities and a Question-Question Game. M3-OPGuided by principles of contextualisation (Ortega, 2009), restructuring (DeKeyser, 1997, 2007), and noticing (Schmidt, 1990), the study pursues two research questions: (1) to what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction develop learner teachers' awareness of strategies to formulate levels of questions, and (2) to what extent can such instruction raise their awareness of strategies to develop divergent questions? M3-APFIn doing so, the study offers new empirical and pedagogical directions for L2 teacher training in questioning.

Educational assessment is an important part of the process of teaching and learning. According to Stiggins and Conklin (1992), regularly teachers spend up to half of their time in the classroom,assessing and analyzing the learning of students. Scholars' and practitioners’ interest in evaluation has always been very strong, and in recent years, evaluation has been one of the key objectives of educational research. As a consequence, the way students are assessed in the classroom has undergone numerous worldwide adjustments The assessment tools used in the classroom in the 21st century go beyond traditional quizzes with paper and pencil. It has many more tasks and is used for various uses such as diagnosis, monitoring, grading, feedback, instructional improvement, motivation, and other (MacMillan, 2014). Formative assessment (MacMillan, 2014) is one of the forms of classroom evaluation aimed at "gathering evidence of student learning and providing feedback to teachers and modifying educational approaches to improve achievement" (p. 93) Formative assessment, a commonly promoted practice in teacher education, is defined as a process for examining one’s own teaching. The utilization of formative assessment, whether it is continuous or occasional, is meant to tell and improve teachers’ understanding while developing their own teaching practice (Yorke, 2003). Traditionally, formative assessment is supported through the processes of reflection and/or self-assessment. Both of these approaches are widely utilized in education as a way for guiding preservice teachers looking inward to further develop their understanding of pedagogy and pedagogical content knowledge (Van Zee & Roberts, 2001). Formative assessment plays an important role in the improvement of student learning and achievement. As Heritage (2007) asserts, effective use of FA can provide sufficient information to move learning forward. The utilization of FA improves students’ knowledge and skills (Bennett, 2011). Nevertheless, there is a limited understanding and application of FA in the context of upper education (Duckor, 2014), despite the pressure on universities to reinforce their teaching and; therefore, improve the quality of student learning assessment (Hattie, 2009). Popham (2014) stresses the term "process" in his concept of FA, stating that it is a calculated process rather than a test. FA is a structured mechanism in which instructors use test-related proof of student status to change their current instructional practices or students to modify their learning strategies (Popham, 2014). Therefore, a pupil is regarded as an active participant responsible for their learning in FA. It offers students the opportunity to prepare their further acts on the suggestions of the teacher. Nevertheless, Shavelson (2006) made a somewhat contradictory statement about the efficacy of FA based on his experience of introducing and researching its effects: After five years of work, our euphoria has become a fact that FA, like so many other changes in education, has a long way to go before a majority of teachers can learn it. In other words, producing positive outcomes in the application of FA is a very long and complicated process and its success does not occur automatically (p. 65). Other researchers have shown that teachers in general are not familiar with different modes of assessment (Watmani, Assadollahfam, & Behin, 2020). School assessments are of two types of formative and summative and both play important roles in education. One major challenge for teachers is to balance formative and summative assessments in their teaching. Since the most important purpose of assessment in education is to support learning (Black & Wiliam, 2006), the value of formative assessment becomes clear. In some countries, like Hong Kong, the educational system has made some changes in the assessment modes of teachers with more emphasis on the formative assessment by making it an inherent part of teaching (Yan & Cheng, 2015). However, pressure from the top of the hierarchal system cannot be effective if those who have to implement formative assessment, i.e., teachers, do not want to employ it in their classes (Rink & Mitchell, 2002). Teachers’ unwillingness for conducting formative assessment can be due to their lack of knowledge or negative beliefs about the subject (Brown, Hui, Yu, & Kennedy, 2011). Therefore, it is clear that successful implementation of formative assessment in schools depends on teachers' understanding, participation, and support as teachers' views have a significant impact on any change in educational systems (Hallinger, 2011) Therefore, it is essential to gain an understanding of teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment. There have not been many studies on the factors which influence teachers’ intentions concerning formative assessment and the impact of attitudinal factors on their formative assessment practices. Formative assessment identifies learners’ strengths and weaknesses, enhances their motivation and metacognition, and provides feedback to inform both teaching and learning (Black & Wiliam, 1998). Empirical studies have shown that integration of formative assessment into teaching has a clear and notable impact on students’ achievement and learning (Black & Wiliam, 1998; Hattie, 2009; Wiliam, Lee, Harrison, & Black, 2004) Although, these benefits of formative assessment are well-accepted among educators, conducting it is a very difficult task and it cannot be added to the teaching practices quickly. Teaching is a very personal task and teachers have their own teaching philosophies and thus their attitudes and beliefs about formative assessment greatly impact their practices (Harrison, 2013). The theory of planned behavior (TPB) proposed by Ajzen (1985, 1991) is a theoretical framework which attempts to predict behavior based on individuals’ attitudes, emotions, and intentions. According to TPB, three factors including attitude towards the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control affect behavior through intentions. This means that those who approve a behavior, have positive subjective norms (social pressure from others), and enjoy a high level of perceived behavioral control (one's perception of the difficulty of and control over performing the behavior) are more likely to perform the behavioor This study employed TPB to identify the contribution of significant factors (affective, subjective norms, control, etc.) to the behavior of performing formative assessment in Iraqi teachers. Most of the studies published on the FA concentrated on the advantages and influences that may affect classroom engagement and the effect of the FA on student learning achievement (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017). There has not been any in-depth study conducted to describe in detail the understanding of FA by teachers and how their perspective affects their ways of doing follow-up actions. The perception of the teachers' in FA certainly affects the kinds of input they provide as well as the actions they take to follow up. Therefore, the current study aims to investigate the attitudes, intentions, and practices in conducting FA in Iraqi EFL classrooms. Also, the study intends to highlight the applicability of FA in EFL classrooms in terms of the use of the correct FA strategy to match the objective or the purpose of the assessment. The study aims to pinpoint the pedagogical implications of using FA To the best knowledge of this researcher, no study was applied with reference to the contributions of attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding FA to student learning improvement in Iraqi universities and schools. 2.1. Research Questions 1. What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards FA? 2. How frequent do Iraqi EFL teachers use FA? 3. To what extent are different components of attitudes to FA related to the application of FA? 4. Do Iraqi teachers’ attitudes to FA differ in terms of sex and level of education?

Any human being may have similarities with others or may have some differences from others. Psychology as an academic field strives to probe these similarities and differences to make generalizable facts about human beings Human beings can act differently even though they have similarities in age, gender, and so on. The reason for this could be associated with the uniqueness of the human mind. This uniqueness particularly is the matter of Individual Differences (IDs) studies within psychology (Dewaele, 2009). IDs in Second Language Acquisition (SLA) accordingly endeavor to anatomize the differences in language learning process, such as different language learning rates, choice of learning styles, and so forth Within this research agenda, motivation has a vital role as it is both intriguing and closely related to other aspects of language learning process. Language learning is an easy process for some people; however, the same situation is not valid for others. Therefore, it is a kind of problematic matter. At this point, if one has motivation at a satisfactory level, he or she may be successful in the end.Therefore, the notion of motivation has attracted so many scholars’ attention, and the research into motivation has led to other constructs to emerge such as Willingness to Communicate (WTC). Even though WTC has emerged within first language (L1) studies, it is unquestionably related with second or foreign language (L2) as it is remarkably proper for L2 learning process and its fundamental point is to make people communicate with each other in L2 (MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément, & Noels, 1998). The early studies on L2 motivation and L2 WTC have emphasized the role of integrative motivation on L2 WTC However, the motivational research paradigm is progressively focusing on the micro level analysis rather than macro level analysis with the emphasis on the individual. Therefore, a relatively new concept in the motivational studies has emerged as a tripartite construct, i.e., L2 Motivational Self System (L2 MSS) (Dörnyei, 2005, 2009). With the present study, L2 MSS is under lens, especially in terms of its relationship between L2 WTC as the notion of integrativeness is not applicable in practice in English as a foreign language (EFL) settings (Yashima, 2009, 2012). Thus, the alternation of integrative motivation to the ideal L2 self is expected and validated (Bursali & Öz, 2017; Khajavy & Ghonsooly, 2017; Öz, 2016). However, the examination of the role of external effects, namely the oughtto L2 self is quite deficient in Turkish EFL contex Therefore, the present study sought to find out the possible association between L2 WTC and L2 MSS (the ideal L2 self and the ought-to L2 self).

Language teaching has long been dominated by the assumption that a target language is best acquired when it is taught through a monolingual medium of instruction. In many foreign language settings, and particularly across the Gulf region, excluding the students' mother tongue from the classroom is widely regarded as the most practical and effective route to proficiency in English. This view rests on the belief that extensive and strict exposure to the target language mirrors the way children acquire their first language and that the classroom offers a controlled environment in which such exposure can be maximised (Cook, 2001). As a result, the separation of languages has become deeply entrenched in foreign language education, where students are treated, in García and Otheguy's (2020) terms, as two monolinguals in one. Recently, however, a more flexible perspective has been gaining prominence. Plurilingualism reconceptualises language competence as a dynamic and evolving repertoire, and holds that learners' full linguistic resources, including their mother tongue, should be deployed without watchful adherence to the boundaries between named languages (Otheguy, García, & Reid, 2015; Piccardo, 2019). Scholars have argued that dismissing the first language restricts the possibilities for language teaching and that exploiting the whole linguistic repertoire can accelerate learning, enhance comprehension and foster metalinguistic awareness (Cook, 2001; Marshall & Moore, 2018). This shift also responds to the sociolinguistic realities of globalisation, in which multiple languages are in constant contact and monolingual hegemonies are increasingly challenged (Blommaert, 2010; Lamb, 2015). Despite these developments, the move towards plurilingual pedagogy continues to meet considerable resistance among second and foreign language teachers, policymakers and parents, who remain attached to the perceived benefits of the target-language-only classroom (Dooly & Vallejo, 2020). While such tensions have begun to be documented in multilingual Anglophone and European contexts, comparatively little is known about how they are experienced in settings where English is a foreign language and where societies are relatively monocultural and monolingual. Saudi Arabia represents precisely such a context, yet EFL teachers' understanding of plurilingualism and its classroom application there remains largely unexamined. The present study addresses this gap by exploring plurilingualism and monolingualism from the perspective of EFL teachers in intermediate and secondary schools in the Qassim region of Saudi Arabia. Adopting a mixed methods case study of 34 teachers, it investigates whether teachers believe English should be taught exclusively through the target language, and what they think about the use of Arabic for teaching, learning and non-academic purposes. In doing so, the study aims to illuminate the interplay between teachers' declared beliefs, their actual classroom practices, and their awareness of plurilingualism as a pedagogical concept.

Despite their diversity, their different methods and cognitive interests, the different approaches largely agree that the category gender cannot be seen as given, but rather represents a complex construction that influences our self-image and our ideas of gender and gender relations as well as our sexuality (Babka/Posselt 2016). Nevertheless, school lessons also “offer the chance to make limiting concepts of gender and sexuality a topic, to encourage a critical discussion of gender-related norms and exclusions, and to open new perspectives” (König/Lewin/Surkamp, 2016, p. 21). Foreign language teaching is particularly suitable for gender thematization and reflection, since it is intended to encourage pupils to engage with 'foreign' cultures, identities and perspectives and to open up new perspectives on their own world. This makes it an excellent opportunity for critical reflection on gender as a dominant category, structuring society to a high degree and creating identity (Lewin 2015). In addition to this, the curricula of most of Germany's federal states include gender-related topics (equality, equal rights, sexual education, sexual self-determination). For modern foreign language teaching, the ability to communicate about sexuality is specifically mentioned. It is precisely the highlighting of linguistic aspects that allows crossconnections to foreign language teaching (e.g. Berliner Rahmenlehrplan). Considering the structure and content of foreign language lessons in the language acquisition phase, materials in general and textbooks in particular are of certain importance, because they do not only serve to instruct learners in their subject matter (Moser/Hannover/Becker 2013), they “contribute to constructing new knowledge and behavioural modes” (Benitt/Kurtz, 2016, p. 171), which leads to the assumption that materials and media can have an impact on the learners perspective, expectations and patterns of behaviour and interpretation related to gender (ibid.). It is undeniable that the global influence of the English language is everywhere we look, whether this is in the media, education, science, tourism, or business. English has permeated all levels of society entering all kinds of domains (Seidlhofer, Breiteneder, & Pitzl, 2006) and this is even more evident in Europe. It is the language of international communication par excellence worldwide but it has become the de facto lingua franca in Europe, where the need for intraEuropean communication pushed this language to take the position but the policies around it are still very controversial in a territory where multilingualism and language diversity is one of the main core values. It is this current status that has awoken many relevant research topics such as linguistic imperialism,the varieties of English, linguistic diversity and conservation, or linguistic and cultural identity, which are often focused in the use of language and not so much integrated in the study of language acquisition. Our research focuses on English language teaching in a plurilingual society and aims to propose a sustainable approach to teach a language that acts as a lingua franca using the first language to learn the second one more effectively while exalting the value of the mother tongue. In a world populated by different “Englishes” and ruled by “nativeness,” it is a complex matter to define what English as a Lingua Franca (ELF thereafter) entails and even more so to teach it as a second language, while at the same time disassociating the language from its “original native speakers” (British or American, for instance). The English language expanded with the British Empire through the colonies, it stayed dominant through the global markets and new technologies, and it has now taken the position of a global language that no longer belongs exclusively to the native speakers. The World Englishes model “does not appear to take into account the fact that English has acquired a new dominant function world-wide” (Mollin, 2006, p. 42) and this has inspired many different research fields within ELF. Despite the different views and understandings of ELF, the idea of the plurilithic English is the common ground, where the focus of international communication is on intelligibility across groups of English speakers of different first language backgrounds (Mckay, 2018) However, not all scholars are on the same page in terms of defining what it actually is and what it represents. For some, ELF is conceptualised as an umbrella term to refer to a language function (Friedrich & Matsuda, 2010; House, 2003), while for others it is becoming a new variety (Jenkins, Modiano, & Seidlhofer, 2001; Seidlhofer, 2009) and focus on the characteristics of a certain group of speakers using English to communicate in an international setting. Nevertheless, we find the definition of ELF as a variety rather incomplete.

Are the frequencies of subsystems linked to the efficiency of the travel brochures, that is, to their power in attracting potential customers

M1-CCThe affective dimension of second and foreign language learning has become a central concern for both researchers and practitioners over the past four decades. Among the various emotional variables that shape the language learning experience, anxiety has attracted particular attention, since it is widely regarded as one of the most influential affective factors capable of interfering with the acquisition and use of a foreign language (Horwitz, 2001; Dörnyei, 2005). Indeed, the debilitating effects of anxiety on language learning have been consistently documented in the literature, and researchers have long stressed the importance of understanding how negative emotional reactions may hinder learners' progress and undermine their willingness to engage with the target language (Young, 1991; Woodrow, 2006). M1-RRA major turning point in this field came with the work of Horwitz, Horwitz and Cope (1986), who conceptualised Foreign Language Anxiety (FLA) not as a general trait but as a situation-specific construct unique to the language learning context. They proposed that FLA comprises three interrelated performance anxieties, namely communication apprehension, test anxiety and fear of negative evaluation, and developed the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS) to measure it. Since then, the FLCAS has become the most widely recognised instrument for assessing general foreign language anxiety, and its reliability and validity have been confirmed across numerous linguistic and cultural settings (Aida, 1994; Rodríguez & Abreu, 2003; Park, 2014). This body of research has repeatedly established a moderate negative relationship between anxiety and language achievement, suggesting that anxiety is not merely a by-product of poor performance but may itself be a cause of unsuccessful learning in some individuals (Horwitz, 2001; MacIntyre & Gardner, 1994). Within this line of enquiry, a considerable number of studies have explored the sources and correlates of FLA. Speaking and oral performance have frequently emerged as particularly anxiety-provoking, with communication apprehension often identified as the most salient component of classroom anxiety (Cheng et al., 1999; Mak, 2011; Choi, 2016). Researchers have also examined how anxiety relates to learners' self-perceptions of their own competence, reporting that lower perceived proficiency tends to coincide with higher levels of anxiety (Phillips, 1992; Liu, 2013). In addition, individual and demographic variables such as gender have been investigated, although findings in this respect have been inconsistent: while some studies report significant gender-related differences in FLA, others find none (Aida, 1994; Park & French, 2013). M1-CCTeachers' ability to detect anxious behaviours and the pedagogical strategies available for reducing anxiety have likewise been the object of scholarly attention (Gregersen, 2007; Young, 1992; Kruk, 2018), underscoring the practical relevance of this research area for the language classroom.
