Pronunciation has long occupied an ambivalent position in English language teaching (ELT). On the one hand, it is universally acknowledged that the way learners produce speech has an immediate and often decisive impact on whether communication succeeds or fails. On the other hand, pronunciation has frequently been described as the neglected or marginalised component of the language curriculum, receiving relatively little attention in teacher education, in commercial teaching materials and in classroom time (Derwing & Munro, 2005; Foote et al., 2016). This paradox is especially relevant in the contemporary context, where English functions as a global lingua franca and where a very large proportion of spoken interaction takes place between non-native speakers, or between non-native and native speakers, rather than exclusively among native speakers. In such circumstances, the priorities that once guided pronunciation instruction are being reconsidered, and the criteria by which learner speech is judged are being redefined. Historically, the teaching of pronunciation has been shaped less by empirical evidence than by ideology and intuition. As Levis (2005, p. 369) observes, '[t]o a large extent, pronunciation's importance has always been determined by ideology and intuition rather than research', with teachers intuitively deciding which features most affect clarity and which are teachable in a classroom. This intuitive orientation is reflected in the history of methodological extremes described by Levis (2005): certain approaches, such as the reform movement and audiolingualism, elevated pronunciation to a position of central importance and relied heavily on drilling and imitation, whereas others, including the cognitive movement and early communicative language teaching, largely set pronunciation aside. The consequence has been a field marked by fluctuation rather than cumulative progress, and by a persistent gap between what research suggests and what actually happens in classrooms. Central to current debate is a paradigmatic shift in the goals of pronunciation teaching. Levis (2005) frames this shift in terms of two competing principles that have long influenced both pedagogy and research: the nativeness principle, which holds that learners should aim for accent-free, native-like speech, and the intelligibility principle, which holds that the essential goal is comprehensible speech regardless of the retention of a foreign accent. The nativeness principle, once dominant, has become increasingly difficult to defend, both because it is rarely attainable and because it is grounded in assumptions about the priority of native models that no longer reflect the realities of global English use. The intelligibility principle, by contrast, accepts that learners will and should retain features of their first-language accent, and it directs pedagogical attention towards those aspects of pronunciation that most affect mutual understanding (Derwing & Munro, 2005; Isaacs, 2008). This reorientation raises a difficult question, however, since intelligibility itself has no universally accepted definition, and there is limited empirical evidence to indicate precisely which pronunciation features are crucial for it (Isaacs, 2008). Teachers seeking to prioritise intelligibility are therefore left with considerable uncertainty about what to teach and in what order. The argument that pronunciation pedagogy should be grounded in research rather than intuition has been articulated most forcefully by Derwing and Munro (2005), who lament the marginalisation of pronunciation within applied linguistics and call for empirical work that can help teachers set realistic goals, establish appropriate priorities and select effective techniques. They emphasise that unqualified or undertrained teachers are prone to misconceptions about phonological phenomena, are often unable to evaluate teaching materials critically, and may set unrealistic objectives such as the elimination of accent. Their appeal for greater collaboration between researchers and practitioners, and for classroom-relevant research framed around intelligibility, functional load and the role of the listener, provides an important rationale for surveying the current state of pronunciation research. Related synthesising work, such as that of Thomson and Derwing (2014) on the effectiveness of L2 pronunciation instruction and Saito's (2012) synthesis of quasi-experimental intervention studies, confirms that instruction can produce measurable gains, while also revealing that some domains, notably the suprasegmental level, remain comparatively underexplored. A further point of contention concerns the relative importance of segmental and suprasegmental features. Traditional phonological description distinguishes between segmentals, the individual vowel and consonant sounds of a language, and suprasegmentals such as stress, rhythm and intonation (Roach, 2009). There is no agreement in the field about which of these deserves greater emphasis in the classroom (Hahn, 2004; Thomson & Derwing, 2014). Some evidence suggests that suprasegmental features, particularly word and sentence stress, exert a strong influence on how listeners process and evaluate non-native speech (Hahn, 2004; Field, 2005), while other work continues to underline the importance of accurate segmental production, especially where sound contrasts carry meaning. In practice, teachers tend to devote the majority of their limited pronunciation time to segmental errors, partly because suprasegmentals are more demanding to teach and require reference to specialised terminology (Foote et al., 2016). This mismatch between what may matter most for intelligibility and what is actually taught illustrates once again the gap between research and classroom practice. The international character of English also complicates the question of which model to teach. The traditional prestige models of Received Pronunciation and General American are increasingly regarded as markers of status rather than as practical targets for learners who will predominantly use English with other non-native speakers. In response, Jenkins (2002) proposed a Lingua Franca Core, a sociolinguistically motivated and empirically grounded set of pronunciation features deemed essential for intelligibility in international communication, together with a set of non-core features that may be desirable but are less critical. This proposal directly challenges the assumption that native accents should serve as the benchmark for teaching and assessment, and it exemplifies the broader move away from nativeness towards comprehensibility. At the same time, the persistence of native models in research designs and in classroom practice indicates that this shift is far from complete. Given these unresolved tensions, there is value in taking stock of what recent empirical research reveals about pronunciation teaching to non-native learners. The present paper therefore reviews twenty selected research studies published after the year 2000 and drawn from peer-reviewed academic journals with an impact factor and from conference proceedings, identified through the World of Science database using keywords relating to pronunciation, teaching, phonemes, suprasegmentals and instructional approaches. Four highly cited review papers (Jenkins, 2002; Derwing & Munro, 2005; Levis, 2005; Thomson & Derwing, 2014) provide the theoretical framework, since they have shaped many subsequent study designs even though they do not themselves report original teaching experiments. The remaining studies, all concerning adult or young adult non-native learners, report original research with a clearly described methodology. The review is organised around two main areas of interest. The first concerns pronunciation classroom practices, examining how the competing principles of nativeness and intelligibility are reflected, or fail to be reflected, in what teachers actually do, and considering issues of teacher training, teaching techniques and learning strategies. The second concerns studies at the segmental and suprasegmental levels, including contrastive analyses of phonetic inventories, investigations of specific pronunciation difficulties, and research into the role of stress and other prosodic features. By bringing these strands together, the paper aims to characterise the current issues in pronunciation teaching, to highlight the enduring gap between research findings and prevailing classroom practice, and to consider the implications of the shift from nativeness towards comprehensibility for the education of both teachers and learners of English as a non-native language.

Listening comprehension plays a central role in second language (L2) acquisition, yet it has long been considered the Cinderella of the four communication skills in terms of both research attention and pedagogical practice (Bloomfield et al., 2010). This relative neglect is striking given that listening occupies more time than any other communication skill and that its importance in the real world continues to grow with the proliferation of new media. Importantly, listening comprehension has recently been identified as a significant predictor of overall language learning, underscoring the need to better understand the variables that shape it (Vandergrift & Baker, 2015). Listening is a complex, dynamic process that draws simultaneously on bottom-up decoding of the speech signal and top-down application of context and prior knowledge (Bloomfield et al., 2010; Goh & Vandergrift, 2021). Because L2 listeners often possess underdeveloped automaticity, they rely more heavily on effortful, controlled processing, which makes them especially vulnerable to features of the aural input such as speech rate and utterance length. Yet, despite the assumption that both accelerated speech and lengthier passages hamper comprehension, the empirical picture remains inconsistent. Studies of speech rate report mixed findings, and much of the research has examined L1 or L1-accented speech rather than L2 listening comprehension per se. Similarly, investigations of passage length have yielded inconclusive results, in part because length has rarely been isolated from confounds such as syntactic complexity and passage type. A further complication is that L2 proficiency, itself operationalized in disparate ways, may moderate these effects, yet few listening studies have employed standardized measures of proficiency. To date, no study has systematically examined how speech rate, utterance length, and L2 oral proficiency jointly influence listening comprehension in L2 Spanish. The present study addresses these gaps by manipulating speed and syllable-based length while controlling for syntactic complexity, and by adopting a standardized oral proficiency test. In doing so, it seeks to clarify the roles and interactions of these variables in the complex process of L2 Spanish listening comprehension, offering implications for pedagogy and materials design.

M1-RRDavison (2006) has set out the foundations of content and language teaching co-operation as a process requiring shared conceptualisation of tasks, a common curriculum, agreed goals and assessment, and clearly defined roles and responsibilities. M1-CCA substantial body of empirical research has accumulated around this issue. M1-RRNumerous studies have examined the attitudes, beliefs, and practices of teachers and students concerning L1 use, and many have documented that both groups tend to support the judicious use of the native language for a range of purposes. In the domain of second language testing, testing language proficiency has always been a major issue regardless of any specific set of instructional materials, examinees educational and linguistic background. Testing specialists have always tested and tried various approaches to invent new procedures for testing language proficiency because they are not satisfied with the existing instruments testing language proficiency. Spolsky (1973) stated that: “In searching for a test of overall proficiency, then, we must try to find some way to get beyond the limitations of testing a sample of surface features and seek rather tap underplaying linguistics competence” (p. 175). To this end, Spolsky has offered two options: The first one is an interview which has been used continuously as a valid measure of language proficiency. But difficulties in administration and establishing the reliability of scoring limited its implementation. The second one is the reduced redundancy principle (RRP). The second option has been well-received by many professionals who have been trying to operationalize this principle through a variety of testing procedures: dictation, the noise test, partial dictation, cloze test, cloze elide, multiplechoice cloze, rational dictation cloze, and the C-Test (Klein-Braley, 1997). Naturally, languages are redundant. Based on RRP native speakers of languages can fix the missing parts of broken sentences, or they have the capability of understanding the meaning of a sentence without having whole information. This characteristic of the human verbal communication system decreases the possibility of making errors and permits communication where there is some interference in the communication channel (Spolsky, 1973). According to Hughes (2003), native speakers of a language can cope well when this redundancy is reduced. For example, they can understand what someone is saying although there are noises in the environment that prevent them from hearing every sound that is made. Likewise, they can infer the meaning of the text of a newspaper that has been left outside in the rain, causing the print to become blurred. Because non-native speakers generally find it more difficult to cope with reduced redundancy, the deliberate reduction of redundancy has been used as a means of estimating foreign language ability. Learners' overall ability has been estimated by measuring how well they can restore a reduced text to its original form Tests that are constructed under the basis of the reduced redundancy principle (RRP) use authentic materials. Authentic materials are those which are not written for learning purposes. These authentic materials are damaged in some way and then examinees are asked to restore the materials. On the other hand, Klien-Barley (1985) believes that no language test is authentic, if what we mean by authentic is normal language in everyday use: normal language is not produced to be assessed. Therefore, the question of test authenticity cannot be solved directly. A large number of test developers and researchers (Baghaei, 2008a, 2008b, 2010, 2011, 2014; Eckes, 2006, 2011; Eckes & Baghaei, 2015; Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006; Forthmann, Grotjahn, Doebler, & Baghaei, 2020; Raatz, 1984, 1985) in the field of language testing confirmed that C-Test is a valid, reliable, economical, and easy to construct, but in the Afghan context of education, the utility, application, validity, and reliability of C-Test have not been researched so far. The purpose of this study is to build validity evidence for the C-Test as a measure of general language proficiency among Afghan students of English English language proficiency tests used in Afghanistan are made with several components like listening, speaking, reading, writing, vocabulary, and grammar; therefore, they are time-consuming both to the examinees and the examiners. Examinees should spend 120 or 150 minutes doing all the items. And finally, it is difficult to score because it consists of a large number of questions. C-Test is an economic test of overall language proficiency with many advantages. It is not only easy to design but also to score and a variety of texts can be used to construct a complete test. Compared to the cloze test, C-Test is shorter and contains more deletions (items) Based on the stated problem the researcher formulated two general questions. They are as follows: Q1: Is the C-Test valid for measuring overall language proficiency among Afghan students of English as a foreign language? Q2: Is the C-Test reliable for measuring overall language proficiency among Afghan learners? Language teachers do not have the expertise and time to write items for examinations. In fact, developing language tests is a very demanding task for teachers and many of them have not received any training for this The family of reduced redundancy tests including C-Tests is very easy to develop and does not require much expertise. Thus, they can be very useful for language teachers (Coniam, 2008). For measuring general language proficiency, Afghans English teachers use teacher-produced tests. According to Gronlund (1985), there are several salient differences between standardized tests and teacher produced test. Standardized tests are much more valid and reliable to the target test-takers as long as they are well constructed and the quality of test items on standardized tests is higher because each item is written by specialists. In contrast, the quality of a teacher-produced test is lower and with more uncertain reliability. Likewise, teacher-produced tests are full of problems since teachers are not skilled at principles of educational measurement (Popham, 2001). If the study shows that C-Test can successfully be used in Afghanistan then it can be very useful in the Afghan English language teaching context as well as test developers, teachers, and learners.

In this context, European and national institutions embraced bilingual education, which was considered to be “the potential lynchpin to counter Europe’s deficient language standards” (Pérez Cañado and Ráez Padilla 2015: 1), and coined their own term for it: CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning). With the support of European and national institutions, CLIL programmes “are burgeoning in European school contexts” (Lasagabasbaster and Doiz 2015: 1), since bilingual education is deemed to be both “a lever for change and success in language learning” (Pérez Cañado and Ráez Padilla 2015: 1), and an “awesome innovation” in education (Tobin and Abello-Contesse 2013: 224). The rapid expansion of CLIL “has concomitantly spawned a substantial amount of publications into the way it is playing out” (Pérez Cañado 2016: 2), and although some authors have shown misgivings about this (Bruton 2011, 2013; Küppers and Trautmann 2013; Paran 2013) in most studies a very positive view of CLIL has been reported (Dalton Puffer 2008, 2011; Nieto Moreno de Diezmas, 2016a, 2016b, 2018a, 2018b; Ruiz de Zarobe 2011; Pérez Cañado 2012), and it is even considered to be “the ultimate opportunity to practice and improve a foreign language” (Pérez-Vidal 2013: 59). However, now that CLIL programmes have been running in Europe for more than a decade, it is important to move beyond the so-called “evangelical picture” of CLIL (Banegas 2011: 183) and conduct investigations that do not simply focus on “exclusively singing the praises of CLIL” (Pérez Cañado 2016: 2), but on reflecting on the strengths and weaknesses of these programmes (Hüttner, Dalton-Puffer and Smit 2013; Doiz and Lasagabaster 2017). In this way, how all the educational processes involving CLIL develop could be better understood, as well as their implications. Furthermore, areas in need of improvement in order to establish CLIL more effectively could be identifiedAn invaluable source of information to be studied before reaching these goals is the perceptions, beliefs and insights of all those involved in the implementation of bilingual education, so as to detect “the main needs and problems stakeholders face in their daily practice” (Pérez Cañado 2012: 330). However, further research is needed in this area (Dalton-Puffer and Smit 2013; Pérez Cañado 2012; Doiz and Lasagabaster 2017), and more information concerning all stakeholders who are committed to establishing CLIL should be gathered and analyzed. Research into beliefs, opinions or perceptions about CLIL programmes have targeted students (Toledo, Rubio and Hermosín 2012; Coyle 2013), parents (Pladevall-Ballester 2015; Relaño-Pastor in press) and teachers. Pena-Díaz and Porto-Requejo (2008) researched the beliefs of primary teachers about bilingual education during the preparation and training process for establishing it; Pavón and Méndez (2017) studied the beliefs of primary and secondary school English and CLIL teachers regarding cross-curricular coordination and professional development; Hüttner, Dalton-Puffer and Smit (2013), investigated the lay theories of upper secondary school teachers and learners involved in CLIL instruction and concluded that they are not always in keeping with those of experts and policy-makers; Durán-Martínez and Beltrán-Llavador (2016) looked into the views bilingual teachers at primary and secondary schools had in connection with teacher training, resources and assessment. In other studies, the thoughts university teachers have on this phenomenon are examined; for example, McDougald (2015) explored the perceptions primary, secondary and university teachers had on CLIL; Fernández-Costales and González-Riaño (2015) looked at how satisfied university teachers in bilingual programmes were, and Dafouz, Núñez, Sancho, and Foran (2007) examined the reactions university teachers and students had to CLIL. Although it seems that investigations conducted so far provide a comprehensive picture of this phenomenon, there is no research that gathers the different points of views of the different categories of teachers involved in establishing CLIL, i.e., members of the management teams, CLIL programme coordinators, CLIL teachers and English teachers. The members of management teams and CLIL programme coordinators are crucial to implementing the bilingual programme on a grass-roots level, but there is little information on how they perceive it or any insights they may have. Only in recent publications, has this issue been addressed. Thus, in a study conducted by Doiz and Lasagabaster (2017) the opinion the members of the management team had were voiced and compared with the beliefs teaching staff had on two controversial issues: Use of L1 and the obligatory nature of CLIL. In turn, Relaño-Pastor (2018) analyzed the narratives of the head teacher, the CLIL programme coordinator, CLIL teachers, parents, and former students of a primary school from an ethnographic perspective; and Nieto Moreno de Diezmas and Ruiz Cordero (2018) evaluated the strengths and weaknesses of bilingual programmes in secondary education in Castilla-la Mancha on the basis of the opinions teachers had, including members of the management team and CLIL programme coordinators To bridge this gap, in this study, student opinions have been gathered, along with the perceptions and views of the different categories of teachers involved in the bilingual programme: members of the management teams: head teachers, heads of studies and academic secretaries; CLIL programme coordinators, who are responsible for counselling and coordination within the bilingual programme (among their other duties); CLIL teachers, who teach non-linguistic subjects in English; and English teachers, who have to adapt the subject to the specific demands of the bilingual school In addition, and given that “shortcomings regarding CLIL programmes have not been fully addressed” (Doiz and Lasagabaster 2017: 93), this paper specifically focuses on detecting points of tension and mutual perceptions among stakeholders, and to thereby identify the main areas in need of improvement. In addition, a wide variety of practices can be found under the CLIL “umbrella” (Dalton-Puffer, Nikula and Smit 2010), and “learning environments differ not only among countries but also among regions within the same country and even among schools” (Navarro-Pablo and García-Jiménez 2018: 72). Therefore, and given that every context needs to be researched specifically (Pérez Cañado 2012), this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the setting, starting with a description of how bilingual programme regulations in the autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha –where this study is set– were created and how they evolved. Later on, the particular circumstances of the schools where this investigation was conducted are explained.

In addition to calculating percentages of agreement, as has been done with many previous tone-tune studies, I also carry out a correlational analysis not only to determine the strength of the relationship between linguistic tone and musical note transitions, but also to ascertain the degree to which the findings observed may be due to chance (i.e., pvalues). In this article, the term “musical notes” is used to refer to the pitch of the sound and not as a measure of relative duration or rhythm Following McPherson, Ryan, & Hall (2017:9), while questions of time signatures are important rhythmic and metrical aspects of tonal text-setting, they are not the main focus of this article. Teaching English has become a widely researched and discussed priority in education, and it is in the joint interest of stakeholders and policy makers to reach the most effective outcomes Parents of very young children are generally on the opinion that it is ideal to start as early as possible (Griva and Chouvarda 2012, Linse 2011, Purdjaková 2006). Language learning is generally believed to have wideranging benefits on the child’s personal, intellectual, educational development and future career prospects (Tekin 2015: 39). Correspondingly, Greek parents were reported to be aware of the benefits of multilingualism and have positive attitudes towards early start provided that learning materials are suitable to young learners and their specific age-related needs are taken into consideration (Griva and Chouvarda 2012: 10–11). However, it is not evident that an early start of learning foreign languages is an advantage in and of itself (Nikolov and Djigunović 2011). For instance, Hanušová and Najvar (2005) investigated the long-term effects of an early start by examining university entrance exam language test scores. They found no evidence of any relationship between test score results and the start of language learning (Hanušová and Najvar 2005: 209–210). According to a public opinion survey carried out in the Czech Republic in 2006, around 68% of the public (nonteachers, generally parents) are of the opinion that children should start learning English as a Foreign Language as early as in kindergarten (Purdjaková 2006). It is essential to note that an early start is not an essential prerequisite to successful outcomes. Eventual learning success for young learners depends on an interplay of various other factors such as continuity, language policy, classroom circumstances, curriculum, or the qualification of the teacher (Hanušová and Najvar 2005, Nikolov and Djigunović 2011, Purdjaková 2006). In spite of the key role of the teacher’s proficiency and language use in the classroom, Nikolov (2006) draws attention to the scarcity of available research focusing on the effect of teachers’ pronunciation and fluency as a major factor contributing to young learners’ language development (Nikolov 2006: 250) However, it has recently become popular and viable to carry out research into stakeholder attitudes since it is very important to have a dialogue between parents and teachers (Linse 2011, Nikolov and Djigunović 2011). For these reasons, it is of interest what views parents have about teachers and teacher accent when it comes to dealing with young learners.

Globally, some 775 million adults have experienced inequitable access to formal instruction in alphabetic print literacy, and the majority of these are women (UNESCO Institute for Statistics, n.d.). As families migrate seeking better economic or political environments, many of these same adults may seek second language learning opportunities to adjust to their new environment. These adults need instruction that differs from a standard second language class: they need instruction in both the new language and, simultaneously, emergent print literacy instruction. In the U.S, such ESL classes are often referred to as “ESL Literacy”, “Pre-Beginning ESL”, or even “Level 0 ESL”, and are found in a variety of contexts: adult schools, community college non-credit programs, library literacy programs, non-profits, community centers, refugee resettlement programs, and churches. While a research domain on children and their acquisition of L1 language and print literacy has been well established, there is very little research on adult emergent print literacy (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012); moreover, research on adult emergent print literacy in the L2 context is relatively unexplored (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004; Strube, 2009; van de Craats, Kurvers, & Young-Scholten, 2006). Correspondingly, instructors of these students have reported feeling greatly unprepared to teach them, as the nuanced pedagogical approaches in teaching first-time print literacy instruction in tandem with the new language are generally not discussed in teacher training programs (Carter, 2020; Vinogradov & Liden, 2009; Young-Scholten, Peyton, Sosinski, & Cabeza, 2015) Fortunately, grassroots materials for teaching L2 adult students with emergent print literacy have been developed over the decades, and many of these can be found online. Organizations such as Literacy Education and Second Language Learning for Adults (LESLLA1 ) have a dedicated research agenda focusing on this population of L2 learners on a global level Yet, while research is emerging it is still generally limited, especially in understanding the trajectory of adult print literacy development in an L2 environment, and best practices involved. While some research has been conducted on teaching initial reading to these learners, research on the teaching of writing is largely missing, especially at the very early stages of writing, like copying. Addressing this gap, this study offers a contextualized account of emergent writing practices in the adult L2 classroom. The purpose of this research is to provide more insight into the developmental process of adult print literacy in an L2 context, with specific attention to the earliest stages. These insights are necessary to inform appropriate standards and curriculum for first-time print literacy instruction for adults. Moreover, understanding the developmental process provides practitioners a platform upon which to build their lessons and pedagogical approaches, as well as design appropriate assessments to track print literacy gains What follows is a review of literature pertaining to initial writing development, to then frame the context and findings of this study.

The role of multiword sequences (MWSs) in second language (L2) learning and use has attracted growing attention among researchers in recent years, largely because of the important part such sequences play in language processing and production (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Wray, 2002). MWSs—combinations of words that recur with high frequency in a target language, ranging from idioms and collocations to lexical bundles and n-grams—are widely believed to offer L2 speakers quick and cost-effective access to correct language, thereby freeing up the attentional resources needed for other aspects of speech production (Boers et al., 2006; Kormos, 2006; Pawley & Syder, 1983). Because MWSs can be retrieved as holistic units, they are theorized to reduce processing load, particularly at the formulation stage of speech production, and thus to facilitate fluent speech (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018; Wood, 2015). Given this theoretical motivation, a substantial body of research has explored the relationship between MWS use and L2 proficiency. However, the majority of these studies have focused on written production, typically through essay-writing tasks (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger, 2018). Findings from this line of work suggest that more proficient writers tend to have richer phraseological knowledge and better control of MWSs. A smaller set of studies, notably those employing corpus-based frequency, proportion, and association measures, has begun to examine oral production (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle et al., 2017), showing that orally proficient speakers produce a greater number of targetlike sequences. A further group of studies has specifically addressed the link between oral fluency and formulaic language, generally reporting positive relationships (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011; Tavakoli, 2011; Wood, 2009). Nonetheless, this emerging evidence is limited in several important respects. First, many of these studies drew on very small samples or on participants spanning only a narrow range of proficiency levels, which constrains the generalizability of their findings. Second, fluency in earlier work was often assessed through subjective ratings, whereas the field of language testing is increasingly moving toward more objective measurement of L2 ability. Third, those few studies that did employ objective measures tended to capture only a single dimension of fluency—typically speed—leaving the multifaceted nature of the construct largely unexplored. Consequently, it remains unclear how different aspects of fluency relate to different types of MWS use across the proficiency continuum. The present study addresses these gaps by examining the relationship between oral fluency and MWS use across four proficiency levels, using objective, corpus-based n-gram measures alongside fine-grained measures of speed, breakdown, and repair fluency. Drawing on speaking test data from 56 learners, we ask (a) to what extent n-gram proportion, frequency, and association relate to proficiency level, and (b) to what extent these measures are associated with the three dimensions of oral fluency. In doing so, we aim to offer a more comprehensive, quantitative and qualitative account of how phraseological competence relates to fluent L2 speech.

M1-CCWriting is arguably one of the most cognitively demanding skills that second language (L2) learners are required to develop, and it has consequently attracted sustained scholarly attention within second language acquisition (SLA) research. As the number of teachers and researchers turning to investigate writing in their classrooms continues to grow, so does the need to understand how various pedagogical decisions shape learners' written output (Hyland, 2016). Among the many variables that influence what learners eventually produce, the selection of the writing topic or prompt occupies a particularly important place, since the topic sets the boundaries within which learners must mobilise their linguistic and cognitive resources. How, and by whom, that topic is chosen therefore carries considerable pedagogical and assessment-related consequences for both classroom instruction and large-scale testing. M1-MTGOne recurring debate in L2 pedagogy concerns whether learners should be given the freedom to self-select the materials and topics they work with, or whether these should be assigned by the teacher. This debate is not merely a practical one; it rests on well-established psychological and behavioural frameworks. M1-RRThe Theory of Reasoned Action (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1980) holds that human behaviour is largely under volitional control and is shaped by attitudes and behavioural intentions, while Choice Theory (Glasser, 1998) maintains that individuals are internally driven and can fully control their own actions. Related motivational accounts, such as self-determination theory, similarly emphasise autonomy, competence, and relatedness as conditions that foster intrinsic motivation and healthy engagement in learning (Ryan & Deci, 2000). Learners' attitudes and dispositions have themselves been shown to be powerful predictors of their subsequent behaviour and performance (Popham, 2005), which lends theoretical plausibility to the idea that allowing learners a voice in choosing what they write about might enhance the quality of what they produce. The manifestation of these theories in SLA is most visible in studies of self-selected materials across the language skills. In reading, learners have consistently been found to demonstrate greater motivation and comprehension when they choose their own texts (Kragler, 2000; Sewell, 2003), although some studies note that learners do not always select material appropriate to their level. In speaking and writing, comparable benefits have been reported, with Wang (2010) documenting how Chinese students' self-selected writing topics differ from the prompts imposed in large-scale tests. This growing body of work suggests that topic autonomy is meaningfully linked to learners' engagement and output. M2-QRWhat remains far less clear, however, is precisely how self-selection affects the linguistic quality of the writing that learners produce, as distinct from more holistic ratings of writing performance. M1-MTGHere it is useful to distinguish writing proficiency, typically captured through rating scales, from writing quality, which SLA researchers have increasingly operationalised through the constructs of complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF). M1-RRLu (2011) has demonstrated that syntactic complexity measures can serve as robust objective indices of ESL writers' language development, and the CAF triad more broadly is now widely regarded as offering a fuller picture of L2 writing development than global proficiency scores alone (Larsen-Freeman, 1976). M2-GapDespite the widespread adoption of CAF as an analytic lens, the existing studies on self-selected topics have focused overwhelmingly on writing performance or perceptions rather than on the fine-grained linguistic quality of the resulting texts. In other words, we still do not know whether, and to what extent, giving learners the freedom to choose their own prompts changes how complex, accurate, and fluent their writing becomes. Several further gaps compound this uncertainty. First, comparatively few studies have examined self-selection specifically in the context of writing instruction, and fewer still have grounded such investigation explicitly in the Theory of Reasoned Action and Choice Theory. Second, most available evidence derives from ESL or foreign contexts other than Iran, and there is a marked paucity of research conducted in the Iranian EFL setting. Third, the potential interaction between prompt selection and learners' proficiency level has been largely overlooked, even though what benefits an advanced writer may not benefit a beginner in the same way. M2-CTGiven the practical stakes involved for both classroom teachers and test designers, these gaps warrant systematic empirical attention. M3-OPThe present study addresses these gaps by investigating the effect of self-selected versus teacher-assigned writing prompts on the writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency of Iranian EFL learners at beginning, intermediate, and advanced proficiency levels. M3-APRDrawing on the tenets of the Theory of Reasoned Action (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1980) and Choice Theory (Glasser, 1998), we asked 52 learners to write about two prompts, one they selected themselves and one assigned by the teacher, and measured the resulting texts using established CAF indices. M3-OPSpecifically, the study seeks to determine whether statistically significant differences exist between the complexity, accuracy, and fluency of learners' writing under the two prompt conditions across the three proficiency levels. M3-APFIn doing so, it aims to offer evidence that may inform both L2 writing instruction and the design of writing assessment tasks, where the choice of topic can substantially shape the ability we are able to observe.

M1-CCIdioms constitute a pervasive yet notoriously challenging feature of English for learners of English as a foreign language (EFL). M1-RRNative speakers of English draw on idiomatic expressions with striking frequency; Polio, Barlow, Fine, and Polio (1977) estimated that an English native speaker produces an average of four idioms per minute of speech. M1-MTGFor EFL learners, however, idioms present inherent difficulties because the meanings of the constituent words do not straightforwardly combine to yield the meaning of the whole expression. Compounding this difficulty is the fact that speakers of different languages tend to conceptualise experience differently, so that the figurative logic underlying an English idiom is often opaque to learners whose first language encodes the same domains of experience in other ways. M1-RRTraditional pedagogical practice has commonly treated idioms as arbitrary, unanalysable chunks to be committed to memory through rote-learning. Such an approach, as Cho (2010) observes, fails to establish associations between new input and learners' prior knowledge and therefore does little to support the formation of durable cognitive structures. M1-CCCognitive linguistics (CL) offers an alternative account of idiomatic language that has attracted growing attention in English language teaching. M1-RRGrounded in cognitive, social, and communicative theories, CL holds that language reflects the ways in which humans encode their embodied interactions with the physical and social world (Evans & Green 2006; Langacker 2008). Within this framework, most idioms are not arbitrary but semantically motivated: they are examples of conceptual metaphors through which meaning is mapped from concrete, spatial domains onto more abstract ones (Lakoff & Johnson 1980; Lakoff 1993). M1-MTGThe recognition that expressions such as 'love is a journey' rest on systematic cross-domain mappings suggests that learners who become aware of the conceptual metaphors underlying idioms may be better able to comprehend and retain them. M1-RRThis meaning-motivated view resonates with theories of meaningful learning, which propose that language items processed in relation to existing knowledge are more likely to be organised, retained, and transferred than items learned in isolation (Ausubel 2000; Hung 2019). The pedagogical implications of CL also align with broader debates in second language teaching between interventionist and non-interventionist positions. Explicit, teacher-led instruction has been argued to foster explicit knowledge that, under appropriate conditions and with opportunities for use, can facilitate language production and even feed into implicit knowledge (Ellis 2005; Ellis 2015). This is especially relevant in EFL contexts, where learners have limited daily exposure to the target language and therefore depend on classroom input as a principal source of learning (Harmer 2015; Ur 2012). M1-MTGA CL-informed pedagogy, delivered explicitly and followed by controlled drills and communicative tasks, thus appears well suited to adult EFL learners. M1-RRA number of CL-motivated experiments have provided empirical support for teaching idioms and other figurative language through awareness-raising of conceptual metaphors. Boers (2000) found that grouping idioms into metaphorical themes aided retention among Dutch EFL learners, while Csabi (2004) and Condon (2008) reported that learners who engaged with the conceptual motivation of idioms outperformed those who learned them as arbitrary units. Comparable advantages for CL-based instruction have been documented for prepositions (Hung 2017; Hung & Vien 2018), tense and aspect (Bielak & Pawlak 2013), and modal verbs (Tyler et al. 2010). M2-GapDespite these encouraging findings, several gaps remain. Much of the existing research has been conducted in European contexts, and previous studies have called for replication elsewhere. Vietnamese EFL learners have received little attention, idioms in business and financial discourse have rarely been targeted, and, notably, most prior treatments have relied on instruction and translation drills without incorporating productive, communicative tasks. M3-APRThe present study addresses these gaps by applying basic concepts in cognitive linguistics to the teaching of twelve English idioms about finance to Vietnamese first-year EFL college students. The X differs according to the testee’s disciplinary choice. Regarding the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), as one of the three compulsory exams in Gaokao, it plays a considerable role in influencing one’s Gaokao final result. Although some provinces implement different exam structures depending on the local educational circumstances, the major content of the NMET is uniformly prescribed by China’s Ministry of Education. The National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA), operating directly under the Ministry of Education, issues a guideline for the NMET each year, which provides an essential guide about the exam for testees’ preparation as well as authorities of individual provinces in designing their own exams (Cheng & Qi, 2006; Farley & Yang, 2020). Throughout the years, the NMET has been gradually reformed toward the direction of examining learners’ communicative skills. For instance, listening has been added as an essential component since 1999 (Cheng & Qi, 2006). In addition, despite a relatively low share of the total score, speaking has been adopted as a separate section beyond the written sections in different cities and provinces (Cheng, 2008). By reforming and diversifying the content of the NMET, the intention of the test constructors is to improve Chinese English learners’ languageuse ability rather than mere linguistic knowledge of English (Ministry of Education, 2017; Qi, 2007); nevertheless, as Gaokao has been remaining as the predominant gatekeeper for most students to pursue higher education and testing grammatical knowledge on paper-based exams continues to take up the major weighting in the NMET, the reality of teaching and learning to the test and focusing on rote memorization stays in the practice of English education in China (Qi, 2005; Yan, 2015). Despite various reforms of the NMET, reading comprehension has always been an essential component of the exam, which takes approximately 25 – 30% of the total points. According to the general guideline from the National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA, 2019a), designing the exams in Gaokao should be based on specific requirements from different universities and the national curriculum standards. The major objectives suggested in the general guideline include being able to understand common topics like announcement, instruction, and advertisement in books, newspapers, and magazines. The testees are expected to obtain useful information from the passage to understand the main ideas and specific details, grasp the major structure, comprehend the author’s purpose, attitude, and opinions, and infer meanings of specific vocabulary and phrases (NEEA, 2019b). Regarding the General High School English Curriculum Standards, the 2003 and 2017 editions both confirm these objectives (Ministry of Education, 2003, 2017). Although the NMET has been acting as the baton of English teaching and learning in China and understanding the longitudinal test development may greatly influence pedagogical practices, few empirical studies have investigated the development of the reading comprehension passages included in the exam from a longitudinal perspective. In particular, to the best of the researcher’s knowledge, no study has used natural language processing tools to analyze the changes of the text complexity of the passages via a systematic and comprehensive manner, including longitudinal analyses at lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels. Therefore, employing corpus-based analyzing methods, the current study aims to provide a comprehensive picture of how the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages in the NMET has changed throughout the past 25 years, from 1996 to 2020. The results of the study are expected to fill the gap in relevant research fields and offer insights for test designing and pedagogical activities. The following research questions led to the investigation of the study: 1. How has the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages at the lexical level changed over the past 25 years (i.e., 1996-2020)? 2. How has the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages at the syntactic level changed over the past 25 years (i.e., 1996-2020)? 3. How has the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages at the discourse level changed over the past 25 years (i.e., 1996-2020)?

Motivation has long been recognised as one of the most influential individual difference factors affecting success in learning a second or foreign language (L2) (Dewaele, 2009; Dörnyei, 2005). Over the past three decades, the study of motivation has undergone considerable transformation, both theoretically and methodologically. Perhaps the most significant of these developments has been the emergence of Dörnyei's (2005, 2009) L2 Motivational Self System (L2 MSS), which has become one of the most influential contemporary frameworks in the field. Building on earlier socio-psychological approaches, most notably Gardner and Lambert's Socio-Educational Model and its notion of integrativeness, the L2 MSS reconceptualises motivation around learners' future self-images. It comprises three components: the ideal L2 self, which represents the attributes one ideally wishes to possess as an L2 user; the ought-to L2 self, which reflects the attributes one believes one ought to possess to meet external expectations and avoid negative outcomes; and the L2 learning experience, which concerns situated aspects of the immediate learning environment (Dörnyei, 2009). This shift towards the self is particularly valuable in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts, where learners' opportunities for direct contact with the target language community are limited and the classical notion of integrative motivation becomes difficult to apply. A related line of inquiry has focused on learners' willingness to communicate (WTC), which MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément, and Noels (1998) defined as the readiness to enter into discourse at a particular time with a specific person or persons using an L2. Rather than a stable personality trait, L2 WTC is now understood as the product of psychological, situational, and linguistic variables, and it has been proposed as the ultimate goal of language instruction. Because communication is central to language learning, understanding what makes learners willing to speak in the L2 has important pedagogical implications. Given that both constructs are grounded in motivational research, it is reasonable to expect a link between the L2 MSS and L2 WTC. A growing, though still limited, body of research has begun to examine this connection, generally reporting that the ideal L2 self predicts L2 WTC, while the relationship between the ought-to L2 self and L2 WTC tends to be indirect or non-significant (Bursalı & Öz, 2017; Khajavy & Ghonsooly, 2017; Öz, 2016; Yashima, 2009). However, findings vary considerably across contexts, and comparatively little research has been conducted in the Turkish EFL setting. The present study therefore seeks to contribute to this emerging literature by investigating the relationship between the two dimensions of the L2 MSS — the ideal L2 self and the ought-to L2 self — and L2 WTC among university preparatory-programme students in Turkey. Specifically, the study explores the participants' perceived levels of motivation and willingness to communicate, and examines whether these self-guides are significantly related to L2 WTC inside the classroom.

The theoretical notion of “English as a Lingua Franca” (henceforth ELF) emerged in the second half of the 1990s. ELF is the form of English used as a contact language by people from varying lingua-cultural backgrounds (Firth 1996). Researchers using the ELF approach distinguish the form of ELF from English as a native language (ENL) and the pedagogic subject English as a foreign language (EFL). Traditionally, the study of English by nonnative speakers is largely based on ENL norms, with the goal of communicating effectively with native speakers; differences from ENL norms in all aspects are regarded as errors that result from learners’ incomplete acquisition and when this takes place, teachers’ correction and remediation are very much needed (Jenkins 2006). However, the aim of English study for an ELF speaker is to communicate with other non-native speakers, so technically, ENL norms should not be applied to set the linguistic agenda of ELF (Jenkins 2012). Instead, the norms of ELF are negotiated by its users for specific purposes by relying on their linguacultural resources and are derived from interactions involving efforts and adjustments from all parties (Jenkins 2009, Cogo 2010). Based on this tenet of the theory, differences from ENL norms are not always signs of language incompetence, but can be indicative of emerging or potential features of ELF (Jenkins et al. 2011). That is, ELF speakers are viewed as language users in their own right who make use of English for their own purposes. According to Cogo and Dewey (2006) and Jenkins (2006), there are three criteria for determining whether features are emerging trends. First, they must be systematic in nature. Secondly, they must occur frequently and are produced by numerous speakers. Finally, they should not cause a breakdown in communication. Modifications that meet these criteria are regarded as “deviations” or “variants”, which are a natural part of language contact and language change, and not as “errors”, which are a result of the incomplete knowledge of English. Despite the focus on linguistic form, there are fewer ELF studies on morphosyntax, compared to phonology and pragmatics. In fact, research at this level is also crucial to the understanding of ELF communication. Many morphosyntactic features are redundant and serve communal, not communicative, purposes, resulting in speakers avoiding them and deviating from ENL norms (Seidlhofer 2008). Furthermore, many studies have analysed ELF forms in Europe (such as France and Italy) and the outer circle of Asian countries (such as Singapore and India); however, studies on the expanding circle of Asian countries (such as Japan and Thailand) are far less common (Bolton 2008). In addition, ELF research has predominantly dealt with spoken interactions (Dewey 2014). Although there has been recent interest in written language, not many implications have been drawn (Jenkins et al. 2011). Thailand is classified as an Asian country in the expanding circle firstly because it does not have a history of British colonisation and secondly, because English is used mainly for inter-cultural communication. There are just a few studies on Thai ELF learners and they mostly focus on socio-cultural aspects, not on the linguistic form of the language. To deal with this limitation and the other limitations of the previous literature as stated above, this study examines ELF’s morphosyntactic system in the academic writing of Thai learners. Given that deviations in tenses and aspects are often found in L2 research (e.g., Ranta 2006, Stapa & Izahar 2010), the target features of the current study include the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive aspect -ing. The objectives of the study are: (1) to examine how Thai ELF learners deviate from ENL norms in their use of the three verbal inflectional suffixes, and (2) to analyse the underlying causes of the emerging patterns. It is hypothesised that Thai ELF learners show some forms of deviations in the three suffixes owing to both linguistic and functional causes. The results help to provide more complete data for the establishment of the empirical description of ELF’s linguistic form.

The role of instructional materials in shaping learners' perceptions of the social world has long been recognised in foreign language pedagogy. Textbooks are not neutral repositories of linguistic input; they transmit values, norms and social constructions, among which representations of gender occupy a particularly influential position. As the principal medium through which learners encounter a new language and culture, textbooks contribute to the formation of learners' worldviews and, potentially, to the reproduction or questioning of social inequalities. Given the continuing centrality of textbooks in German secondary schools, and the sustained popularity of Spanish as a second foreign language (Statistisches Bundesamt, 2018; Bär, 2012), the question of how gender is portrayed in Spanish as a Foreign Language (ELE) materials is a matter of considerable pedagogical relevance. Gender has become an established object of inquiry across the humanities and social sciences, informed by feminist scholarship, gender studies and queer theory (Babka & Posselt, 2016; Schößler, 2008). Within foreign language education, several distinct lines of research have developed: studies on gender differences in language learning (Schmenk, 2002), on gender-specific approaches to teaching, on the explicit thematisation of gender in the classroom (Decke-Cornill, 2009; König, 2015; König et al., 2016), and on the role of gender in instructional materials (Benitt & Kurtz, 2016; Elsen, 2018). Approaches drawing on literature, film and image didactics have been proposed as particularly productive means of stimulating gender reflection among learners (König, 2018; Lewin, 2015; Volkmann, 2007; Elsner & Lohe, 2016). Understandings of gender have also shifted over time: whereas early textbook studies of the 1970s and 1980s concentrated on sexism and biological sex, more recent research foregrounds sexual identity, heteronormativity and social inequality, informed by constructivist and queer-theoretical perspectives (Gutenberg, 2013; Grein, 2012; Mittag, 2015). Despite this growing conceptual sophistication, gender-related issues have not become a central concern of foreign language and, more specifically, ELE textbook research, either nationally or internationally (Bengoechea & Simón, 2010; Benitt & Kurtz, 2016; Sunderland, 2010). Sunderland (2010) explicitly stresses that gender research remains especially scarce in foreign language contexts in which English is not the target language. The available ELE analyses, which can be presented chronologically, have examined sexist representation (Galiano Sierra, 1993), the depiction of men and women in illustrations (Robles Fernández, 2005, 2007), the verbal and graphic representation of the sexes (Barceló Morte, 2006), the social consideration of women and minorities (de Santiago Guervós, 2009), and language, job titles and professional identity (Bengoechea & Simón, 2010; Morales-Vidal & Cassany, 2020). Taken together, these studies reveal a persistently stereotypical treatment of gender: men and women are portrayed unequally, the generic masculine is used almost without exception, gender-sensitive language is rare, and male occupations are both more frequent and prioritised over female ones. However, most of these analyses approach the object of investigation from a strictly binary perspective, and the level of language itself is examined far less frequently than illustrations or thematic content. Moreover, the findings of the international studies are embedded in different national and educational contexts and are therefore only partially transferable to the German setting. Crucially, no ELE textbook analysis of gender-related aspects can be found in the German research context at all, even though analyses of foreign language English and of German-language textbooks in Germany have already developed more differentiated foci, including language, homosexuality and LGBTIQ+ identities (Bittner, 2011; Benitt & Kurtz, 2016; Elsen, 2018; Moser, Hannover & Becker, 2013; Ott, 2017). There thus remains a clear gap: recent, German-context ELE textbooks have not been examined in a way that integrates a detailed linguistic analysis with a thematic one, nor in a way that moves beyond binary gender constructions to consider non-binary and LGBT representations. It is this gap that the present study seeks to address. Accordingly, this article investigates how gender is represented in modern ELE textbooks used for Spanish as a second foreign language at lower secondary level in Germany, examining both a broad thematic and a detailed linguistic perspective. A corpus of five frequently used textbooks published between 2012 and 2019, drawn from various publishing houses and covering different years of learning, is analysed both quantitatively and qualitatively. Building on existing analysis models and evaluation instruments (Moser, Hannover & Becker, 2013; Nova Scotia Department of Education, 2001; Ott, 2017), an analysis grid is developed that networks the level of language with the presentation of gender-related topic areas such as family, leisure, profession, household, appearance and celebrities, while also allowing for the identification of non-binary gender constructions (Bittner, 2011). Because Spanish offers particular grammatical possibilities for gender specification and abstraction, an excursus on gender-sensitive language use in Spanish precedes the presentation of the results. Following the state of research and a rationale for the study, the analysis, findings and their discussion are set out, and implications for teachers are deduced, together with recommendations for promoting and deepening learners' gender awareness (Linke, 2012; Cunningsworth, 1995).

SECOND LANGUAGE (L2) SPEECH FLUENCY has been widely studied from various angles, including the connections between fluency measurements and judgments of fluency (utterance fluency and perceived fluency, respectively, Segalowitz, 2010; e.g., Baker–Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2013), fluency development (notably during study abroad; e.g., Lennon, 1990; Mora & Valls–Ferrer, 2012; Towell & Dewaele, 2005; Towell, Hawkins, & Bazergui, 1996), and the differences between learners at different proficiency levels (e.g., Hilton, 2014; Kormos & Dénes, 2004). Native speakers, representing a relatively homogenous group of ‘ideally’ fluent speakers, have traditionally been the implicit or explicit points of comparison for learners in L2 fluency studies. Yet studies examining the temporal aspects of L1 speech have shown that individuals vary in their fluency (e.g., Goldman–Eisler, 1968). Furthermore, fluency studies including a native speaker control group have also demonstrated variation in fluency not only among L2 speakers, but also among L1 speakers (e.g., Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014). These findings have significant implications for L2 fluency research, assessment, and teaching: If individuals vary in how they speak their native language, the factors influencing their L1 speech fluency are likely to influence L2 speech as well. In other words, temporal measures, which have been used as indicators of L2 oral proficiency in L2 speech fluency research, can, at least to some extent, also reflect L1 fluency. Empirical research on the connections between L1 and L2 speech fluency has, nevertheless, been scarce, as L2 speech fluency studies have usually not incorporated data from the same speakers in their L1 and L2 (but see early exploratory studies, e.g., Lehtonen, 1979; Möhle, 1984; Raupach, 1980). However, in recent years, the effects of L1 speech patterns on L2 speech fluency have attracted more interest, and the studies suggest that at least some of the variance in L2 speech fluency can be explained by the learners’ L1 speech patterns (De Jong et al., 2015; Derwing et al., 2009; Huensch & Tracy–Ventura, 2017). Examining the connections between L1 and L2 speech fluency can thus help in pinpointing aspects of L2 fluency that are prone to L1 speaking style effects and aspects that are more clearly linked to L2 (oral) proficiency. Therefore, this line of research not only contributes to increasing the reliability of measuring L2 speech fluency, but also has implications for the development of reliable and valid L2 fluency assessment practices, which would ideally emphasize proficiency-related aspects of L2 fluency and focus less on aspects influenced by L1 fluency (see also Segalowitz, 2010, pp. 35, 40–41). In the present study, 42 Finnish learners of English from two school levels, ninth grade (i.e., the final year of compulsory education) and the second year of upper secondary school, were examined for their L1 and L2 fluency. Compared to previous, mainly quantitative studies, the present study employed a mixed methods approach including both group level (quantitative) and individual level (qualitative) analysis to achieve a holistic picture of the connections between L1 and L2 fluency. First, in the quantitative analysis, correlations between L1 and L2 fluency measures were studied, followed by regression analyses exploring the predictive power of L1 fluency measures in explaining L2 fluency measures. Second, the complementary qualitative analysis involved examining individual differences in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency by focusing on six subjects’ productions with high frequencies of so-called stalling mechanisms (e.g., repetitions and filled pauses, FPs; see Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998). As previous studies have shown stalling mechanisms to be potentially multifunctional and prone to individual variation (e.g., Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014), examining these features from individuallearners’ productions with a qualitative analysis along with group level tendencies is particularly important; individual differences in L1 and L2 patterns regarding stalling mechanisms may be more prominent than group level patterns. Seeking to uncover individual patterns in fluency-related features across L1 and L2, the qualitative component of the present study thus provides a new angle to the study of connections between L1 and L2 fluency.

M1-CCLanguage curriculum sits at the heart of language education, shaping not only what learners come to know but also, more subtly, who they are invited to become. M1-RRCurrent understandings of curriculum are closely tied to the field's evolving views of language, learning, and pedagogy (Garton & Graves, 2014; Tarone, 2014), and can be understood as informed by three theoretical orientations: a linguistic cognitive perspective that treats curriculum as a body of linguistic knowledge to be transmitted and mastered; a social contextual perspective that foregrounds curriculum as a negotiated process of enactment situated within sociocultural contexts of teaching and learning; and a critical ideological perspective that maintains curriculum is politically and ideologically endorsed and often reproduces existing power relations. Scholars working within the last of these have shown how curriculum content, especially in commercially published materials, can reproduce inequalities and normative ideologies through exclusion or misrepresentation, whether of culture, gender, social class, or sexuality (Gray, 2013). Others have shown that curriculum enactment is a dynamic, negotiated process in which materials frequently afford emergent rather than intended possibilities for language use, and in which teachers and students bring their identities and lived experiences into classroom interaction (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013). M2-GapDespite the richness of these two lines of inquiry, both the analysis of curriculum content and the study of curriculum enactment have, with few exceptions, paid little attention to learners' subjectivity. The dominant framing has been Marxist, examining how ideologies are reproduced in curriculum texts, rather than how curriculum texts constitute subjectivities for learners. M1-RRA notable exception is Gray's (2013) analysis of ELT textbooks, which showed that narrative texts constructed particular subject positions for learners in ways aligned to prevailing ideologies. M2-GapYet what remains underexamined is how curriculum, and the interactions built around it, constructs subject positions for students and how students, in turn, negotiate those positions in the moment-to-moment life of the classroom. This is a significant gap, particularly for minoritized and immigrant youth, whose classroom participation is entangled with racialized and gendered discourses that circulate far beyond the classroom walls. M2-CTAddressing this gap requires a theoretical vocabulary that connects language, discourse, and subjectivity. M1-RRPerformativity theory offers such a lens, positing that subjectivity is constituted through repeated linguistic and bodily acts within regulatory normative frames (Butler, 1990; Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004). Coupled with Butler's (1997) account of subjectivation, in which power is understood as productive rather than merely repressive, this perspective invites a shift from a referential view of classroom language use toward an ontological one that asks how students use classroom talk to produce themselves as particular kinds of learners and persons (Kramsch, 2009). Integrating performativity theory with critical race theory (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995) further allows immigrant youths to be understood as racialized subjects, read through racial ideologies coupled with essentializing gender stereotypes. M2-GapWhile prior sociolinguistic and applied linguistic research has examined how immigrant youths perform identities through language, racialized subjectivities and their entanglement with curriculum content have not been foregrounded. M3-OPExtending these two lines of research, and building on feminist poststructuralist work on the constituting power of school discourses (Davies & Banks, 1992), the present study brings a poststructuralist perspective to bear on the relationship between curriculum and the learner. It marries the critical ideological and social contextual approaches by theorizing curriculum and its enactment through a lens of criticality while reimagining these foci through a poststructuralist theorization of language, discourse, and the learner. Drawing on data from a critical ethnography in one U.S. secondary multilingual classroom, this classroom discourse study analyzes instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews to address two questions: how a teacher-designed vocabulary curriculum, centered on a routinized sentence-starter language practice, constructed subjectivity for students; and how three immigrant adolescents negotiated their racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to that curriculum content. M3-APFThe analysis illustrates how the sentence starters, designed as scaffolding tools, served an implicit goal of constituting students as 'good learners,' and how the focal students appropriated them to challenge, subvert, or conform to prevailing discourses. In doing so, this article argues that curriculum can constitute a discursive and performative space in which students negotiate subjectivity and meaning in relation to power, and considers the implications of this theorization for research and practice.
